abase.definition: to humiliate or degrade, especially oneself
abase.sentence: He abased himself before the committee, apologizing so profusely that even his critics grew uncomfortable.
sentences: The courtier abased himself so thoroughly that the king grew embarrassed on his behalf.

abash.definition: to embarrass or unsettle someone's composure
abash.sentence: Nothing abashed her: heckling, hostile questions, and open laughter left her delivery entirely unshaken.
sentences: Nothing abashed the toddler, who continued singing after the entire restaurant fell silent.

abate.definition: to lessen in intensity or degree
abate.sentence: Only when the storm abated did the crew venture onto the deck to assess the damage.
sentences: The fever abated by morning, leaving him weak but no longer talking to the curtains.

abdicate.definition: to formally give up power or responsibility
abdicate.sentence: By refusing to investigate the fraud, the board effectively abdicated its duty to shareholders.
sentences: A king may abdicate a throne; a parent cannot abdicate a child.

aberrant.definition: departing sharply from what is normal or expected
aberrant.sentence: A single aberrant reading did not trouble her; it was the pattern of anomalies that demanded explanation.
sentences: One aberrant swan does not overturn the rule, but it does end the word "never."

aberration.definition: a departure from what is normal or expected
aberration.sentence: The senator dismissed his outburst as an aberration, though colleagues recalled several similar episodes.
sentences: He called the loss an aberration until it happened four Saturdays running.

abet.definition: to help or encourage, usually in wrongdoing
abet.sentence: The clerk who forged the signatures was convicted, as was the manager who abetted him.
sentences: The lookout never touched the safe, yet the law counts abetting as the same crime.

abeyance.definition: a state of temporary suspension or inactivity
abeyance.sentence: The lawsuit was held in abeyance while both parties pursued a private settlement.
sentences: The feud lay in abeyance for a decade, waiting like a bill nobody had paid.

abhor.definition: to regard with disgust and hatred
abhor.sentence: She abhorred flattery, and courtiers who praised her extravagantly found themselves quickly out of favor.
sentences: Nature abhors a vacuum; he abhorred small talk with roughly the same force.

abide.definition: to tolerate; to endure or remain
abide.sentence: He could abide criticism of his methods but not of the motives behind them.
sentences: She could abide the noise, the cold, and the hours, but not the pointlessness.

abject.sentence: The report described abject poverty that decades of aid had somehow failed to relieve.
sentences: His apology was abject enough to make the victim feel, oddly, like the villain.

abjure.definition: to renounce formally, especially under oath
abjure.sentence: Forced to abjure his findings publicly, the astronomer nonetheless kept circulating them among colleagues.
sentences: Galileo abjured his findings aloud and, legend insists, muttered the truth on his way out.

abound.definition: to exist in great numbers or quantity
abound.sentence: Rumors abounded after the merger, though executives insisted nothing had been decided.
sentences: Theories abound; evidence, as usual, is on back order.

aboveboard.sentence: The auditors found the transaction entirely aboveboard, however unusual its timing appeared.
sentences: The phrase comes from card tables: hands above the board could hide nothing underneath.

abrasive.sentence: His abrasive style alienated allies who agreed with nearly every position he took.
sentences: Sandpaper and his personality shared a property: both removed a layer on contact.

abreast.definition: up to date with current information
abreast.sentence: Keeping abreast of the literature consumed the hours she had hoped to spend on experiments.
sentences: Keeping abreast of the field means running beside it, never quite catching up.

abridge.definition: to shorten while keeping the essentials
abridge.sentence: The editor abridged the memoir severely, cutting three hundred pages without losing the argument.
sentences: The abridged epic kept every battle and cut every reason anyone was fighting.

abrogate.sentence: The new government abrogated the treaty within weeks, citing terms it called unenforceable.
sentences: A treaty takes years to sign and one signature to abrogate.

abscission.definition: the act of cutting off; natural shedding of leaves
abscission.sentence: Abscission of the leaves follows a chemical signal, not merely the arrival of cold weather.
sentences: Autumn is mass abscission: the tree fires its leaves before winter can starve it.

abscond.definition: to leave secretly, especially to avoid capture
abscond.sentence: The treasurer absconded with the endowment, and auditors traced the funds through four countries.
sentences: The bookkeeper absconded on a Friday, which bought him two days before anyone counted.

abstain.definition: to refrain deliberately from doing something
abstain.sentence: Two members voted against the measure and a third abstained, citing a conflict of interest.
sentences: He abstained from the vote, from dessert, and from every argument he might lose.

abstemious.definition: sparing, especially in eating and drinking
abstemious.sentence: Abstemious by habit, he ate lightly at banquets that left other guests immobile.
sentences: The word contains a, e, i, o, u in order, which is more fun than the diet it describes.

abstract.definition: existing as an idea rather than a physical thing
sentences: In the abstract everyone supports the reform; in the budget nobody does.
Justice is abstract until it arrives as a specific person in a specific room.

abstruse.sentence: Her argument was sound but so abstruse that only specialists could follow its middle section.
sentences: The proof was abstruse enough that its author needed a week to reread his own reasoning.

abut.sentence: The new development abuts protected wetlands, which is why the permit drew such scrutiny.
sentences: Their properties abut, which is why the fence has its own filing cabinet at the courthouse.

abysmal.sentence: Attendance was abysmal, and the theater closed before the season ended.
sentences: An abysmal performance: the audience's applause was mostly relief that it had ended.

abyss.definition: a deep or seemingly bottomless chasm
abyss.sentence: Between his stated principles and his conduct lay an abyss no rhetoric could bridge.
sentences: Stare long into the abyss, Nietzsche warned, and the abyss stares back.

accede.definition: to agree or yield to a demand
accede.sentence: The administration acceded to the students' demands only after a month of daily protests.
sentences: He acceded to every demand, which taught the negotiators to keep inventing more.

accentuate.definition: to emphasize or make more noticeable
accentuate.sentence: The stark lighting accentuated flaws the painter had spent months trying to conceal.
sentences: Black clothing accentuates whatever you were hoping nobody would notice.

access.definition: the right or means of approaching something
access.sentence: Access to the archive was granted grudgingly, and only for a single afternoon.
sentences: He had access to the archive, the code, and the accounts, which the auditors called a design flaw.

accessible.sentence: She wrote an accessible account of quantum theory without diluting a single essential idea.
sentences: The best physics writing is accessible without pretending the mathematics is optional.

acclaim.sentence: The novel met with critical acclaim abroad long before publishers at home would touch it.
sentences: Acclaim arrived thirty years late, addressed to a painter who had died in a rented room.

accolade.definition: an award or expression of praise
accolade.sentence: The prize was the highest accolade in her field, and she received it at thirty-one.
sentences: The accolade was once a sword tap on the shoulder; now it is a plaque and a lukewarm dinner.

accord.sentence: The two delegations reached an accord on trade but remained divided over fishing rights.
sentences: They reached an accord on everything except what the accord actually meant.

accretion.definition: gradual growth by addition or accumulation
accretion.sentence: The doctrine developed by accretion, each generation of judges adding a qualification.
sentences: Planets form by accretion: dust that keeps bumping into dust until it can bully the neighborhood.

acerbic.sentence: His acerbic reviews were feared by playwrights and quoted with delight by everyone else.
sentences: Her acerbic wit made enemies quickly and dinner invitations even quicker.

acidulous.definition: somewhat sour in taste or manner
acidulous.sentence: She offered an acidulous compliment that left the honoree unsure whether to thank her.
sentences: An acidulous "how brave of you" can end a conversation faster than an insult.

acme.sentence: The cathedral is often called the acme of a style that took two centuries to mature.
sentences: Acme is the peak, which is why the cartoon company selling doomed rockets was named it.

acolyte.sentence: The economist was trailed by acolytes who repeated his phrases more faithfully than his reasoning.
sentences: Every guru collects acolytes who repeat the conclusions and skip the doubts that produced them.

acquiesce.definition: to accept or comply reluctantly, without protest
acquiesce.sentence: She acquiesced to the schedule change, though her silence was plainly not approval.
sentences: Silence in a meeting is not agreement, but it acquiesces just as effectively.

acquisitive.definition: eager to acquire possessions or wealth
acquisitive.sentence: An acquisitive collector, he bought whole libraries merely to secure a few manuscripts.
sentences: So acquisitive that he bought the neighboring house for its bookshelves and left the rooms empty.

acrid.definition: sharply bitter in smell, taste, or tone
acrid.sentence: Acrid smoke drifted through the corridors hours after the fire had been put out.
sentences: Acrid smoke has a taste, and everyone who has smelled a housefire remembers it.

acrimonious.sentence: The negotiations grew so acrimonious that mediators separated the parties into different buildings.
sentences: The divorce was acrimonious enough that the lawyers billed for reading each other's insults.

acrimony.sentence: Decades of acrimony between the families ended, improbably, over a shared legal problem.
sentences: Two decades of acrimony evaporated over a shared dislike of a third cousin.

activism.definition: vigorous action to bring about political or social change
activism.sentence: Her activism began with a local zoning fight and ended in the national legislature.
sentences: Activism is what happens when writing letters stops feeling like enough.

actuate.definition: to set in motion; to motivate
actuate.sentence: What actuated the reform was not principle but the threat of losing federal funding.
sentences: Fear, not conviction, actuated the sudden reform.

acumen.sentence: Her political acumen let her count votes weeks before the whips could.
sentences: Business acumen is knowing which numbers are lying before the auditors arrive.

adage.definition: a traditional saying expressing common wisdom
adage.sentence: He answered every objection with an adage, which passed for wisdom until someone examined it.
sentences: "Look before you leap" is an adage; so is its opposite, which is the trouble with adages.

adamant.sentence: She was adamant that the data be released in full, whatever the political cost.
sentences: Adamant once named a stone believed unbreakable, which is exactly how she said no.

adept.sentence: Adept at reading a room, he abandoned his prepared remarks after the first minute.
sentences: Adept at excuses, he had one ready before anyone asked for the report.

adequate.sentence: The funding was adequate to keep the clinic open, not to expand the services it offered.
sentences: "Adequate" on a report card is the politest word in English for disappointment.

adhere.definition: to stick fast; to follow closely
adhere.sentence: Researchers who adhere rigidly to the protocol sometimes miss what the anomalies are telling them.
sentences: Adhere to the recipe or to the tradition, but stop claiming you did both.

adherent.definition: a supporter of a cause or person
adherent.sentence: The movement attracted adherents faster than it could articulate what it actually wanted.
sentences: A theory gains adherents faster than evidence, since belief is cheaper than experiment.

adjudicate.definition: to judge or settle a dispute formally
adjudicate.sentence: The panel was asked to adjudicate a claim that neither side could document convincingly.
sentences: Someone had to adjudicate whether the cat belonged to the house or the neighborhood.

adjure.sentence: The letter adjured him to withdraw before the vote, invoking loyalties two decades old.
sentences: She adjured him, by everything they had survived together, to leave the letter unopened.

admonish.sentence: The judge admonished counsel for the remark but declined to declare a mistrial.
sentences: A parent admonishes; a judge sentences. The difference is what happens next.

admonitory.sentence: His admonitory tone made the advice sound like a verdict already delivered.
sentences: The fable ends with an admonitory moral nobody heeds until they have paid for it.

adroit.definition: clever and skillful, especially in handling situations
adroit.sentence: An adroit negotiator, she conceded the small points loudly and the crucial ones never.
sentences: An adroit answer conceals the fact that no answer was actually given.

adulation.sentence: The adulation of his early admirers did more damage to his prose than any critic could.
sentences: Adulation ruins more talent than neglect ever has, because nobody notices it happening.

adulterate.definition: to make impure by adding inferior substances
adulterate.sentence: Merchants adulterated the spice with ground husks, a fraud detectable only under magnification.
sentences: Honey is the most adulterated food on earth: syrup wearing a bee costume.

adumbrate.sentence: The preface adumbrates an argument the book itself never quite develops.
sentences: The first chapter adumbrates a tragedy the reader spends three hundred pages hoping to avoid.

adventitious.sentence: The resemblance is adventitious, arising from convergent pressures rather than shared ancestry.
sentences: The scratch on the lens was adventitious, but three astronomers published it as a moon.

adverse.sentence: The drug was withdrawn after adverse effects appeared in a small fraction of patients.
sentences: Adverse conditions do not build character so much as reveal how much you already had.

adversity.sentence: Her reputation rests less on her triumphs than on her composure in adversity.
sentences: Adversity introduces a man to himself, usually without an appointment.

advert.definition: to refer to something in speech or writing
advert.sentence: He adverted briefly to the scandal, then returned to the budget as though nothing had happened.
sentences: He adverted to the missing money the way one mentions weather: briefly, then never again.

advocate.sentence: She advocated a gradual transition, warning that abrupt reform would collapse under its own costs.
sentences: To advocate is to be called for: the word once meant a voice summoned to your side.

aerie.definition: a lofty nest or dwelling high above
aerie.sentence: From his aerie on the top floor, the editor rarely saw the reporters he directed.
sentences: Eagles build aeries where nothing without wings can argue with them.

aesthete.definition: one devoted to beauty and art
aesthete.sentence: An aesthete to the end, he chose his furniture more carefully than his friends.
sentences: The aesthete rearranged his bookshelves by spine color and read none of them.

aesthetic.definition: concerned with beauty or artistic taste
aesthetic.sentence: The objection was aesthetic rather than practical: the bridge worked, but nobody could bear looking at it.
sentences: The complaint was aesthetic: the bridge held perfectly, and nobody could stand to look at it.

affable.definition: friendly and easy to talk to
affable.sentence: His affable manner concealed a bargaining style that gave away almost nothing.
sentences: Affable people get the parking space, the upgrade, and the truth from strangers.

affect.definition: to put on a pretense of; to influence
affect.sentence: He affected an indifference to the prize that nobody who knew him believed.
sentences: He affected a limp for sympathy and forgot, by Thursday, which leg it was.

affectation.sentence: The accent was pure affectation, acquired at university and abandoned whenever he was tired.
sentences: The monocle was an affectation; his eyesight was better than everyone's at the table.

affected.sentence: Her affected modesty irritated colleagues who had watched her campaign openly for the appointment.
sentences: An affected laugh always arrives half a second after the joke.

affinity.definition: a natural attraction or close resemblance
affinity.sentence: He felt an affinity for the older painters, whose difficulties resembled his own.
sentences: Cats show an unerring affinity for the one guest who is allergic to them.

afflict.sentence: The drought afflicted the northern provinces most severely, though the capital drew the coverage.
sentences: Journalism, the saying goes, should comfort the afflicted and afflict the comfortable.

affluent.sentence: The policy benefited affluent districts that had lobbied for it and few others.
sentences: The word once described rivers flowing freely; money apparently borrowed the metaphor.

afford.sentence: The vantage point affords a view of the whole valley, which is why the fort was built there.
sentences: The hilltop affords a view that the guidebook affords three exclamation marks.

affront.sentence: The omission of her name was taken as an affront, and she declined to attend.
sentences: Being seated at the children's table was, at forty-one, an affront he mentioned for years.

aggrandize.definition: to increase power, wealth, or importance
aggrandize.sentence: Each reorganization aggrandized the department that proposed it, a pattern nobody named aloud.
sentences: Every reorganization aggrandized whoever proposed it, which explained the reorganizations.

aggravate.sentence: The tariff aggravated a shortage that the government had spent a year trying to relieve.
sentences: Scratching aggravates the itch, which is the entire argument against most quick fixes.

aggregate.definition: a total formed by combining separate parts
aggregate.sentence: In aggregate the reforms saved money, though several districts paid substantially more.
sentences: In aggregate the town was richer; house by house, most people were not.

aggrieve.definition: to treat unjustly; to cause grief to
aggrieve.sentence: Aggrieved shareholders sued, arguing the board had concealed the losses for two quarters.
sentences: Only the aggrieved party may sue, which is why lawyers ask first who was actually hurt.

aghast.sentence: Aghast at the proposal, the trustees adjourned without taking a vote.
sentences: She looked aghast at the bill, then aghast at the friend who had ordered the wine.

agitate.definition: to stir up feeling; to campaign vigorously
agitate.sentence: For a decade she agitated for the reform that her successors would take credit for passing.
sentences: Washing machines and reformers do the same job: agitate until something comes clean.

aide.definition: an assistant to an important person
aide.sentence: An aide leaked the memo, and the minister's denials collapsed within a day.
sentences: Every scandal has an aide who knew first and said nothing until the subpoena arrived.

alacrity.sentence: She accepted the assignment with an alacrity that surprised colleagues expecting resistance.
sentences: He accepted the free ticket with an alacrity he never showed for actual work.

alchemy.definition: a seemingly magical process of transformation
alchemy.sentence: By some alchemy of editing, a shapeless draft became the year's most admired essay.
sentences: Alchemists never made gold, but they invented the laboratory, which turned out to be worth more.

alcove.definition: a small recessed space in a room
alcove.sentence: He worked in an alcove off the main hall, hidden from anyone who might interrupt.
sentences: Every good library has an alcove where someone is hiding from someone else.

alienate.sentence: The tone of the announcement alienated the very donors it had been written to reassure.
sentences: The apology alienated the last people still willing to defend him.

allay.definition: to calm or reduce fear or doubt
allay.sentence: Nothing in the statement allayed the concerns of parents who had read the inspection report.
sentences: Nothing allays a rumor faster than a duller rumor arriving on time.

allege.sentence: The complaint alleges misconduct spanning four years, none of it yet corroborated.
sentences: Newspapers write "allegedly" for the same reason climbers use rope.

alleviate.sentence: The grant alleviated the immediate crisis without addressing why it kept recurring.
sentences: Aspirin alleviates the headache and has no opinion about why you keep getting them.

allusion.sentence: The speech was thick with allusions to a scandal the speaker never mentioned by name.
sentences: An allusion flatters the reader who catches it and quietly excludes the one who does not.

allusive.sentence: Her allusive style rewards rereading and frustrates anyone hoping for a plain statement.
sentences: His allusive toast praised the bride by describing, at length, a Greek shipwreck.

aloof.sentence: He remained aloof from factional quarrels, which made him acceptable to both sides.
sentences: The sailing term meant steering away from shore; aloof people have kept the habit.

altruism.sentence: Economists have long puzzled over altruism toward strangers who can never reciprocate.
sentences: Altruism confuses economists: the anonymous donor gets nothing, not even credit.

altruistic.sentence: The gesture was less altruistic than it appeared, as the donor's name went on the building.
sentences: An altruistic gift with a plaque attached is a purchase with extra steps.

amalgam.definition: a mixture or blend of different things
amalgam.sentence: The style is an amalgam of local craft traditions and imported industrial technique.
sentences: The dentist's amalgam and the city's culture share a definition: separate things forced to set together.

amalgamate.definition: to combine into a single whole
amalgamate.sentence: The two societies amalgamated in 1908, though their journals stayed separate for decades.
sentences: The two rival choirs amalgamated and spent a year arguing over which name came first.

amalgamation.definition: the process of combining into one
amalgamation.sentence: The amalgamation of the archives simplified access and destroyed some useful distinctions.
sentences: The amalgamation saved money and destroyed both institutions' reasons for existing.

ambience.definition: the atmosphere or character of a place
ambience.sentence: The restaurant traded on its ambience, since the food itself was unremarkable.
sentences: Dim lighting is what restaurants call ambience and opticians call a hazard.

ambiguous.definition: open to more than one interpretation
ambiguous.sentence: The wording was deliberately ambiguous, letting both delegations claim victory at home.
sentences: Diplomats prize ambiguous language because both sides can go home claiming victory.

ambivalence.definition: the state of having conflicting feelings
ambivalence.sentence: Her ambivalence about the promotion showed in the three weeks she took to answer.
sentences: Ambivalence is wanting both doors, then blaming the hallway.

ambivalent.sentence: Critics were ambivalent: they admired the ambition and distrusted nearly every result.
sentences: He was ambivalent about the promotion: more money, more meetings, same person.

ambrosia.definition: something delicious; food of the gods
ambrosia.sentence: After a week of rations, the plain bread tasted like ambrosia to the survey team.
sentences: Ambrosia made the Greek gods immortal; the fruit salad named after it has not repeated the feat.

ameliorate.definition: to make a bad situation better
ameliorate.sentence: The subsidy ameliorated conditions in the short term without changing what caused them.
sentences: Painting the ward ameliorated the mood without adding a single nurse.

amenable.definition: willing to agree or be persuaded
amenable.sentence: He proved amenable to compromise once the deadline made delay more costly than concession.
sentences: He became amenable to compromise the moment delay grew more expensive than defeat.

amend.definition: to change or improve a text or law
amend.sentence: The clause was amended twice before anyone noticed it now contradicted the preamble.
sentences: The constitution can be amended, which is why it has outlived every document that could not.

amiable.sentence: An amiable colleague, he was nonetheless ruthless about deadlines he had not set.
sentences: An amiable colleague, ruthless only about deadlines and other people's coffee.

amicable.sentence: The dispute ended in an amicable settlement that neither party would discuss publicly.
sentences: "Amicable settlement" means both sides are equally unhappy and equally tired.

amorous.sentence: The letters are amorous in tone yet oddly formal, as though written for an audience.
sentences: The pigeon's amorous display involved a great deal of strutting and no visible success.

amorphous.sentence: The movement remained amorphous, with no leaders, no platform, and remarkable staying power.
sentences: Glass is amorphous: a solid that never bothered to arrange itself properly.

amortize.definition: to pay off a debt gradually
amortize.sentence: The loan is amortized over thirty years, which conceals how much interest it carries.
sentences: The word hides a corpse: amortize comes from "to kill," which is what payments do to debt.

amply.sentence: The evidence amply supports the narrower claim and says nothing about the broader one.
sentences: The evidence amply supports the small claim and is silent about the headline.

amuck.sentence: Left unsupervised, the process runs amuck and produces results nobody can reconstruct.
sentences: A single loose goat can run amuck through a supermarket for nineteen minutes.

amulet.definition: a charm worn to ward off evil
amulet.sentence: The amulet was buried with its owner, suggesting protection was expected to continue after death.
sentences: The amulet failed to stop the plague but was found, intact, on its owner's skeleton.

anachronism.definition: something out of its proper historical time
anachronism.sentence: The wristwatch in the battle scene is an anachronism that reviewers noticed immediately.
sentences: A clock strikes in Julius Caesar, which is Shakespeare's most famous anachronism by about two millennia.

anachronistic.definition: belonging to the wrong time period
anachronistic.sentence: His anachronistic courtesies charmed some colleagues and struck others as a performance.
sentences: His anachronistic bow at the door charmed half the room and confused the rest.

analgesia.definition: the absence or relief of pain
analgesia.sentence: The compound produced analgesia without the sedation that limited earlier treatments.
sentences: Analgesia without anesthesia means you feel the surgeon's hands but not the knife.

analgesic.sentence: The analgesic dulled the pain enough for her to work, though not to sleep.
sentences: Willow bark was the first analgesic; aspirin is simply the version that stopped ruining stomachs.

analogous.definition: similar in a way that permits comparison
analogous.sentence: The situation is analogous to the earlier crisis, but the differences matter more than the parallels.
sentences: A wing and a fin are analogous: same job, entirely separate inventors.

anarchy.sentence: What followed the collapse was not anarchy but a patchwork of local authorities.
sentences: Anarchy rarely lasts a week; someone always starts collecting the garbage and charging for it.

anathema.definition: something intensely detested; a formal curse
anathema.sentence: Compromise was anathema to the faction that had built its identity on refusing it.
sentences: Compromise was anathema to a faction that had built its identity on refusing it.

ancillary.sentence: The ancillary services cost more than the treatment they were meant to support.
sentences: The ancillary fees exceeded the tuition, which the brochure declined to mention.

androgynous.definition: having both male and female characteristics
androgynous.sentence: The sculpture's androgynous features have frustrated attempts to identify the figure.
sentences: The statue's androgynous face has kept archaeologists arguing for a century about whom it honors.

anemic.sentence: Growth was anemic for three straight quarters despite the incentives announced with such confidence.
sentences: Sales were anemic, a word chosen so the memo would not have to say "terrible."

anesthetic.definition: a substance that produces loss of sensation
anesthetic.sentence: The anesthetic wore off sooner than expected, and the procedure had to be paused.
sentences: Before anesthetic, surgeons were judged on speed: two minutes for a leg was a good day.

animosity.sentence: Personal animosity, not policy, kept the two committees from meeting for a year.
sentences: The animosity between the departments predated everyone currently working in either.

animus.definition: hostility or ill will motivating action
animus.sentence: The court found no evidence of animus, only administrative carelessness of an impressive scale.
sentences: Courts look for animus: the difference between a bad decision and a targeted one.

annul.sentence: The election was annulled after observers documented irregularities at a third of the polling stations.
sentences: The marriage was annulled, which legally means it never happened, whatever the photographs show.

anodyne.sentence: The statement was so anodyne that both factions quoted it approvingly the same afternoon.
sentences: The statement was so anodyne that both sides quoted it approvingly by lunchtime.

anoint.sentence: The retiring chairman anointed a successor, and the board discovered it had no real say.
sentences: Kings were anointed with oil; modern successors are anointed with a leaked memo.

anomalous.sentence: The anomalous result was reproduced twice before anyone dared publish it.
sentences: The anomalous reading survived three instruments, which is when it stopped being an error.

anomaly.definition: something that deviates from the norm
anomaly.sentence: The anomaly persisted across instruments, which is precisely why it could not be dismissed.
sentences: Neptune was found by taking an anomaly in Uranus's orbit seriously.

antagonize.sentence: He antagonized the only committee whose support his proposal actually required.
sentences: He antagonized the one committee whose approval his proposal actually needed.

antecedent.sentence: The reform had antecedents in a proposal rejected forty years earlier for the same reasons.
sentences: Every overnight success has antecedents stretching back a decade nobody photographed.

antedate.sentence: The manuscript antedates the invention it describes, which is why scholars suspect a forgery.
sentences: The cave paintings antedate agriculture by roughly the span separating us from the pyramids twice over.

antedated.definition: came before in time; dated earlier than actual
antedated.sentence: The contract was antedated by two months, a detail the auditors found immediately.
sentences: The contract was antedated by two months, which the auditors spotted before the coffee arrived.

anthology.sentence: The anthology preserved a dozen poets whose individual volumes had long gone out of print.
sentences: Anthology means "gathering of flowers," which is generous treatment for most poetry collections.

anthropocentrism.definition: regarding humans as the central concern
anthropocentrism.sentence: Her critique targets the anthropocentrism implicit in valuing forests only for what they yield us.
sentences: Anthropocentrism values a forest by its lumber and a whale by its oil.

anthropomorphic.definition: attributing human traits to nonhuman things
anthropomorphic.sentence: Anthropomorphic descriptions make the behavior vivid and quietly smuggle in assumptions about motive.
sentences: Calling the storm "angry" is anthropomorphic, and every weather report does it anyway.

antic.sentence: The antics that delighted audiences early on wore thin by the third season.
sentences: The antics that charmed the first season were a contractual obligation by the fourth.

antipathy.sentence: His antipathy toward the press predated any particular story they had run about him.
sentences: His antipathy toward small talk was so total that he learned three languages to avoid it.

antiquated.definition: outdated; belonging to an earlier era
antiquated.sentence: The antiquated filing system survived because replacing it would expose how little had been recorded.
sentences: The antiquated filing system survived because replacing it would reveal how little was filed.

antithesis.sentence: Her patient, evidence-first method was the antithesis of his taste for bold conjecture.
sentences: Her patient method was the antithesis of his taste for the brilliant guess.

antithetical.sentence: Secrecy of that kind is antithetical to the transparency the charter demands.
sentences: Secrecy of that kind is antithetical to the transparency the charter promises.

apathetic.sentence: Voters were not hostile so much as apathetic, having heard the same promises three elections running.
sentences: Apathetic voters are not persuaded by louder arguments, only by shorter queues.

apathy.sentence: The campaign's real opponent was apathy, not the rival party's thin platform.
sentences: The opposite of love is not hatred but apathy, which requires no effort at all.

apex.sentence: The company reached its apex just before the technology it depended on became obsolete.
sentences: The company hit its apex the year before its only product became obsolete.

aphorism.definition: a short saying expressing a general truth
aphorism.sentence: He wrote in aphorisms, which made him quotable and occasionally unintelligible.
sentences: An aphorism is a truth cut short enough to fit on a mug.

aphoristic.sentence: Her aphoristic prose compresses arguments that other writers would spend chapters unfolding.
sentences: His aphoristic style compressed whole chapters into sentences you had to read twice.

aplomb.sentence: She handled the hostile questioning with an aplomb that unnerved her interrogators.
sentences: She answered the hostile question with such aplomb that the questioner apologized.

apocryphal.sentence: The story about the burnt manuscript is apocryphal, though biographers repeat it fondly.
sentences: The story of the falling apple is apocryphal, which has never slowed its retelling.

apogee.definition: the highest or most distant point
apogee.sentence: The movement reached its apogee in 1968 and fragmented within three years.
sentences: The moon is farthest from us at apogee; movements reach theirs just before fragmenting.

apologist.definition: one who defends a doctrine or practice
apologist.sentence: He became an apologist for a policy he had privately called indefensible.
sentences: An apologist never apologizes; the word means he is explaining why nothing was wrong.

apostate.definition: one who abandons a belief or allegiance
apostate.sentence: Denounced as an apostate, she pointed out that the doctrine itself had changed, not her.
sentences: Every apostate insists the faith moved first.

apostle.definition: an ardent early advocate of a cause
apostle.sentence: He was an apostle of open data long before institutions found the idea respectable.
sentences: He was an apostle of open data back when the phrase got you removed from committees.

apothegm.sentence: The lecture ended with an apothegm students copied down without quite understanding.
sentences: The general's apothegm — "no plan survives contact" — has outlived every plan he made.

apotheosis.definition: the highest example; elevation to divine status
apotheosis.sentence: The chapel is the apotheosis of a style that elsewhere looks merely ornate.
sentences: Roman emperors were granted apotheosis after death, becoming gods by paperwork.

apparent.definition: clearly visible; seeming rather than actual
apparent.sentence: The apparent contradiction dissolves once you notice the two studies measured different populations.
sentences: The word does double duty: an apparent heir may be obvious, an apparent motive merely alleged.

appeal.definition: to make an earnest request; to be attractive
sentences: She appealed for volunteers and forty people arrived on a wet Saturday.
The design appeals to everyone under thirty and baffles the committee approving it.

appease.definition: to pacify by giving in to demands
appease.sentence: Concessions meant to appease the faction only convinced it that more could be extracted.
sentences: Appeasement feeds the crocodile hoping to be eaten last, as Churchill put it.

append.sentence: She appended a dissent that eventually proved more influential than the majority opinion.
sentences: She appended a two-page dissent that outlived the ruling it was attached to.

appoint.definition: to assign to a position or office
appoint.sentence: He was appointed to the panel after two better-qualified candidates declined.
sentences: He was appointed after two better candidates read the job description carefully.

apposite.sentence: Her example was apposite, cutting off an objection before anyone could raise it.
sentences: Her example was so apposite that the objection died before it was fully spoken.

appreciable.definition: large enough to be noticed or measured
appreciable.sentence: There was no appreciable difference between the groups, though the press release implied otherwise.
sentences: There was no appreciable difference between the groups, though the press release found one.

apprehension.sentence: She approached the review with apprehension that the first ten minutes entirely dispelled.
sentences: Apprehension means both dread and understanding, which anyone awaiting test results can confirm.

apprise.sentence: Nobody apprised the committee of the change until after the contracts were signed.
sentences: Nobody apprised the committee of the merger until the letterhead had already changed.

approach.definition: a way of dealing with something
approach.sentence: Their approach was empirical where his was theoretical, and the two rarely spoke.
sentences: Their approach was empirical, his theoretical, and the corridor between offices stayed empty.

approbation.sentence: He craved the approbation of colleagues whose work he had spent years dismissing.
sentences: He spent thirty years seeking the approbation of critics he publicly called irrelevant.

approbatory.sentence: An approbatory nod from the chair was the closest thing to praise the department offered.
sentences: An approbatory grunt from the chair was, in that department, a standing ovation.

appropriate.definition: to take for one's own use, often without permission
appropriate.sentence: The ministry appropriated funds earmarked for schools and reported the shift only years later.
sentences: The ministry appropriated the school fund and reported it three budgets later.

appurtenance.definition: an accessory or minor accompanying item
appurtenance.sentence: The title came with appurtenances of office that cost more to maintain than the salary covered.
sentences: The title came with appurtenances — a car, a crest, a driver — that cost more than the salary.

appurtenant.definition: belonging to as a subordinate part
appurtenant.sentence: The easement is appurtenant to the land and passes automatically to the next owner.
sentences: The right of way is appurtenant to the land and follows it to every new owner.

apropos.sentence: Her question was apropos, though it derailed a presentation the speaker had rehearsed for weeks.
sentences: Her question was apropos and derailed a presentation rehearsed for a month.

apt.sentence: The metaphor is apt: the institution really does resemble a machine nobody remembers designing.
sentences: The metaphor is apt: the institution really is a machine nobody remembers designing.

aquiline.sentence: The portrait exaggerates his aquiline profile, which contemporaries described as unremarkable.
sentences: Roman portrait busts flatter aquiline noses the way modern cameras flatter cheekbones.

arbiter.definition: one with power to settle disputes
arbiter.sentence: For thirty years the journal was the arbiter of what counted as serious work in the field.
sentences: For thirty years the journal was the arbiter of what counted as serious work.

arbitrary.definition: based on whim rather than reason
arbitrary.sentence: The cutoff was arbitrary, and students a single point below it were treated entirely differently.
sentences: The cutoff was arbitrary, and one point below it changed a student's entire decade.

arbitrate.definition: to settle a dispute as a neutral party
arbitrate.sentence: She was asked to arbitrate a quarrel that both sides preferred to keep alive.
sentences: She was asked to arbitrate a quarrel both sides were enjoying far too much.

arcane.sentence: The rules were arcane enough that compliance depended on a handful of long-serving clerks.
sentences: The tax code is arcane by accident; medieval alchemy was arcane on purpose.

arch.sentence: Her arch remarks about the committee's efficiency were funnier than anyone there admitted.
sentences: Her arch remark about punctuality landed exactly on the person who had arrived last.

archaic.definition: belonging to an earlier period; outdated
archaic.sentence: The statute's archaic language required a specialist to determine what it actually prohibited.
sentences: "Thou" is archaic, which is why it now sounds grander than the plain "you" it replaced.

archetype.definition: an original model or typical example
archetype.sentence: The novel established an archetype that a hundred imitators diluted within a decade.
sentences: The hard-boiled detective is an archetype: invented once, photocopied a thousand times.

ardent.sentence: An ardent defender of the program, she nonetheless conceded its costs had been understated.
sentences: Ardent comes from burning, which explains why such supporters are exhausting.

ardor.sentence: The ardor of his early letters gave way to the caution of a man with something to lose.
sentences: The ardor of his early letters cooled into the caution of a man with a mortgage.

arduous.sentence: Cataloguing the collection was arduous work that three previous archivists had abandoned.
sentences: Cataloguing the collection was arduous work that three previous archivists had quietly abandoned.

aria.definition: an elaborate solo song in an opera
aria.sentence: The aria is technically brutal, which is why so few singers attempt it twice.
sentences: The aria is brutal enough that sopranos schedule the rest of the week around it.

armada.definition: a large fleet of ships or vehicles
armada.sentence: An armada of trucks arrived at dawn, and the site was cleared before noon.
sentences: The Spanish Armada was defeated less by the English navy than by the weather.

arrant.definition: complete; utter, in a negative sense
arrant.sentence: The claim was arrant nonsense, and repeating it confidently did not improve it.
sentences: Arrant nonsense is nonsense with no redeeming ambiguity whatsoever.

arrest.definition: to stop or check the progress of
arrest.sentence: The treatment arrests the disease's progress without reversing the damage already done.
sentences: The treatment arrests the decline without repairing anything already lost.

arresting.sentence: The opening image is arresting enough that few viewers notice how conventional the rest becomes.
sentences: The opening image is so arresting that few notice the film has nothing to follow it with.

arriviste.definition: an ambitious newcomer to wealth or status
arriviste.sentence: The old families treated him as an arriviste long after his fortune exceeded theirs.
sentences: The old families called him an arriviste long after his fortune had swallowed theirs.

arrogate.definition: to claim or seize without right
arrogate.sentence: The agency arrogated to itself powers the legislature had deliberately withheld.
sentences: The agency arrogated powers the legislature had deliberately refused to grant.

artful.definition: clever, often in a cunning way
artful.sentence: His artful phrasing conceded nothing while sounding, to most listeners, like an apology.
sentences: Dickens named his pickpocket the Artful Dodger, which is a definition disguised as a name.

articulate.sentence: She was the most articulate member of a panel that badly needed one.
sentences: Being articulate wins arguments you should have lost, which is why it deserves suspicion.

artifact.definition: an object made by humans; a spurious result
artifact.sentence: The spike proved to be an artifact of the instrument rather than a feature of the sample.
sentences: The spike turned out to be an artifact of the instrument, not a signal from the sky.

artifice.sentence: The apparent spontaneity was pure artifice, rehearsed over several afternoons.
sentences: The apparent spontaneity was pure artifice, rehearsed across three afternoons.

artless.sentence: Her artless account of the meeting revealed more than the official minutes ever would.
sentences: Her artless account of the meeting revealed everything the official minutes had smoothed away.

artlessness.definition: sincerity; freedom from deceit or affectation
artlessness.sentence: The memoir's artlessness is its charm and, in places, its most serious limitation.
sentences: The memoir's artlessness is its charm until, near the end, it becomes its limitation.
The faction's ascendancy lasted exactly as long as the leader who had assembled it.
Rome's ascendancy over the Mediterranean began with a navy it had to invent from a wrecked ship.
Investigators could not ascertain whether the fire began in the kitchen or the wiring above it.
Before arguing about the cause, ascertain that the thing actually happened.

ascetic.definition: severely self-denying, especially for spiritual reasons
sentences: His ascetic routine allowed one meal, one hour of talk, and no exceptions for holidays.
Ascetic monks slept on stone to keep the body from voting in the soul's decisions.

ascribe.definition: to attribute a cause or origin to
sentences: Never ascribe to malice what is adequately explained by a spreadsheet error.
Historians ascribe the collapse to drought; the survivors ascribed it to their neighbors.
Aseptic technique cut surgical deaths faster than any new instrument ever did.
His prose is aseptic: clean, safe, and entirely free of anything living.
The committee looked askance at a budget that balanced only in the final column.
To look askance is literally to look sideways, which is what suspicion does to a face.
He corrected the intern with an asperity the mistake did not deserve.
Asperity shares a root with "rough": the word is sandpaper for the voice.

aspersion.definition: a damaging or false remark about someone
sentences: He cast aspersions on her research without once naming a paper or a page.
Casting aspersions is cheap; retracting them requires a lawyer.

aspersions.definition: damaging or false remarks about someone
sentences: The letter was three pages of aspersions and one paragraph of verifiable fact.
Aspersions travel faster than corrections and never share a route home.

assail.definition: to attack violently, physically or verbally
sentences: Critics assailed the plan for a week before anyone read past its summary.
Doubts assailed her at three in the morning, which is when doubts do their best work.

assay.definition: to test or analyze the quality of
sentences: The mint assays every bar, since gold is the one metal people bother to fake well.
He assayed the mood of the room and quietly folded his prepared speech.
Royal assent turns a bill into law and has not been refused since 1708.
Her nod was the only assent the motion received, and it carried.

assert.definition: to state firmly; to insist upon a right
sentences: To assert a claim is easy; the burden begins with the next sentence.
She asserted herself for the first time in the meeting and the agenda changed.

assertive.definition: confident and forceful in stating one's position
sentences: Assertive is what we call it when we approve; aggressive is the same behavior we don't.
One assertive question from the audience unraveled forty slides of confidence.

assiduous.definition: showing great care and persistent effort
sentences: Assiduous note-taking saved the project when the only server failed.
The root means "sitting down to it" — assiduity is mostly refusing to get up.
He assiduously avoided the one colleague who might have corrected him.
She worked assiduously for six years and became an overnight success.
It takes a week to read the manual and a year to assimilate it.
The empire assimilated the gods of every province, which made its temples very crowded.

assuage.definition: to soothe or make less intense
sentences: A public apology assuaged nobody, since the private conduct continued unchanged.
Ice cream assuages grief for about eleven minutes, which is still eleven minutes.
To general astonishment, the unknown candidate carried three districts.
His astonishment lasted a second; his recalculation of everything took a month.

astringent.definition: sharp or severe; causing tissue to contract
sentences: Her astringent review of the draft removed both flattery and forty pages.
Unripe persimmons are astringent enough to make the mouth feel upholstered.

astute.definition: shrewd and quick to see advantage
sentences: An astute buyer noticed the roofline sagging and left before the tour ended.
She was astute about people and hopeless about deadlines, a common combination.
What the treaty joined, three bad harvests tore asunder.
The word survives almost entirely inside wedding vows and dramatic weather reports.

atavism.definition: the reappearance of an ancestral trait
sentences: The whale calf born with hind limbs is an atavism, an old blueprint briefly resurfacing.
Mob violence, he argued, is atavism: the crowd remembering something the individual forgot.

attenuate.definition: to weaken or reduce in force
sentences: Distance attenuates the signal until static wins the argument.
Vaccines use attenuated virus: the enemy, sent in weak enough to be studied safely.

attitude.definition: a settled way of thinking or feeling
sentences: His attitude toward deadlines was less defiance than serene disbelief.
Attitude also means an aircraft's angle: both senses describe how something is leaning.

attribute.definition: a quality or characteristic of something
sentences: Patience is the attribute every job listing wants and no interview can test.
In paintings, saints carry attributes — a wheel, a lion — so illiterate viewers could name them.

attuned.definition: receptive to or in harmony with
sentences: Attuned to the room's mood, she cut the presentation in half and won the vote.
Sailors grow attuned to the sound of rigging the way parents do to breathing.
The audacious plan required six strangers to be punctual, which is why it failed.
Audacious enough to ask for the raise in writing, twice, with a chart.
He had the audacity to bill the client for the apology letter.
Audacity swings both ways: the same word praises the explorer and condemns the gatecrasher.

augment.definition: to make greater by adding to
sentences: She augmented her salary by teaching two evening classes she came to prefer.
The choir augmented by twenty voices sounded, to everyone's surprise, quieter.

augury.definition: a sign of what will happen; an omen
sentences: Roman generals delayed battles when the sacred chickens refused to eat — a bad augury.
Empty seats at the premiere were an augury the producers chose to ignore.

august.definition: inspiring respect through dignity and grandeur
sentences: The august hall had hosted four coronations and one very awkward wedding.
An august body of scholars can still be wrong, only more slowly and in better clothing.
The dig proceeded under the auspices of a museum that never sent anyone to see it.
Auspices began as bird-watching for omens; now it means whose logo is on the banner.
Snow on opening night was, the superstitious cast insisted, auspicious.
The launch had an auspicious start and a very expensive middle.
The austere chapel contained one window, one bench, and no explanation.
His austere manner softened exactly once a year, in the presence of his dog.
The authoritarian coach won titles and lost every player who could afford to leave.
Authoritarian regimes rarely announce themselves; they arrive as emergency measures.
Her autocratic editing improved the book and ended the friendship.
The committee was democratic in structure and autocratic in practice.

automate.definition: to make a process operate by machine
sentences: They automated the reporting and discovered nobody had ever read the reports.
Automating a broken process gets you the same mistakes at a much higher speed.
The region became autonomous in name while its budget stayed in the capital.
An autonomous vehicle is only as autonomous as its worst-mapped intersection.
Doctors defend patient autonomy even when the patient chooses badly.
The department traded autonomy for funding and spent a decade regretting the exchange.
The auxiliary generator ran for nine hours and saved the entire experiment.
"Have" and "will" are auxiliary verbs: they carry no meaning, only other verbs.
Avarice is the only deadly sin that improves your credit score.
Dante placed the avaricious face-down, since they had spent life looking at the ground.
The avaricious landlord raised rents twice in a year and wondered why the building emptied.
He was avaricious about money and oddly generous with time.
She averred under oath that the meeting never happened; the parking records disagreed.
To aver is to stake your credit on it, which is why the word appears in court.
His aversion to meetings was strong enough to make him unusually productive.
One bad oyster can install a lifelong aversion in a single evening.

avert.definition: to prevent, or to turn away
sentences: A single phone call averted a strike that had been fifteen months in the making.
She averted her eyes from the screen, which did nothing about the numbers on it.
An avid reader, he owned four thousand books and had shelves for perhaps six hundred.
The word shares a root with avarice: an avid fan is greedy for more.

avocation.definition: a hobby pursued alongside one's job
sentences: Beekeeping was his avocation until the honey outsold his consulting.
Vocation calls you; avocation calls you away, which is the whole difference.

avow.definition: to declare openly and without shame
sentences: He avowed his change of mind in print, which cost him two friends and gained three.
To avow is to own it publicly; to disavow is to hope nobody kept the receipt.

avuncular.definition: kindly and tolerant, like an uncle
sentences: His avuncular advice was warm, confident, and almost entirely wrong.
The anchor's avuncular delivery made even the market crash sound survivable.

axiom.definition: a principle accepted as self-evidently true
sentences: Geometry begins with five axioms; two thousand years of doubt fell on the fifth.
"Follow the money" is treated as an axiom by every reporter under forty.
It is axiomatic in the trade that the last ten percent takes half the time.
What seems axiomatic in one century becomes a research question in the next.
She badgered the office for six weeks until the permit simply appeared.
The verb comes from baiting the animal: relentless, and enjoyed by the wrong party.
An hour of badinage passed before either negotiator mentioned a number.
Their badinage was affectionate and, to everyone else at the table, incomprehensible.
The cat fixed the new sofa with a baleful stare and made its plans.
A baleful glance is not merely unfriendly; it is a forecast.

balk.definition: to hesitate or refuse to proceed
sentences: He balked at the price, then paid it two days later without comment.
The horse balked at the ditch, and the rider continued alone, briefly airborne.
Costs ballooned from a modest estimate to a number nobody would say aloud.
The two-page memo ballooned into a policy, then a department.
The speech was banal enough to be applauded by people who disagreed with it.
Evil, Arendt argued, is often banal: a clerk, a form, a routine afternoon.
The condolence card offered three banalities and one sentence that actually helped.
Banality is what remains after everyone has agreed not to say anything risky.

bandy.definition: to exchange words or pass around casually
sentences: Names were bandied about the newsroom hours before anyone confirmed a single one.
Do not bandy statistics with someone who has read the appendix.

bane.definition: a cause of ruin or persistent misery
sentences: Damp was the bane of the archive, defeating three generations of librarians.
Wolfsbane and henbane are named honestly: the suffix once meant "killer."

banish.definition: to send away permanently; to drive out
sentences: Dante was banished from Florence and spent his exile assigning its citizens to hell.
One good night's sleep banished a fear that had survived a week of argument.
The banter stopped the moment the client walked in, which told him everything.
Their banter had rules older than the friendship itself.
The tax scheme was baroque enough to require its own flowchart and two lawyers.
Baroque originally described a misshapen pearl — an insult that became a period.
A barrage of questions met the announcement, and none of them were friendly.
The artillery barrage lasted a week; the ground never recovered its shape.

barren.definition: unable to produce; bleak and empty
sentences: The barren season yielded one paper, and even that one was mostly footnotes.
The soil looked barren until someone tested it and found the problem was salt.
He acted from base motives and a genuinely good instinct, which confused everyone.
Base metals corrode; noble metals do not — the moral vocabulary came from chemistry.

bastardization.definition: a corrupted or debased version of something
sentences: Purists called the adaptation a bastardization; audiences called it Tuesday.
Every bastardization begins as a shortcut somebody was in a hurry to justify.
The crowd waited with bated breath, which is breathing held back, not baited.
He bated his criticism only after learning the author was in the room.

bauble.definition: a showy trinket of little value
sentences: The medal was a bauble, and he wore it every day for thirty years.
A shop full of baubles will still outsell one honest, expensive thing.
Chaucer is bawdy in a way school editions quietly translate into fog.
The toast started bawdy and ended, unexpectedly, in tears.
The press was baying for a resignation before the facts had finished arriving.
Hounds baying in the valley meant the hunt had turned toward the river.

beatific.definition: showing radiant blessedness or serene joy
sentences: She wore a beatific smile through an hour of criticism, which unsettled the panel.
The infant's beatific expression usually indicates digestion rather than grace.

becoming.definition: flattering or appropriate to the person
sentences: Modesty was becoming in a champion and irritating in a candidate.
The color was becoming; the price was not.
The announcement produced bedlam: three microphones, forty questions, no answers.
Bedlam was a real asylum in London, whose name the city turned into a synonym.

befuddled.definition: confused and unable to think clearly
sentences: Befuddled by the new forms, applicants queued at the wrong desk for two days.
Six hours of jargon left the jury visibly befuddled and quietly resentful.

beg.definition: to ask earnestly; to evade a question
sentences: To beg the question originally meant assuming what you set out to prove.
He begged for one more week and delivered, remarkably, in four days.

begrudge.definition: to resent someone's possession or success
sentences: Nobody begrudged her the prize; several begrudged the speech that followed.
He begrudged every minute spent on paperwork and cheerfully lost hours to the crossword.
The brochure beguiled them into booking a hotel that no longer had a roof.
She beguiled the afternoon with letters she never intended to send.

behoove.definition: to be necessary or proper for
sentences: It would behoove the committee to read the report before praising it.
The word survives almost exclusively in sentences that are about to deliver a warning.
It behooves anyone signing a lease to read the clause about the roof.
"It behooves you" is how English says "you will regret it otherwise."

belabor.definition: to explain or attack at excessive length
sentences: He belabored the obvious for ten minutes while the actual problem waited.
There is no need to belabor the point once the room has visibly agreed.
The beleaguered mayor answered questions about potholes for the ninth straight week.
Creditors beleaguered the office until the phones were simply unplugged.

belfry.definition: a bell tower or the part housing bells
sentences: The belfry held four bells, three of them cracked, one of them illegal to ring.
"Bats in the belfry" locates madness in the tower, which is where the noise is.

belie.definition: to contradict or give a false impression of
sentences: Her calm voice belied a pulse the paramedics later described as impressive.
The tidy figures belied a warehouse in which nothing could be found.
He belittled the discovery until a rival institution announced the same thing.
Jefferson is credited with coining belittle, and critics belittled him for it.
His bellicose speech was aimed at supporters at home, not the enemy abroad.
Bellicose in meetings, he became remarkably reasonable in writing.
A belligerent passenger delayed the flight by ninety minutes and one arrest.
In law, a belligerent is simply a party at war; in life, it is a party at dinner.

bemoan.definition: to express regret or grief about
sentences: Editors have bemoaned the decline of reading in every decade since printing began.
He bemoaned the traffic he had joined by choosing to drive.
The instructions bemused everyone except the child, who assembled it in eight minutes.
Bemused means puzzled, not amused — a distinction most writers have already lost.
He wore a bemused expression through the entire ceremony honoring him.
The bemused silence lasted until someone finally asked what a "synergy audit" was.
The foundation's beneficent grants rebuilt a library and, incidentally, a reputation.
A beneficent tyrant is still a tyrant with better public relations.

benevolent.definition: kind and wishing to do good
sentences: A benevolent stranger paid the fare and disappeared before anyone could object.
Benevolent means wishing well; beneficent means doing well — intention against delivery.
Every generation calls the previous one benighted and is repaid within thirty years.
The word means overtaken by night, which is a kinder image than the insult it became.
The growth was benign, a word that has never sounded so beautiful.
A benign neglect let the meadow return without a single committee meeting.
She had a mathematical bent that the school's curriculum did its best to hide.
Follow your bent, the advice goes, provided somebody pays for it.

bequeath.definition: to leave property or a legacy to someone
sentences: He bequeathed his library to the town and his debts to his nephew.
Shakespeare bequeathed his wife the second-best bed, and scholars have argued ever since.

berate.definition: to scold angrily and at length
sentences: He berated the crew for a delay caused entirely by his own late arrival.
To berate is to scold with the volume up and the clock ignored.
The epidemic bereaved half the village within a single winter.
War bereaves twice: once at the front, and again at every kitchen table.
The argument was bereft of evidence and remarkably confident about it.
Bereft of his notes, he improvised the lecture and was never as good again.
She beseeched the board for one more term and got three more weeks.
Beseeching works on people; it has never once worked on a deadline.

besiege.definition: to surround and press hard upon
sentences: Reporters besieged the house until the family left by a neighbor's garden.
Troy was besieged for ten years and fell, allegedly, to carpentry.
A single anonymous post besmirched a career built over twenty years.
To besmirch is to smear: the metaphor was mud long before it was media.

besotted.definition: infatuated to the point of foolishness
sentences: Besotted with the prototype, investors ignored the fact that it never worked twice.
He was besotted enough to move countries and sensible enough to keep the lease.

bestow.definition: to confer or give as a gift
sentences: The university bestowed an honorary degree on a donor who had never read a book.
Titles bestowed cheaply are worn loudly.

betoken.definition: to be a sign of; to indicate
sentences: Empty shelves betokened a shortage the government was still denying.
A red sky at night betokens nothing except that people love a rhyme.

betray.definition: to be disloyal; to reveal unintentionally
sentences: His steady voice betrayed nothing; his hands betrayed everything.
The map betrayed the route long before the guide admitted they were lost.

betrothed.definition: the person one is engaged to marry
sentences: Her betrothed arrived two days late and blamed a river that had not flooded.
In the letters he calls her his betrothed, a word already old-fashioned in 1890.

bevy.definition: a large group of people or things
sentences: A bevy of consultants arrived, produced a chart, and left before anything was decided.
The collective noun began with quails and swans and has since escaped into offices.
The sample was biased toward people willing to answer a twenty-minute phone survey.
Everyone can spot a biased referee except the crowd that is winning.
The trail bifurcates at the ridge, and both branches are labeled "summit."
The case bifurcated into a criminal trial and a civil one, each blaming the other's delay.
His bilious column attacked the mayor, the weather, and a passing dog.
Medieval doctors blamed bad temper on bile, and the insult outlived the medicine.

bilk.definition: to cheat someone out of money
sentences: He bilked investors out of millions with a fund that owned one photocopier.
Bilking works best on people too embarrassed to admit they were bilked.

blanch.definition: to turn pale; to briefly scald food
sentences: He blanched at the estimate and asked, hopefully, whether it included tax.
Blanch the almonds and the skins slip off like bad excuses.

bland.definition: lacking flavor, interest, or strong feeling
sentences: The statement was so bland it could have been issued by any of the four parties.
Hospital food is bland by design, which is its only design.
The foul was so blatant that even the home crowd stopped arguing.
Blatant errors survive longest, since everyone assumes someone else has flagged them.
The forecast was bleak, and the second forecast was worse and better documented.
A bleak landscape has its admirers; a bleak balance sheet has none.
Potato blight emptied a country and rewrote the map of two continents.
The empty lot was a blight the council discussed annually for eleven years.
A blighted harvest meant the village ate seed corn and hoped for a mild spring.
His blighted career recovered abruptly when the accusation collapsed.
A blinkered focus on quarterly numbers cost the company its only patent.
Blinkers keep a horse from panicking and a person from noticing.
His blithe assurance that "it'll be fine" preceded every disaster of the trip.
She showed a blithe disregard for rules that had, admittedly, never been explained.

bluster.definition: loud, aggressive talk with little substance
sentences: Behind the bluster was a negotiator who had already accepted the terms.
Bluster is what wind and executives have in common.

boast.definition: to speak with excessive pride; to possess
sentences: The town boasts two museums, one of which is a shed with a plaque.
He boasted about the deal until the details were published.
The bogus certificate hung in the lobby for four years before anyone checked.
Bogus once named a machine for making counterfeit coins, which is a fittingly fake origin.
A boisterous crowd filled the hall and drowned out the string quartet entirely.
Boisterous at nine, silent at ten: the class had discovered the substitute's limits.
New data bolstered a theory that had been surviving on charm alone.
The word is a pillow: to bolster is to prop something up so it does not sag.

bolt.definition: to run away suddenly; to eat hurriedly
sentences: The horse bolted at the umbrella and stopped, sheepishly, four fields later.
He bolted his lunch in ninety seconds and spent the afternoon regretting it.
Strip the bombast from the speech and one modest proposal remains.
Bombast was originally cotton padding — the word means stuffing, and always did.
His bombastic introduction lasted longer than the lecture it introduced.
Bombastic prose is easy to write and impossible to finish reading.
The conference ran on bonhomie, coffee, and a shared dread of the closing plenary.
His bonhomie evaporated the instant the contract was on the table.
The new bridge was a boon to everyone except the ferryman.
Rain in June is a boon; the same rain in August ruins the harvest.
The boor talked through the entire quartet and complained about the acoustics.
Boor once simply meant farmer, which says more about cities than about farmers.
His boorish remarks emptied the table faster than the fire alarm had that morning.
Boorish behavior at a wedding is remembered longer than the vows.
A cube of bouillon rescued a soup that had otherwise given up.
The word shares a root with "boil," which is the entire recipe.

bowdlerize.definition: to censor by removing offensive parts
sentences: The film was bowdlerized for television until the plot no longer made sense.
Thomas Bowdler cleaned up Shakespeare and earned the rare fate of becoming a verb.

brandish.definition: to wave something threateningly or ostentatiously
sentences: He brandished the report like a weapon and never once opened it.
Brandishing an umbrella at a taxi is the most British form of combat.

bravado.definition: a show of courage meant to impress
sentences: The bravado lasted until the first question he could not answer.
Bravado is courage's understudy: same costume, no rehearsal.
The job needed brains and brawn, and the budget covered one of them.
Brawn moved the piano; brains had already measured the doorway.
A brazen forgery signed with the wrong century's spelling fooled two experts anyway.
She made a brazen request and, because nobody expected it, got exactly that.
Brevity is the soul of wit, said a character in a very long speech.
The email's brevity was mistaken for anger, which cost three days of clarification.
She bridled at the suggestion that the discovery had been lucky.
Bridle your enthusiasm long enough to read the contract.
The committee bristled at being called ceremonial, which rather proved the point.
A cat bristles to look larger; people do it to sound larger.

broach.definition: to raise a subject for discussion
sentences: Nobody would broach the topic of the missing funds until the auditor did.
The word means to pierce a barrel: broaching a subject lets the pressure out.

broadside.definition: a forceful attack in speech or writing
sentences: Her broadside against the proposal filled two pages and ended three careers.
A ship's broadside fired every gun at once, which is how the metaphor earned its force.
The speech offered bromides about teamwork to a room that had just been laid off.
Bromide was once a sedative, which explains what the word came to mean.

brooch.definition: an ornamental pin worn on clothing
sentences: The brooch was paste, and the insurance claim was not.
She chose her brooch the way other diplomats chose their words.
The chairman brooked no interruption, which made the meetings short and useless.
She would brook criticism of her methods but never of her data.

browbeat.definition: to bully with words or threats
sentences: He browbeat the junior staff into agreeing and called it consensus.
Browbeating produces compliance and, reliably, a resignation letter six weeks later.
"No," he said brusquely, and turned back to the screen.
She answered brusquely, then spent the afternoon writing an apologetic paragraph.
The small studio bucked the trend and released a two-hour film with no explosions.
The horse bucked, the trend bucked, and both threw somebody off.
The painting's bucolic calm hid the fact that the field had been worked by children.
A bucolic weekend cured him of wanting a bucolic life.
A film buff spotted the continuity error the director's whole crew had missed.
Fire buffs once wore buff-colored coats, which is where the fan got his name.

buffer.definition: something that lessens a shock or conflict
sentences: Savings acted as a buffer between one bad month and total catastrophe.
The neutral state was a buffer, which is a polite word for battlefield.

bullion.definition: gold or silver in bulk form
sentences: The vault held bullion worth more than the building housing it.
Bullion is money that has not yet been asked to be interesting.

bulwark.definition: a defensive wall or strong protection
sentences: A free press is the standard bulwark cited in speeches and cut in budgets.
The dunes were the town's only bulwark against a sea that kept auditioning.
A bumbling attempt at repair turned a leak into an indoor fountain.
The bumbling detective solves the case by tripping over the evidence, which audiences forgive.

buoyant.definition: cheerful and resilient; able to float
sentences: She stayed buoyant through the rejections and kept a folder of them for scale.
Markets described as buoyant have a habit of remembering gravity.
Three signatures were needed, and the bureaucracy required them in an impossible order.
Bureaucracy literally means rule by desk, which anyone who has visited one can confirm.
The side project burgeoned into a company with an office and a legal department.
Burgeon began as a word for buds opening, and it still carries the spring in it.

burnish.definition: to polish; to improve a reputation
sentences: The donation burnished a reputation that three lawsuits had dulled.
He burnished the anecdote with each retelling until it gleamed and was untrue.
He buttressed the argument with three studies, two of which he had not read.
Flying buttresses let cathedral walls become windows, which is architecture's best magic trick.
The word once meant obedient, then cheerful, and only lately what it means now.
The portrait's buxom subject was, the label revealed, the painter's landlady.
The hotel preserved a bygone elegance and, unfortunately, bygone plumbing.
Let bygones be bygones, says the person who wrote everything down.
The approval process was byzantine enough that consultants existed solely to navigate it.
Byzantine court intrigue was so tangled that the empire's name became an adjective for it.
A cabal of three deans reversed a decision the full faculty had spent a year making.
Every committee that meets before the meeting is, technically, a cabal.
The orchestra's tuning is cacophonous by design and the best part of the evening.
Cacophonous debate is still better than a silence somebody enforced.
A cacophony of alarms went off, none of them indicating an actual fire.
The Greek roots mean "bad sound," which is a fair review of most group chats.
Three weeks of exams left him cadaverous and fluent in medieval trade law.
The portrait's cadaverous face was the painter's revenge for an unpaid fee.

cajole.definition: to persuade by flattery or coaxing
sentences: She cajoled the landlord into fixing the boiler with compliments and one small pie.
Cajoling works where demanding fails, which every toddler discovers before age three.
The callous reply to a grieving family was read aloud in court.
Skin grows callous to protect itself, which is exactly what the metaphor means.
A callow recruit argued with the safety officer once and never again.
The word meant featherless: a callow bird cannot yet fly, and neither can he.

calumny.definition: a false statement meant to damage a reputation
sentences: The pamphlet was pure calumny, and it outsold every honest account of the trial.
Calumny needs no evidence, only repetition and a willing audience.

cameo.definition: a brief notable appearance or portrayal
sentences: The author's cameo lasts eleven seconds and is the film's most discussed scene.
The chapter is a cameo of the whole era, cut small and carved deep.

campaign.definition: an organized effort toward a goal
sentences: The campaign to save the theater raised half the money and all of the attention.
Campaign comes from "open field": armies fought there before marketers borrowed the word.

canard.definition: an unfounded rumor or false story
sentences: The canard that the bridge was sinking survived four engineering reports.
Canard is French for duck; the fake story apparently waddles.
Her candid assessment cost her the promotion and earned her the department's trust.
A candid photograph catches you before you can arrange your face.
His candidness in the interview was refreshing until it reached the legal department.
Candidness costs nothing to give and a great deal to receive.
The memo's candor about the failure is why the company survived it.
Candor is honesty without the flattering angle.

canny.definition: shrewd and careful, especially in business
sentences: A canny buyer waited three weeks and got the same house for less.
Canny is astute with its wallet already closed.

canon.definition: an accepted body of works or rules
sentences: Ten novels entered the canon that decade, and eight were by people nobody had published before.
Every argument about the canon is really an argument about who assigns reading.
The canonical version of the experiment omits the three attempts that failed.
Which recipe is canonical depends entirely on whose grandmother is in the room.

canonize.definition: to declare a saint; to treat as authoritative
sentences: Critics canonized the novel so quickly that its flaws became features.
The church canonized her four centuries after burning her records.
The speech was cant: virtue words arranged around a contract award.
Cant also means the private jargon of a trade, which is often the same thing.
The cantankerous neighbor objected to the fence, the color, and the concept of neighbors.
He grew cantankerous with age, having decided politeness had never once helped him.

canto.definition: a major division of a long poem
