sentences: The Inferno's first canto gets read in every survey course; the other thirty-three do not.
Each canto ends on a cliff, which is how epic poems kept audiences awake.

capacity.definition: the ability or maximum amount possible
sentences: The hall's capacity is four hundred, and six hundred tickets were somehow sold.
She has the capacity for the work and no appetite for the meetings.
The studio capitulated after nine weeks and restored the original ending.
To capitulate was originally to negotiate terms in chapters — surrender with paperwork.

caprice.definition: a sudden unpredictable change of mind
sentences: The schedule changed on the caprice of a director who had not read it.
Caprice comes from a word for a hedgehog-headed shudder, which is how whims feel.
Funding was capricious, generous one year and invisible the next.
Mountain weather is capricious enough to require three coats and one apology.

captious.definition: eager to find fault over trifles
sentences: The captious reviewer devoted a paragraph to a misplaced comma and none to the argument.
Captious questions are designed to catch, not to learn.
The cardinal rule of the lab was to label everything, and it was broken weekly.
Cardinal comes from "hinge": the things everything else swings on.

careen.definition: to lurch or swerve while moving fast
sentences: The cart careened down the hill and ended its career in a hedge.
The negotiations careened between collapse and celebration twice in one afternoon.

caricature.definition: an exaggerated portrayal for comic effect
sentences: The cartoon was a caricature: one enormous nose and a policy nobody could defend.
Argue against a caricature of a view and you have won nothing at all.
A carping colleague can drain more energy than an outright enemy.
The carping notes in the margin outnumbered the sentences they surrounded.

carrion.definition: the decaying flesh of dead animals
sentences: Vultures find carrion by smell from a mile up, which is a horrifying talent.
The metaphor is unkind but exact: the lawyers circled like birds over carrion.
The cartographer left the interior blank rather than invent rivers, which was rare honesty.
Medieval cartographers filled empty space with monsters; modern ones use logos.

cartography.definition: the art and science of making maps
sentences: Cartography is never neutral: what gets named and centered is an argument.
Satellite imagery finished the geography and left cartography arguing about borders.
The report castigated the agency for delays it had documented in its own memos.
He castigated the team publicly and apologized privately, in that revealing order.
The castigation lasted twenty minutes and taught nothing that two sentences would not have.
Public castigation buys obedience and sells loyalty.
The eruption was a cataclysm that ended a civilization and preserved its bread.
Financial cataclysms are always obvious afterward and unthinkable the week before.
The asteroid's arrival was cataclysmic for dinosaurs and career-making for mammals.
A cataclysmic first act leaves a play nowhere to go.
The strike was not the cause but the catalyst; the grievances were a decade old.
A catalyst speeds the reaction and walks away unchanged, which is enviable.
He issued a categorical denial on Monday and a careful clarification on Friday.
Kant's categorical imperative admits no "unless," which is why it is so hard to live by.
Writing the letter was cathartic; sending it would have been catastrophic.
Greek audiences went to tragedies for a cathartic cry and a clean walk home.
Her taste in music was catholic enough to include both plainsong and speed metal.
Lowercase catholic means all-embracing, which is where the capitalized word got its ambition.

caucus.definition: a closed meeting of a faction
sentences: The caucus met at seven and had decided the vote before the public session opened.
Iowa's caucuses require standing in a corner of a gym, which is democracy at its most literal.
Her caustic aside was quoted for years, usually by people who had not been insulted.
Caustic soda eats through pipes; caustic remarks manage friendships.
His cavalier attitude toward safety ended when the inspector arrived unannounced.
A cavalier answer to a careful question is its own kind of insult.

cease.definition: to stop or bring to an end
sentences: Production ceased in March and resumed, under a new name, in April.
"Cease and desist" says the same thing twice, which lawyers charge for separately.

cede.definition: to give up power or territory formally
sentences: The company ceded the market rather than fight a competitor with deeper pockets.
Nations cede territory on paper long before anyone moves a fence.
The refund arrived with a celerity that suggested somebody feared the press.
Celerity shares a root with accelerate and nothing at all with celery.

censor.definition: to suppress objectionable parts of material
sentences: The letters were censored so heavily that the surviving words formed a haiku.
Censoring a book is the most reliable way to guarantee it is read.
The senate's censure carried no penalty and ended a thirty-year career.
Censure is disapproval with the minutes taken.

centrifuge.definition: a machine spinning to separate substances
sentences: The centrifuge sorts blood into layers that tell a doctor more than the patient can.
Spun long enough in a centrifuge, even loyalty separates by density.
The film is cerebral to a fault: three ideas, no pulse.
His approach was cerebral, hers instinctive, and the argument they had was inevitable.

chaff.definition: worthless material; husks separated from grain
sentences: Separating wheat from chaff is easy with grain and nearly impossible with advice.
The report was ninety pages of chaff around four useful paragraphs.
To his chagrin, the error was on the slide behind him, enlarged and backlit.
Chagrin is embarrassment with a bruise on the pride.

chamber.definition: an enclosed space or legislative body
sentences: The lower chamber passed the bill, and the upper chamber buried it politely.
The burial chamber had been sealed for three thousand years and looted for two thousand nine hundred.

champion.definition: to support or defend a cause vigorously
sentences: She championed the unglamorous reform that saved more lives than any drug that decade.
He championed the idea until it succeeded, then championed his role in it.
The charlatan sold a cure, a certificate, and a follow-up appointment he never kept.
Charlatan comes from an Italian word for chatter — the credential is the talking.
Burned once by a forged provenance, the museum was chary of private sellers.
He was chary with praise and generous with everything else.
The coach chastised the squad for a lapse that lasted four seconds and cost the season.
She chastised herself for the error long after everyone else had forgotten it.

chauvinism.definition: excessive loyalty to one's own group
sentences: Nicolas Chauvin's fanatical devotion to Napoleon gave the world a word for it.
Culinary chauvinism insists no country abroad has ever seasoned anything correctly.

chauvinist.definition: one who believes their group is superior
sentences: The chauvinist praised local engineering while driving an imported car.
Every chauvinist believes the accident of his birthplace was a verdict.

chauvinistic.definition: aggressively convinced of one's group's superiority
sentences: The chauvinistic editorial insulted three neighboring countries in a single paragraph.
Chauvinistic pride survives entirely on not looking anywhere else.

check.definition: to restrain or halt the progress of
sentences: Only a cold spring checked an insect population that had doubled every year.
Checks and balances exist because power, left alone, does not check itself.

checkered.definition: marked by both successes and failures
sentences: He arrived with a checkered past and a genuinely impressive set of references.
The firm's checkered history included two bankruptcies and one Nobel laureate.
She cherished the battered dictionary more than the prizes on the shelf above it.
We cherish what we might lose; nobody cherishes tap water.
Legal chicanery delayed the trial until the key witness had moved abroad.
The contract's chicanery lived entirely in a footnote about renewal.
She chided him for skipping breakfast, then handed him half of hers.
Chiding is scolding with the affection still switched on.
Cheap fusion power remained a chimera through four decades of confident forecasts.
The original chimera had a lion's head, a goat's body, and no chance of existing.

chivalrous.definition: courteous and honorable, especially toward others
sentences: His chivalrous gesture at the door lost some charm when he let it swing back.
Chivalrous conduct was invented by knights who mostly did the opposite.
The choleric conductor snapped his baton twice in one rehearsal.
Medieval medicine blamed choleric tempers on yellow bile; modern offices blame email.

chortle.definition: to laugh in a gleeful, snorting way
sentences: He chortled at his own joke before the punch line, which spoiled it entirely.
Lewis Carroll invented chortle by welding chuckle to snort.
The exhibit's chronological order made a two-century argument in a single corridor.
His account was chronological, thorough, and missing the only afternoon that mattered.
It would be churlish to complain about a free upgrade, so he complained quietly.
A churlish reply to a kind letter says everything about the writer.
After ten minutes of circumlocution he admitted the money was gone.
Circumlocution means talking around; the word itself takes six syllables to say so.
The new rules circumscribed the agency's power without reducing its budget.
Her role was carefully circumscribed and gradually, quietly, ignored.
Within his circumscribed authority he did remarkable things; beyond it, nothing.
A circumscribed study of one village produced the decade's broadest conclusion.
Circumspect in public and blunt in private, she survived four administrations.
The word means looking around, which is what caution physically resembles.
Under different circumstances the same decision would have been called courageous.
He explained the circumstances at length and never once mentioned his own part in them.

circumvent.definition: to get around a rule or obstacle cleverly
sentences: The shell company existed solely to circumvent a law written the previous spring.
Every new rule creates a small industry devoted to circumventing it.

cite.definition: to quote or refer to as evidence
sentences: He cited four studies, none of which said what he claimed they said.
Cite your sources, or someone eventually will cite them against you.
The tower is clad in copper that has spent a century turning green.
Clad only in a raincoat and confidence, he addressed the press.

clamber.definition: to climb awkwardly using hands and feet
sentences: They clambered over the rocks with all the grace of falling furniture.
He clambered up the ranks by routes nobody else considered dignified.

clamor.definition: loud noise or vehement public demand
sentences: The clamor for an inquiry grew louder than the scandal that had started it.
A clamor outside the chamber ended a debate no argument could.
Clamorous gulls made the harbor unusable for anyone hoping to think.
The clamorous minority got the interview; the silent majority got the bill.

clandestine.definition: kept secret, especially for illicit reasons
sentences: Their clandestine meetings were held in a café directly opposite the ministry.
Clandestine funding built the road; nobody would say which country's.
The clangor of the foundry set the whole street's windows vibrating.
Church bells produce clangor; alarm clocks produce something less forgivable.
The report was a clarion call that four committees agreed to study further.
Her clarion voice carried to the back of a hall built before microphones.

cleave.definition: to split apart, or to cling to
sentences: Cleave is its own opposite: an axe cleaves wood, and a vine cleaves to the wall.
The party cleaved into two factions that cleaved stubbornly to the same name.
The governor granted clemency an hour before the sentence was to be carried out.
Clemency also describes mild weather, since both spare you what was coming.
One phone call clinched a deal that eighteen months of dinners had not.
The final witness clinched the case in eleven minutes of testimony.
The policy cloaked a cut in the language of reform.
Fog cloaked the harbor so completely that the ferry docked by memory.
The film's cloying score told the audience how to feel every eleven seconds.
One spoonful is delightful; the whole jar is cloying.

coagulate.definition: to thicken into a semisolid mass
sentences: Blood coagulates in seconds, which is the only reason paper cuts are survivable.
The group's vague complaints slowly coagulated into a formal petition.

coalesce.definition: to come together to form a whole
sentences: Scattered protests coalesced into a movement with a name and a bank account.
The notes coalesced into an argument only after the third rewrite.
He coasted through the first year and met the second one at full speed.
The company coasted on one invention for eleven years.
She coaxed the engine into starting with a technique the manual did not describe.
You cannot coax a deadline, though everyone tries.

coda.definition: a concluding section or final addition
sentences: The last chapter is a coda: nothing happens, and everything is finally explained.
His retirement speech was a coda to a career that had ended, quietly, years earlier.
The startup was coddled by investors until its first honest quarter.
Coddle an egg gently in water; coddle a person and you get something less useful.

codicil.definition: an addition or supplement to a will
sentences: A codicil written three days before his death redirected the entire estate.
The codicil was valid, witnessed, and written in crayon, which delighted the lawyers.

coercion.definition: the use of force or threats to compel
sentences: A confession obtained by coercion is worthless in court and in life.
Coercion gets you compliance today and sabotage every day after.

coercive.definition: using force or threats to compel
sentences: The contract's coercive clause was struck out by a judge who called it "remarkable."
Coercive measures work quickly and expire the moment attention wanders.

coffer.definition: a chest for valuables; financial reserves
sentences: The city's coffers were empty, and the fountain still needed repairing.
Three centuries of donations filled the coffers of a chapel that seats forty.
Her cogent two-page rebuttal ended a debate that had run for two years.
Cogent arguments change votes; loud ones only change the volume.
He cogitated over the problem for a week and solved it on a bus.
To cogitate is to think slowly enough that people notice you doing it.
English "father" and Latin "pater" are cognate, which is why the pattern repeats everywhere.
The two disciplines are cognate and have not spoken since 1974.
Fully cognizant of the risk, she signed anyway and said so in writing.
The board was cognizant of the deficit and unwilling to name it.

cohere.definition: to hold together logically or physically
sentences: The essay's parts never quite cohere, though each is fine alone.
Wet sand coheres; dry sand has opinions of its own.
A cohesive team of average players beat a fractured team of stars.
The chapter is cohesive; the book around it is a filing cabinet.

cohort.definition: a group sharing a characteristic or time
sentences: The 1994 cohort produced three ministers and one very famous defendant.
A Roman cohort was six hundred soldiers; a research cohort is six hundred spreadsheets.
Her coiffure survived the storm better than the umbrella did.
The portrait was commissioned mainly to document the coiffure.

coin.definition: to invent a new word or phrase
sentences: Shakespeare coined "assassination," which is a striking gift to leave a language.
The phrase was coined in a memo and lived to embarrass three generations.

collaborate.definition: to work jointly; to cooperate with an enemy
sentences: They collaborated for a decade and never once agreed on the first paragraph.
The word carries a shadow: in wartime, to collaborate meant something unforgivable.

collation.definition: the act of collecting and comparing texts
sentences: Collation of the manuscripts revealed a missing line in every printed edition.
The collation took four months and changed one word.

collude.definition: to cooperate secretly for a wrongful purpose
sentences: The three suppliers colluded to fix a price nobody could afford to refuse.
To collude is to cooperate with the lights off.

collusion.definition: secret cooperation for a dishonest purpose
sentences: The identical bids, down to a typo, suggested collusion rather than coincidence.
Collusion is the crime that requires two people to keep one secret.
One bad experience colored her view of the entire profession.
The witness's memory was colored by six months of newspaper coverage.
The Colossus of Rhodes gave us the adjective and then fell over in an earthquake.
It was a colossal error, executed with impressive attention to detail.
The chamber's comity survived until the cameras were installed.
Comity between nations means recognizing each other's courts without being forced to.
Proceedings commenced at nine and adjourned, unresolved, at nine forty.
Graduation is called commencement because it names the beginning, not the ending.
Her commendable honesty about the failure was the reason she kept the job.
"Commendable effort" on a report is praise with a small knife in it.
The punishment was not commensurate with an offense involving one traffic cone.
Salary commensurate with experience is a phrase that means bring your own leverage.

commiserate.definition: to express sympathy for another's misfortune
sentences: They commiserated over identical rejection letters and split a very large dessert.
Commiserating is grief shared until it becomes portable.

commission.definition: to formally order or authorize work
sentences: The city commissioned a study, received it, and commissioned a second one.
She was commissioned to paint the hall and given nine days.

commit.definition: to pledge oneself; to carry out an act
sentences: He committed to the plan in public and hedged it in every email afterward.
One word covers marrying, memorizing, and murdering, which is English at its strangest.

compel.definition: to force or drive to do something
sentences: The court compelled disclosure of documents the firm had described as nonexistent.
Curiosity compelled her to open the box the label warned against.
The evidence was compelling enough that even the defense stopped objecting.
A compelling first chapter forgives a great deal of what follows.
The compendium fit two centuries of case law into four hundred pages.
His notebook was a compendium of other people's best ideas, carefully attributed.
Competent is the highest compliment some professions ever need.
A competent surgeon beats a brilliant one with a bad night's sleep.

complacent.definition: smugly satisfied and unaware of danger
sentences: Three good years made the company complacent and the fourth one instructive.
Complacent is not the same as content: one has stopped looking, the other has stopped wanting.
Her complaisance was mistaken for weakness by everyone who later worked for her.
Complaisance pleases; complacence sleeps. One letter, two very different failings.
A complaisant assistant said yes to four impossible deadlines in one morning.
He was complaisant with superiors and remarkably firm with everyone else.

complement.definition: to complete or enhance by adding
sentences: The wine complemented the fish, which is the only sentence sommeliers actually need.
Her caution complemented his recklessness for exactly one profitable year.

complementary.definition: combining well to form a whole
sentences: Their complementary skills covered everything except deciding who was in charge.
Complementary completes; complimentary flatters — and only one is free.
A compliant workforce is easy to manage and impossible to learn anything from.
The building was fully compliant with a code written before elevators.
Silence in that room was not neutral; it was complicit.
He was complicit by signature, which the court found sufficient.

comply.definition: to act in accordance with a rule or request
sentences: They complied with the letter of the order and buried its purpose entirely.
Comply first, complain in writing afterward: the bureaucrat's survival rule.

comport.definition: to behave in a specified way; to agree with
sentences: He comported himself with dignity through a hearing designed to remove it.
The testimony did not comport with the timeline the phone records established.

compound.definition: to make worse by adding to
sentences: He compounded the error by explaining it at length on television.
Interest compounds, and so does neglect.
The comprehensive review took two years and confirmed what the interns said in week one.
Comprehensive insurance covers everything except what happened to you.

compromise.definition: to settle by concession; to endanger
sentences: They compromised on everything except the one clause that mattered.
A single reused password compromised the entire system.
She conceded the point graciously and won the argument twenty minutes later.
He conceded the election before the last district had finished counting.

conceit.definition: excessive pride; a fanciful literary device
sentences: His conceit was so complete that criticism registered as jealousy.
The novel's central conceit is that the house remembers everyone who lived there.

concept.definition: an abstract idea or general notion
sentences: The concept survived four redesigns and one complete change of purpose.
"Fairness" is a concept everyone endorses and nobody defines the same way.

concern.definition: worry, or a matter of interest
sentences: Her only concern was whether anyone would read past the summary.
The auditors expressed concern, which in their language is a scream.
He tried to conciliate both factions and was distrusted by each for it.
A small apology conciliated a neighbor who had been silently furious for years.
His conciliatory tone surprised a room that had prepared for a fight.
A conciliatory gesture costs little and is remembered for years.
The DNA result was conclusive, which the four eyewitnesses had never been.
Nothing in that field is conclusive; it merely becomes expensive to disagree.
Growth came with the concomitant traffic that nobody had budgeted for.
Fame and its concomitant loss of privacy arrive as a package deal.
Three judges concurred with the outcome and disagreed about every reason for it.
The experts concur, which historically means check again in ten years.

condemn.definition: to express strong disapproval; to sentence
sentences: The building was condemned, which was the first official acknowledgment of the smell.
He condemned the practice in public and continued it in the accounts.

condolence.definition: an expression of sympathy for grief
sentences: The letter of condolence arrived a month late and was worth the wait.
Condolences are easiest to give and hardest to phrase.

condone.definition: to overlook or tacitly accept wrongdoing
sentences: The board did not condone the conduct; it merely declined to notice it twice.
To explain is not to condone, though the distinction rarely survives a headline.

conducive.definition: tending to promote or help bring about
sentences: An open-plan office is conducive to conversation and hostile to concentration.
Nothing about the schedule was conducive to actually finishing anything.
His conduct at the hearing was faultless, which made the evidence worse.
The code of conduct ran forty pages and omitted the situation that arose.

confer.definition: to grant, or to consult together
sentences: The degree confers a title and no useful powers whatsoever.
They conferred in the corridor for ninety seconds and reversed a year of policy.
A dropped lamp became a conflagration that redrew the city's map.
The dispute grew from a memo into a conflagration involving four departments.

conflate.definition: to merge two distinct things confusingly
sentences: The article conflates correlation and cause, then builds a policy on top.
Do not conflate being busy with being useful; the calendar cannot tell the difference.
The city grew at the confluence of two rivers and one very old road.
A confluence of cheap credit and bad memory produced the bubble.
The result confounded a theory that three textbooks had already printed.
Weather confounded the forecast, the schedule, and the caterers.
The gravy congealed while the argument about politics reached its second hour.
Vague resentment congealed into a formal complaint sometime that winter.

congenial.definition: pleasant and agreeable in company or nature
sentences: The library was congenial to thought and hostile to conversation, which suited him.
They made congenial neighbors for nine years and never once entered each other's houses.

conjectural.definition: based on guesswork rather than evidence
sentences: The reconstruction is conjectural: two walls survive, and the rest is confident drawing.
His dating of the manuscript remains conjectural and is quoted as fact.
Conjugal duties in the old law codes were listed alongside property and cattle.
Their conjugal arrangement involved two cities and one very reliable train.

conjure.definition: to summon or produce as if by magic
sentences: He conjured a budget out of nothing and a resignation out of the treasurer.
The smell of pine conjures a specific December he has never described to anyone.
The conniving deputy leaked one paragraph and toppled a minister.
Conniving requires patience, which is why it so rarely fails.

connoisseur.definition: an expert judge in matters of taste
sentences: A connoisseur can name the vineyard; the rest of us can name the color.
He was a connoisseur of bureaucratic excuses and had a favorite.

connotation.definition: an implied meaning beyond the literal
sentences: "Thrifty" and "stingy" denote the same behavior with opposite connotations.
The word's connotation had drifted so far that the dictionary gave up.

connote.definition: to imply in addition to the literal meaning
sentences: "Home" denotes a residence and connotes everything the residence is not.
The uniform connotes authority even when its wearer is nineteen and lost.

conscientious.definition: careful, thorough, and guided by principle
sentences: A conscientious editor caught the error on page four hundred and eleven.
Conscientious objectors accepted prison rather than a rifle, which required its own courage.

consecrate.definition: to declare sacred; to dedicate solemnly
sentences: The ground was consecrated in 1103 and paved over in 1974.
He consecrated thirty years to a dictionary that reached the letter G.
The consensus formed in the corridor and was ratified, ceremonially, in the room.
Scientific consensus is not a vote; it is what survives repeated attempts to break it.
The most consequential decision of the decade was made by four people on a Friday.
Small consequential changes beat large ceremonial ones every time.

conservatory.definition: a music school, or a glass-walled room for plants
sentences: She trained at a conservatory where practicing after midnight was a tradition, not a rule.
The conservatory held four hundred plants and one very confused cat.

consider.definition: to think about carefully; to regard as
sentences: Consider the alternatives before announcing that there are none.
He considered himself misunderstood; his colleagues considered him understood perfectly.
Nothing consoled her until a colleague admitted making the same mistake in 1998.
He consoled the team by pointing out how much worse it could have been, which did not help.
They consolidated six databases into one and lost only two years of records.
He spent the first term consolidating power and the second wondering what for.
He was conspicuous by his absence, which is the loudest way to attend.
Conspicuous consumption is spending designed to be seen, not enjoyed.

conspire.definition: to plot secretly; to combine toward an effect
sentences: Rain, roadworks, and a lost key conspired to make him forty minutes late.
They conspired for months and were undone by one enthusiastic group email.
A constant friend and an inconstant correspondent, he wrote twice a decade.
The only constant in the department was the coffee machine's failure.
To the consternation of the organizers, the guest of honor brought a rival.
The announcement produced consternation in the office and celebration in the pub.

constituency.definition: a body of supporters or voters
sentences: The policy had no constituency except the person who wrote it.
Her constituency was small, loyal, and impossible to poll accurately.
Break the compound into its constituents and the mystery becomes chemistry.
He answered every constituent letter personally, which is why he had no evenings.
Three missed payments constitute default, whatever the customer intended.
Women constituted a majority of the workforce and a fifth of its management.
Constrained by budget and pride, they rebuilt the roof themselves, badly.
His constrained smile in the photograph tells the story the caption omits.
The only real constraint was time, which is the only one that cannot be negotiated.
Poets choose constraints deliberately, which is either discipline or masochism.
Cold constricts the blood vessels, which is why fingers go white before they hurt.
New rules constricted lending until the smallest firms stopped applying.

construe.definition: to interpret in a particular way
sentences: Silence was construed as consent by everyone who benefited from that reading.
The clause can be construed two ways, and both parties chose the profitable one.
A consummate professional, she rewrote the speech in the car and delivered it flawlessly.
He is a consummate bore, which requires as much dedication as any other mastery.

consumption.definition: the using up of resources; an old term for tuberculosis
sentences: Water consumption fell eight percent when the meters became visible in the kitchen.
Nineteenth-century novels killed off half their heroines with consumption.
Familiarity breeds contempt, and so does reading the minutes of any committee.
He was held in contempt of court for laughing, which was accurate and unwise.
A contemptuous glance at the proposal was the only feedback ever received.
Contemptible earns the scorn; contemptuous delivers it.

contend.definition: to assert; to compete or struggle
sentences: She contends that the data were misread, and three replications now agree.
Four teams contended for a title that was decided by weather.

contention.definition: an assertion in an argument; dispute
sentences: His central contention survived the review; his evidence did not.
The border remained a point of contention for two centuries and one afternoon of talks.

contentious.definition: causing or likely to cause argument
sentences: The most contentious clause was three words long.
A contentious colleague can make even the coffee order a constitutional matter.
The forty-eight contiguous states leave Alaska and Hawaii permanently in the footnote.
Their offices were contiguous, and they communicated exclusively by email.
Funding was contingent on results that required the funding to produce.
Every plan was contingent on a ferry that ran when it felt like it.

contract.definition: to shrink; to acquire an illness
sentences: Metal contracts in the cold, which is why the bridge sings in January.
He contracted a fever abroad and a lifelong distrust of buffet tables.
Blake believed contraries were necessary: without opposition there is no progression.
The two policies were contraries dressed in the same vocabulary.

contravene.definition: to violate a law or rule
sentences: The sale contravened a statute that everyone had assumed was repealed.
To contravene is to go against, in the literal Latin sense of walking the other way.
A small contretemps over seating consumed the first hour of the summit.
The contretemps at the buffet was later described in three memoirs, differently.
He looked contrite until the cameras left the room.
A contrite apology names the harm; the other kind names the misunderstanding.
The statement offered explanations where contrition was expected.
Contrition is measured in changed behavior, never in adjectives.
She contrived to be seated next to the one person who could sign the check.
He contrived a solution from two paperclips and a genuinely dangerous amount of confidence.
The ending was contrived: three coincidences arriving in a single afternoon.
His contrived spontaneity took two assistants and a schedule.
The contumacious witness was fined daily and enjoyed every minute of it.
Contumacious silence in court is expensive and, occasionally, principled.
The report listed contusions, a sprain, and a strong opinion about the referee.
Contusion is what medicine calls a bruise when it wants to be paid more.
The conundrum was scheduling: everyone was free at exactly no common hour.
A riddle has an answer; a conundrum has a committee.
He convalesced for six weeks and wrote the best chapter of his career.
The company convalesced slowly, one quiet quarter at a time.
The convalescent patient was ordered to rest and immediately reorganized the ward's library.
A convalescent economy still walks with a stick.

convention.definition: an accepted custom, or a large assembly
sentences: Convention required a black tie; the invitation required nothing of the sort.
The convention filled four hotels and produced one memorable sentence.
The conventional wisdom was wrong for six years and then, briefly, right.
A conventional solution nobody argues with beats a brilliant one nobody adopts.

converge.definition: to come together from different directions
sentences: Three independent methods converged on the same number, which is how facts get made.
The roads converge at a roundabout that has defeated two generations of drivers.
Conversant in four languages and fluent in none, he traveled cheerfully anyway.
She was conversant with the regulations and openly contemptuous of them.
Cheap credit fuels growth; conversely, its withdrawal ends the party abruptly.
He hated crowds and, conversely, could not bear an empty house.

conversion.definition: a change from one form or belief to another
sentences: The conversion of the mill into flats took three years and one heroic architect.
His conversion to caution came directly after a very expensive lesson.

conviction.definition: a firm belief; a formal guilty verdict
sentences: He argued with the conviction of a man who had not checked.
The conviction was overturned after eleven years and one persistent journalist.

convince.definition: to cause someone to believe something
sentences: Data convinced nobody; one anecdote convinced everyone.
He convinced himself first, which is always the hardest audience to leave.
The convivial dinner ran four hours and settled nothing on the agenda.
Convivial comes from living together — the word was always about the table.

convoke.definition: to call together for a meeting
sentences: The dean convoked the faculty at short notice, which itself announced bad news.
Parliaments are convoked, and occasionally regret answering.

convoluted.definition: extremely complex and difficult to follow
sentences: The plot was so convoluted that the actors kept a chart backstage.
Convoluted rules protect whoever wrote them.
She took copious notes and could never find the one line she needed.
Copious evidence, poorly organized, loses to one clear page.
Relations stayed cordial, which is diplomatic for nobody has shouted yet.
A cordial greeting from someone who has just read your review is a small miracle.
The archive was a cornucopia of misfiled letters and one forgotten treaty.
The horn of plenty came from a goat that fed the infant Zeus, which seems a raw deal.
A corollary of open data is that mistakes become public property.
Fame's corollary is a mailbox nobody can answer.
The ghost story works because the footprints are stubbornly corporeal.
His corporeal needs were three coffees and a chair by the window.
The corpulent cat refused every diet and outlived two veterinarians.
Corpulent is the polite word, which is why it appears in wills and portraits.
Ice cream sales correlate with drownings, and neither causes the other.
The two datasets correlate beautifully and explain nothing.
A parking ticket corroborated an alibi that nobody had believed.
One witness asserts; two corroborate; three usually contradict each other.

corrosion.definition: gradual destruction, especially by chemical action
sentences: Corrosion had eaten the bolts, and the inspection had been scheduled for next spring.
The slow corrosion of trust rarely announces itself until something falls.

cosmopolitan.definition: worldly; at home in many cultures
sentences: The port was cosmopolitan a century before the capital learned the word.
Cosmopolitan tastes and a provincial budget make for interesting weekends.
The team cosseted its star until he could no longer tolerate ordinary weather.
Cosset originally meant a lamb raised by hand, which explains the tone.
A cosseted childhood left him unprepared for a queue.
The cosseted prototype worked perfectly in a room built for it alone.
A coterie of six decided which poems the century would remember.
Every coterie thinks of itself as a movement.

coterminous.definition: having the same boundaries or duration
sentences: The parish and the county were coterminous until a boundary review invented three exceptions.
His tenure was coterminous with the building's only functional decade.
The board would not countenance a delay, having already announced the date.
As a noun it means the face; as a verb, keeping a straight one while permitting something.

counterintuitive.definition: contrary to what common sense suggests
sentences: The counterintuitive result held up: adding a road made the traffic worse.
Most good advice sounds counterintuitive until you have paid for the alternative.
Headquarters countermanded the order four hours after the trucks had left.
One phone call countermanded a policy three departments had spent a year drafting.

counterpoint.definition: a contrasting element that sets off another
sentences: Her steady prose is the counterpoint to a story that would otherwise be hysterical.
In music, counterpoint is two melodies refusing to yield and somehow agreeing.

counterproductive.definition: having the opposite of the intended effect
sentences: Banning the book was counterproductive: it sold out in a week.
Working eighty hours became counterproductive somewhere around hour fifty.

court.definition: to seek favor or invite something risky
sentences: The airline courted controversy with an advertisement it withdrew in six hours.
He courted investors for a year and disaster in a single afternoon.
The covert operation was described in three memoirs before it was declassified.
Covert hostility in a meeting is far more efficient than the open kind.

covet.definition: to desire something belonging to another
sentences: He coveted the corner office and got it just as the building was sold.
The commandment against coveting is the only one about a feeling.
The crowd was not cowed by the threat and arrived the next day in greater numbers.
He tried to cow the intern, who cited the handbook back at him.
The dog cowered at thunder and hunted wild boar without hesitation.
They cowered behind procedure rather than make a decision.
The company was coy about the launch date and precise about the price.
A coy answer is a refusal wearing a smile.
He cozened the old man out of a farm with a document and a fountain pen.
Cozen is what con artists did before the word "con" existed.

crabbed.definition: irritable; or cramped and hard to read
sentences: His crabbed handwriting hid a generous mind and one very rude marginal note.
A crabbed reply to a friendly email costs more than it saves.
The chair showed craft in every joint and no imagination whatsoever.
Craft cuts both ways: witchcraft and handicraft share the same word.
A crafty amendment buried the exemption in a definition.
The crafty raccoon defeated three locks and one engineer.
The craven retreat was described in the minutes as "a strategic pause."
Craven silence when it mattered is remembered longer than any speech.

credence.definition: belief in or acceptance of something
sentences: The photograph lent credence to a story nobody had believed for thirty years.
Give no credence to a rumor whose source improves with each telling.
Credibility takes a decade to build and one press conference to spend.
The witness lost all credibility over a detail about a bus timetable.
The threat was credible enough to close the airport for four hours.
A credible denial requires details; a guilty one requires adjectives.
A creditable third place, given that half the team had food poisoning.
Creditable means good enough to mention and not good enough to celebrate.

credo.definition: a statement of beliefs or guiding principles
sentences: "Measure twice" was his entire credo, and it built forty houses.
The company credo was printed on mugs and contradicted in every meeting.

credulity.definition: readiness to believe on flimsy evidence
sentences: The scheme relied on credulity and a very convincing letterhead.
The plot twist strains credulity past the point of politeness.
A credulous audience is worth more to a fraud than a rich one.
Credulous means you believe; incredulous means you cannot — one letter, opposite people.

crescendo.definition: a gradual increase toward a peak
sentences: The complaints reached a crescendo the week the elevator finally stopped entirely.
Purists insist a crescendo is the rise, not the peak, and lose that argument daily.
He returned crestfallen from an interview that had gone, he thought, brilliantly.
The image is a bird's crest collapsing — disappointment with feathers.
Ferns grew from a crevice in the wall where nothing should survive.
Every crevice in the argument was probed, and one of them opened.

crew.definition: a group working together, especially on a vessel
sentences: The crew mutinied over food, which is how most mutinies actually start.
A film crew of eighty people waited four hours for one cloud.

crone.definition: a withered old woman, often in folklore
sentences: The fairy tale's crone gives the best advice and is always ignored.
Folklore keeps the crone; history keeps her herbal knowledge under someone else's name.

croon.definition: to sing or speak softly and sentimentally
sentences: He crooned to the engine as though flattery might restart it.
Microphones made crooning possible; before them, singers had to shout.

cryptic.definition: having a hidden or obscure meaning
sentences: The cryptic note said "check the second drawer," and there were nine drawers.
Cryptic crosswords are a national pastime for people who enjoy being insulted by a newspaper.
The plan crystallized on a napkin in a station café at midnight.
Vague unease crystallized into a specific fear when the auditor asked for the second file.

culminate.definition: to reach a climax or final stage
sentences: Twenty years of work culminated in a paper that four people read carefully.
The festival culminates in a bonfire that the fire service watches nervously.
The inquiry established culpability at every level and consequences at none.
Culpability is shared easily and admitted rarely.
The report found the contractor culpable and the supervisor merely unlucky.
Culpable negligence is carelessness the law decided to take personally.
A cultured voice and a savage opinion make a memorable dinner guest.
The cultured pearl is real, grown deliberately — which is also true of most cultured people.
The cumbersome approval process took six weeks to say no.
Early mobile phones were cumbersome enough to double as weapons.
A cunning clause let either party withdraw and only one party knew it.
The cunning fox of fables would, in reality, mostly like to be left alone.
Cupidity, not need, emptied the pension fund.
The word comes from Cupid, whose arrows apparently also hit wallets.
A single tax curbed a habit that four campaigns had failed to touch.
Curb your enthusiasm until the contract is signed.
The office curmudgeon was also the only one who read the safety manual.
Every curmudgeon believes the world got worse the year he stopped enjoying it.
A cursory glance missed the clause that later cost two million.
Cursory shares a root with "course": the eye runs over the page without stopping.
The trip was curtailed by weather and one extremely persuasive harbormaster.
Rights are rarely abolished; they are curtailed, quietly, in appendices.
He was too cynical to be surprised and too curious to stop investigating.
The original Cynics were philosophers who lived in barrels; the modern kind live on committees.

dais.definition: a raised platform for a speaker or seat of honor
sentences: The guests on the dais could see everything and hear almost nothing.
A dais raises the speaker eighteen inches and the stakes considerably.

dalliance.definition: a brief casual romance or idle dawdling
sentences: A brief dalliance with modern art left him with two canvases and no explanation.
The dalliance cost him a marriage and a rather good house.

damp.definition: to dull or lessen the force of
sentences: The rain damped the crowd's enthusiasm without reducing its size.
Good springs damp the shock; bad news damps everything else.
The dapper little man in the corner turned out to own the entire building.
Dapper at seventy, he still had his shoes made by the same shop.
The size of the archive daunted three researchers and delighted the fourth.
Nothing daunted her except the telephone.
The reading list was daunting until she realized half of it was footnotes.
A daunting task shrinks the moment somebody starts it in front of you.

dawdle.definition: to waste time; to move slowly
sentences: He dawdled over the first page for a week and wrote the rest in two days.
Children dawdle on the way to school and sprint home, which is a whole philosophy.
There was no dearth of opinions and a striking dearth of evidence.
The word is a cousin of "dear": scarcity is what makes things expensive.
The launch was a debacle: two crashes, one apology, and a resignation by Friday.
Every debacle has a moment where somebody could have said stop.

debase.definition: to lower in quality, value, or dignity
sentences: Rome debased its coinage until the silver was mostly optimism.
He debased the award by giving it to donors.
A debased currency buys the same bread at four times the price.
The debased version of the story kept the scandal and lost the point.
A weekend of debauchery cost him a job he had wanted for six years.
The emperor's debauchery is better documented than his administration, which is unfair to both.
A debilitating fever kept her from the trial she had spent two years preparing.
Debilitating doubt is harder to treat than any of the certainties it replaces.
Debonair in a borrowed jacket, he talked his way into the reception.
The word once meant "of good disposition" and has since acquired a tuxedo.

debunk.definition: to expose as false or exaggerated
sentences: The myth was debunked in 1957 and appears in three textbooks printed last year.
Debunking travels at half the speed of the claim it corrects.

debutante.definition: a young woman formally entering society
sentences: The debutante ball survived two wars and finally died of embarrassment.
She was presented as a debutante in June and was organizing a strike by October.
Every generation diagnoses decadence in the one that follows it.
The empire's decadence was described enthusiastically by historians who had never visited.

decadent.definition: self-indulgent to the point of moral decline
sentences: A decadent dessert menu is a marketing category; a decadent age is a verdict.
The decadent poets took the insult as a name and wore it beautifully.
A jet at takeoff reaches 140 decibels, which is the point where sound becomes injury.
Decibels are logarithmic: ten more is ten times the energy, not ten percent more noise.

decimate.definition: to destroy a large portion of
sentences: The blight decimated the orchards and the argument about the word decimate.
Roman legions decimated mutinous units by killing one man in ten, chosen by lot.

decimation.definition: destruction of a large part of something
sentences: The decimation of the fishery took nine years and one very efficient trawler design.
Decimation of the archive was accidental, which made it no less permanent.

decipher.definition: to make out the meaning of something obscure
sentences: It took nine months to decipher a shopping list written in shorthand.
Linear B was deciphered by an architect in his spare time, which infuriated the professionals.
He declaimed against the budget for forty minutes and voted for it.
Declaiming is what speaking becomes when the speaker can hear himself.
The path ended in a declivity too steep for the cart and too long to carry.
Acclivity goes up, declivity goes down, and both are usually called "the hill."
A decorous silence followed the announcement, broken by one very audible laugh.
Decorous behavior at a funeral is a performance everybody agrees to give.
Decorum required a black tie; the emergency required running.
Parliamentary decorum forbids calling someone a liar, so members have invented forty phrases meaning it.

decree.definition: an official order with legal force
sentences: The decree arrived by fax and abolished a department of two hundred.
By decree the calendar lost eleven days, and riots followed over the missing time.
Editorials decried the decision all week and none proposed an alternative.
He decried waste in a speech that cost forty thousand to stage.

deduce.definition: to reach a conclusion by reasoning
sentences: From a tan line and a train ticket she deduced the whole holiday.
Holmes claimed to deduce; usually he was inferring, which is less impressive and more useful.
The letter was deemed inappropriate by a committee that never quite said why.
What one century deems genius the next deems a phase.
Someone defaced the portrait with a mustache that historians now defend as period-appropriate.
Defacing a banknote is illegal, which has stopped precisely nobody.

default.definition: failure to fulfill an obligation; a preset option
sentences: The country's default in 2001 rewrote every textbook chapter on sovereign debt.
Nobody changes the default setting, which is why defaults are the most powerful design decision.

defer.definition: to postpone, or to yield to another's judgment
sentences: They deferred the decision twice and inherited it a third time, unchanged.
She deferred to the surgeon on medicine and to nobody at all on grammar.
Out of deference to the family, the report withheld two names.
Deference to expertise is wisdom; deference to seniority is often just furniture.
His deferential manner disappeared the moment the contract was signed.
A deferential junior asks the question everyone senior was afraid to.
She deflected the question with a joke and answered a different one entirely.
The shield deflected the blow; the argument deflected the blame.
A small grant defrayed the travel and none of the actual research.
Ticket sales defrayed about a third of what the festival cost.
A deft edit removed two hundred words and improved every remaining one.
Deft hands and a bad temper made him the best and least popular repairman in town.
The deftness of her reply left the interviewer with nowhere to go.
Deftness looks like ease and is made entirely of repetition.

degrade.definition: to reduce in quality, status, or dignity
sentences: Plastic degrades over centuries, which is a fact best considered before opening the packet.
The policy degraded the service and was reported as an efficiency.
Fans deified the coach in October and demanded his dismissal in March.
Rome deified emperors after death, which was cheaper than doing so while they lived.

deign.definition: to do something considered beneath one's dignity
sentences: He finally deigned to answer the email, three weeks and one lawsuit later.
She did not deign to reply, which was itself an eloquent reply.
The verdict dejected everyone except the lawyer, who had planned for it.
Nothing dejects a team faster than a leader who has already given up.

delegate.definition: to entrust a task to another
sentences: He could not delegate, so he worked eighty hours and everyone else worked twenty.
Delegate the task, not the blame.
The deleterious effects showed up eight years after the product was discontinued.
Constant interruption is more deleterious to thought than outright noise.
The jury deliberated for nine days over evidence that took two hours to present.
As an adjective it means intentional; as a verb, taking your time about it.

delicacy.definition: fineness or tact; a choice food
sentences: The matter required delicacy, so naturally it was handled by memo.
One country's delicacy is another's evidence of something having gone badly wrong.
The treaty delimited the border and left the river to change its mind annually.
First delimit the question, or the answer will keep growing.
The memo delineated four responsibilities and assigned all of them to one person.
She delineated the character in three sentences and the plot never caught up.
The delusion that everyone reads the appendix has ruined many careful reports.
A delusion held by one person is madness; held by a crowd, it is a market.

delve.definition: to research or dig into deeply
sentences: She delved into the parish records and emerged with an entirely different family.
Delve first meant to dig with a spade, which research still resembles.

demagogue.definition: a leader who exploits popular fears
sentences: A demagogue offers a villain where a statesman offers a budget.
The word means "leader of the people," which is how every demagogue introduces himself.

demarcate.definition: to mark boundaries or separate clearly
sentences: A single hedge demarcated two counties, three parishes, and one very long feud.
Science and pseudoscience are hard to demarcate, which is why philosophers still have jobs.
He would not demean himself by answering the accusation, which everyone read as guilt.
The job did not demean her; the way it was described did.

demonstrable.definition: able to be proven or shown
sentences: A demonstrable improvement in three metrics is worth more than a compelling story.
The claim was demonstrable, which is why nobody bothered demonstrating it.
He was undemonstrative for sixty years and wept openly at a dog's funeral.
A demonstrative greeting from a colleague usually means bad news is close behind.
Nothing demoralizes a team like watching a good idea die in committee.
The siege was designed to demoralize rather than destroy, which took longer and cost less.
She demurred at the price and accepted the terms.
He demurred, coughed, and then agreed to everything anyway.
Her demure reply concealed the fact that she had already bought the company.
Demure in public and ferocious in committee, she got everything she asked for.

denigrate.definition: to criticize unfairly; to blacken a reputation
sentences: He denigrated the work publicly and borrowed its method quietly.
The Latin root means to blacken, which is exactly what the gossip was for.
A red flag on the beach denotes danger; a red face denotes something else entirely.
Words denote their dictionary meaning and connote everything they have been used for.

denouement.definition: the final resolution of a plot
sentences: The denouement explained everything and satisfied nobody.
French for "untying": the plot is a knot, and the denouement undoes it.
He denounced the deal from the podium and signed a version of it in June.
To denounce is to condemn with an audience present; without one it is just grumbling.

dense.definition: thick and compact; hard to understand
sentences: The chapter is dense in the good way: nothing wasted, everything load-bearing.
Dense fog and dense prose share the property of hiding what is directly ahead.

deportment.definition: the way a person behaves or carries themselves
sentences: Her deportment under cross-examination impressed the jury more than her answers.
Schools once graded deportment, which was a polite word for sitting still.

depose.definition: to remove from office; to testify under oath
sentences: The king was deposed by a committee that met in a stable.
She was deposed for eleven hours and contradicted herself twice.
Every new medium has been accused of depraving the young, from novels to radio.
The censor claimed the play would deprave audiences who had already read the book.
The court described the crime's depravity in language usually reserved for weather.
Depravity requires effort; ordinary selfishness manages fine on its own.

deprecate.definition: to express disapproval of; to belittle
sentences: He deprecated his own contribution so persistently that people believed him.
Programmers deprecate a feature to warn you it is about to disappear.

depredation.definition: an act of plundering or destruction
sentences: Centuries of depredation left the temple with three columns and a very good story.
The depredations of damp did more damage to the library than any war.
The derelict warehouse became flats, then a landmark, then flats again.
Derelict in his duty, the guard had been asleep for the entire robbery.
Critics derided the design for a decade and now call it visionary.
It is easy to deride an idea and hard to build a better one.
The proposal was met with derision and adopted, quietly, four years later.
Derision is the cheapest form of criticism and the hardest to answer.
A derisive snort from the back row ended the presentation early.
The derisive nickname stuck for thirty years and outlived everyone who had meant it unkindly.
The album is derivative, competent, and completely unnecessary.
Every style looks derivative until enough time passes to call it a tradition.

derive.definition: to obtain or trace from a source
sentences: Half the vocabulary derives from Latin and pretends otherwise.
She derives more satisfaction from the footnotes than from the argument.
The figure is derived, not measured, which the headline declined to mention.
A derived unit like the newton is built from ones you can actually feel.
A derogative aside in the margin was the only comment the manuscript received.
The nickname was derogative in 1890 and is now printed on the school crest.

descry.definition: to catch sight of something distant
sentences: From the tower they descried a sail an hour before it mattered.
One can descry, in the early drafts, the shape of the book it became.

desecrate.definition: to treat something sacred with disrespect
sentences: The tomb was desecrated by looters who left the gold and took the inscriptions.
To desecrate is to undo a consecration, which apparently takes far less time.
The wind desiccated the topsoil until the fields simply blew away.
Bureaucracy can desiccate a good idea without ever formally rejecting it.
The desiccated flower fell out of the book intact after ninety years.
His prose was accurate, thorough, and desiccated past the point of readability.
Speed was desirable; accuracy was the desideratum.
The great desideratum of the field is a dataset nobody has yet been willing to fund.
Despair arrives quietly, usually disguised as being realistic.
He was the despair of his teachers and the delight of his readers.
He did it in despite of every instruction he had been given.
Now almost always a preposition, despite once meant the contempt itself.

despoil.definition: to plunder or strip of possessions
sentences: The coast was despoiled by developers who named the streets after what they removed.
Armies despoil; committees merely deplete.
History remembers the despoiler and forgets the archivist who saved the rest.
Every despoiler of a landscape has a brochure explaining why it was necessary.

despot.definition: a ruler with absolute, oppressive power
sentences: The despot built a road, a dam, and nine thousand statues of himself.
Enlightened despot is a term historians use when the roads were good.
The department was run on despotic lines by a man with no formal authority whatsoever.
Despotic rule is efficient right up until the succession.
He died destitute in a rented room and is now on the currency.
The argument was destitute of evidence and rich in adjectives.
A desultory search of the attic turned up three lamps and no will.
The word comes from a circus rider leaping between horses — motion without a route.
Her detached account of the disaster was the only readable one published that year.
A surgeon must be detached; a witness usually cannot manage it.
He described his own bankruptcy with the detachment of a weather report.
Detachment is a virtue in a judge and a warning sign in a friend.

detente.definition: an easing of hostility between rivals
sentences: The detente lasted four years and one particularly badly worded press release.
Detente between the two departments began, as usual, with a shared enemy.
Higher fines deterred nobody; visible enforcement deterred everybody.
Rain deterred the fair-weather protesters and revealed who was serious.
Postcode remains the strongest determinant of outcomes, which is an indictment of everything else.
The determinant was not talent but timing, as it usually is.
The lock is not a deterrent to a professional and works fine on everyone else.
The best deterrent is the belief you will be caught, not the size of the penalty.

detraction.definition: the act of belittling or disparaging
sentences: The review was three columns of detraction and one grudging final line.
Detraction subtracts: the word admits exactly what it does.
The delay was detrimental to the patient and convenient for the schedule.
Detrimental effects appear in the appendix; benefits appear on the cover.
Sociologists study deviance and discover mostly that societies enjoy defining it.
Yesterday's deviance is today's subculture and tomorrow's advertisement.

deviate.definition: to depart from an established course
sentences: The pilot deviated from the route by six miles and avoided the storm entirely.
He never deviated from the recipe, which is why the cake was never memorable.
A deviation of two degrees put the ship on the wrong side of the island.
Standard deviation measures how much reality wanders from its own average.

device.definition: a tool, or a scheme or technique
sentences: The unreliable narrator is a device, not an accident.
Left to his own devices, he built a boat in the garden and never sailed it.

devolve.definition: to transfer power downward; to degenerate
sentences: Powers devolved to the regions and the budget stayed exactly where it was.
The debate devolved into an argument about who had said what in 2011.
The puzzle was diabolic: solvable, elegant, and designed to waste your evening.
A diabolic plan requires a level of organization most villains cannot sustain.
The weather was diabolical, the pitch was worse, and the match went ahead anyway.
His diabolical timing meant the resignation landed during the annual gala.
The diadem was sold in 1923 and bought back by the museum for forty times the price.
A diadem signals sovereignty; a hat signals weather.
Diaphanous curtains turned the harsh afternoon into something almost kind.
Her argument was diaphanous: you could see straight through it, beautifully.
The letter began as a correction and became a diatribe by the second page.
A diatribe convinces nobody and relieves the author enormously.

dichotomy.definition: a division into two opposed parts
sentences: The nature-versus-nurture dichotomy has survived a century of evidence that it is false.
Most dichotomies are arguments that stopped looking for a third option.
Geography dictated the route long before engineers were consulted.
He dictated terms to a room that had already decided to refuse them.
His dictatorial editing produced a superb magazine and a permanent staffing crisis.
Dictatorial leadership works until somebody has to think without being told.
The old dictum that form follows function has been quoted by everyone who ignores it.
A judge's dictum is not binding, which does not stop lawyers from citing it.
The novel is didactic to the point of lecturing, and it sold four million copies.
Aesop is didactic; the fables survive anyway because the animals are funny.
Nothing differentiated the two proposals except the letterhead.
Wine experts can differentiate vintages; the rest of us can differentiate red from white.
Her diffidence in meetings hid a mind three steps ahead of the discussion.
Diffidence cost him the promotion; competence eventually got it back.
The diffident candidate answered brilliantly and apologized for doing so.
Diffident about his singing and fearless about everything else, he made an odd impression.
The argument is diffuse: good ideas scattered across sixty pages of throat-clearing.
Diffuse light flatters everyone, which is why photographers spend so much on it.

digress.definition: to depart from the main subject
sentences: He digressed for twenty minutes about a boat and somehow made the point better.
If I may digress — a sentence that guarantees the digression is already planned.

digression.definition: a temporary departure from the main topic
sentences: The book's best chapter is a digression about a bridge that never got built.
Two hours of digression left eleven minutes for the actual decision.
The dilapidated pier was condemned, photographed, and put on every postcard.
The Latin root involves stones falling off, which is exactly the image.

dilate.definition: to widen or expand; to speak at length
sentences: Pupils dilate in the dark and in the presence of someone you like, unhelpfully.
He dilated upon the subject until the audience dilated toward the exits.

dilatory.definition: tending to delay; slow to act
sentences: Dilatory tactics kept the case out of court for six years.
The dilatory reply arrived after the problem had solved itself.
A dilettante in six fields, he was interesting at dinner and useless on deadline.
The word once meant simply a lover of art; contempt was added later.
Diligent checking caught an error that would have cost a year's work.
The diligent student and the brilliant one meet at the same finish line, differently tired.
The diminutive conductor was invisible behind the score and audible three streets away.
A diminutive ending like "-let" makes a book a booklet and a pig a piglet.
The din of the market made conversation an act of shouting and faith.
Above the din, one voice asked the only useful question of the evening.
The dingy office produced the decade's most elegant mathematics.
One coat of paint took the room from dingy to merely plain.

dint.definition: force or means, as in "by dint of"
sentences: By dint of sheer repetition he learned every irregular verb in the language.
The word survives in one phrase and nowhere else, like a fossil in amber.

dirge.definition: a mournful song for the dead
sentences: The band played something between a dirge and a march, and nobody knew when to stand.
His victory speech had the cadence of a dirge, which the polls had predicted.

disabuse.definition: to free someone from a mistaken belief
sentences: Allow me to disabuse you of the notion that anyone reads the terms.
One week on the ward disabused him of every idea medical school had installed.
A disaffected faction leaked the memo and the leadership never recovered.
Disaffected voters do not switch sides; they stay home, which is worse.
Public disapprobation did more than any fine could have.
She met his explanation with silent disapprobation, which lasted the whole drive home.
It is hard to discern a pattern in four data points and very easy to invent one.
She discerned the forgery from the ink, not the brushwork.

discernible.definition: able to be perceived or recognized
sentences: There was no discernible difference between the two batches, which ended the lawsuit.
A faint but discernible improvement showed up in the third month.
A discerning reader will notice the second narrator halfway through chapter two.
"For the discerning buyer" is what catalogues say instead of "expensive."
One quiet question discomfited a speaker who had handled forty loud ones.
Discomfit once meant to defeat in battle, which explains its force.
There was a discomfiting pause before anyone agreed with him.
The most discomfiting reviews are the accurate ones.
It disconcerted him that the audience laughed in the wrong place and kept laughing.
Nothing disconcerts a liar like being asked to repeat the story backwards.

disconsolate.definition: unable to be comforted; deeply unhappy
sentences: The disconsolate team sat in the changing room for an hour without speaking.
He was disconsolate over a dog and composed at his own diagnosis.
Discord over one paragraph delayed a treaty for eleven months.
The apple of discord started a war, which is a lot to ask of fruit.
A discordant note in the third movement was, the composer insisted, deliberate.
The one discordant voice in the meeting turned out to be right.

discount.definition: to disregard or treat as unimportant
sentences: Investors discounted the warning because the warner had been early twice before.
Discount the first review and the last; the middle ones are usually honest.
Public discourse improved briefly when the comment section broke.
His discourse on bees lasted ninety minutes and converted three people to beekeeping.

discredit.definition: to damage the reputation or believability of
sentences: Rather than answer the study, they set out to discredit its author.
One fabricated detail discredited an otherwise accurate account.
A discreet cough from the doorway ended the argument instantly.
Discreet keeps the secret; discrete keeps things separate. The extra E hides.

discrepancy.definition: an inconsistency between facts or figures
sentences: A four-pound discrepancy in the accounts uncovered a decade of theft.
The discrepancy between the brochure and the building was visible from the road.
The process has four discrete stages, and everybody skips the second.
Digital means discrete: steps, not slopes.

discretion.definition: freedom to decide; good judgment in conduct
sentences: The fine is at the officer's discretion, which is another way of saying it depends.
Discretion is the better part of valor, said a character who was pretending to be dead.
The discretionary fund paid for whatever the director found interesting that year.
Discretionary spending is the first thing cut and the last thing missed.
The ear can discriminate between two notes a fraction apart and cannot describe how.
The same word covers fine judgment and gross injustice, which is a lesson in itself.
A discriminating palate can be a curse in an airport.
She was discriminating about books and cheerfully indiscriminate about films.

discursive.definition: rambling; moving from topic to topic
sentences: His discursive lectures wandered for an hour and landed, always, exactly on time.
A discursive footnote can be the best part of a dull book.

disdain.definition: contempt for something regarded as unworthy
sentences: Her disdain for small talk was legendary and slightly performative.
He looked at the spreadsheet with the disdain of a man who preferred paper.

disembark.definition: to go ashore from a ship or leave a vehicle
sentences: Four hundred passengers disembarked into a port with two taxis.
They disembarked at dawn and were lost by breakfast.

disenfranchise.definition: to deprive of a right, especially voting
sentences: The new rule disenfranchised thousands who owned no photo identification.
To disenfranchise quietly is easier than to argue openly.

disentangle.definition: to free from complication or knots
sentences: It took two accountants a month to disentangle the accounts from the excuses.
She disentangled the necklace and, in the same evening, herself from the engagement.

disgorge.definition: to discharge or give up unwillingly
sentences: The court ordered the bank to disgorge profits earned from the scheme.
The stadium disgorged sixty thousand people into a street built for two hundred.
Disheartened by the third rejection, he sent it to a fourth publisher out of spite.
The team looked disheartened at halftime and unrecognizable after it.

disillusion.definition: to free from a pleasant but false belief
sentences: A summer in the industry disillusioned her and improved her writing enormously.
Nobody thanks you for disillusioning them, however accurate you were.
It is disingenuous to call it a consultation when the decision was printed already.
The disingenuous apology apologized for the reaction, not the act.
Judicial disinterest is a requirement, not a personality trait.
The word is being lost to "boredom," and English is worse for it.

disinterested.definition: impartial; not influenced by personal stake
sentences: They needed a disinterested party, which ruled out everyone in the building.
Disinterested means fair; uninterested means asleep.
The disjointed testimony improved once the witness was allowed to sit down.
A disjointed film can be forgiven if any single scene is unforgettable.

dismiss.definition: to reject as unworthy of consideration
sentences: He dismissed the objection in a sentence and spent two years answering it.
The court dismissed the case; the newspapers did not.

disparage.definition: to belittle or speak slightingly of
sentences: He disparaged the method until his own results depended on it.
To disparage a rival's work is to advertise that you have read it.
The book joins disparate fields with a confidence no specialist would risk.
Two disparate datasets were merged, and the result meant nothing at all.

dispassionate.definition: calm and free of emotion or bias
sentences: A dispassionate account of the riot was published, and both sides called it hostile.
Dispassionate does not mean uncaring; it means the caring is not driving.

dispatch.definition: to send off promptly; to deal with quickly
sentences: She dispatched the correspondence in an hour and the difficult call in nine minutes.
The messenger was dispatched at dawn and arrived after the surrender.
A papal dispensation permitted the marriage and started a national schism.
He received a special dispensation to submit late, which everyone then requested.
The machine dispensed coffee, tea, and a liquid the label declined to name.
Let us dispense with the introductions and get to the disagreement.
The crowd dispersed after the rain arrived, having outlasted every argument.
Seeds disperse by wind, water, and the reliable carelessness of birds.
The team is dispersed across four time zones and meets, unhappily, at seven.
Dispersed populations preserve dialects that cities flatten in a generation.
Otters disport themselves in the current while everyone else works.
The word gave us "sport" after losing its first syllable somewhere in the fifteenth century.

disposition.definition: a person's usual temperament; an arrangement
sentences: A sunny disposition survives most things except an open-plan office.
The disposition of the troops was clever; the timing was not.
The most disquieting detail was how normal the office looked afterward.
A disquieting silence followed the question and answered it.

disquisition.definition: a long, formal discussion of a subject
sentences: His disquisition on medieval taxation lasted two hours and converted nobody.
The email opened with a disquisition and closed without a request.
Disregard the previous email, said the email that made everything worse.
He disregarded the warning label and became a statistic in someone's presentation.

dissemble.definition: to conceal one's true motives or feelings
sentences: He dissembled beautifully for an hour and gave himself away with a receipt.
To dissemble is to lie with your face rather than your words.

dissembler.definition: one who conceals true feelings or motives
sentences: The dissembler agreed with everyone in the room and reported all of them.
Every good dissembler is eventually undone by someone with a long memory.
The findings were disseminated by press release before the reviewers had finished.
The Latin root is sowing seed, which is optimistic about what gets spread online.
Her dissent ran twelve pages and became law twenty years later.
A body that tolerates no dissent will hear no warning either.
The dissident's essays circulated in carbon copies and outlasted the regime.
Yesterday's dissident is often on the next generation's stamps.
She dissimulated her disappointment so well that they offered her the job again.
Simulate is showing what isn't there; dissimulate is hiding what is.

dissipate.definition: to scatter and disappear; to squander
sentences: The tension dissipated the moment somebody laughed.
He dissipated a fortune in nine years and described each one as an investment.

dissolution.definition: the formal ending or breaking up of something
sentences: The dissolution of the partnership took longer than its entire productive life.
Parliament's dissolution sends everyone home to campaign for their own jobs.
Cognitive dissonance is what happens when belief and evidence share a room.
The dissonance in the opening bars was scandalous in 1913 and is a ringtone now.

distaff.definition: relating to women or the female side
sentences: The estate passed down the distaff line, which the lawyers found unusually complicated.
A distaff held wool for spinning, and the word came to stand for the women who held it.

distend.definition: to swell or expand from internal pressure
sentences: The balloon distended until the room went quiet in anticipation.
The budget distended year by year without ever being formally increased.

distill.definition: to extract the essential meaning of
sentences: He distilled forty pages into one paragraph and lost nothing but the throat-clearing.
Whiskey is distilled; so, occasionally, is wisdom, and both take years.

distinction.definition: a difference; or excellence and honor
sentences: The distinction between the two policies fits inside a comma.
She graduated with distinction and no idea what to do next.

distort.definition: to twist out of true shape or meaning
sentences: The headline distorted a careful finding into a confident prediction.
Heat distorted the rails, and the timetable followed.

distraught.definition: deeply agitated with worry or grief
sentences: The distraught owner searched three streets calling a cat that was asleep upstairs.
He was distraught for a week and functional throughout, which fooled everyone.
Distressed assets are bought by people who can afford to wait.
She sounded distressed on the phone and perfectly calm in person.
They dithered over the offer until it expired, which counted as a decision.
He dithered about the color for a month and painted it white.

diurnal.definition: occurring in the daytime or daily
sentences: Diurnal animals are simply the ones we happen to have met.
The diurnal rhythm of the office is coffee, complaint, and a brief burst of work.

diverge.definition: to move or differ in different directions
sentences: Their accounts diverge at exactly the point where the money moved.
