Two roads diverged, and the poem has been misread ever since.
Two divergent interpretations of the same clause reached opposite courts.
Divergent thinking generates options; someone else has to close the list.
A diversified portfolio is an admission that nobody knows which one will fail.
The diversified farm survived the year that ruined the specialists.
Funds were diverted to a project nobody could later name.
The magician diverted four hundred people with one hand while working with the other.

divest.definition: to rid oneself of; to sell off
sentences: The university divested from coal in 2018 and from the debate immediately after.
He divested himself of the title, the office, and every responsibility except the parking space.

divine.definition: to discover by intuition or guesswork
sentences: From two sentences of the memo she divined the entire reorganization.
Water diviners hold a stick and, reliably, find water where water usually is.
The proposal was divorced from any budget anyone recognized.
His theory is elegant and entirely divorced from what happens in a kitchen.
He would not divulge the source and spent eleven weeks in a cell for it.
The letter divulged nothing and implied a great deal.
The docile horse became a different animal at the sound of a plastic bag.
A docile committee approves everything and notices nothing.

doctrinaire.definition: rigidly attached to a theory regardless of practicality
sentences: The doctrinaire approach worked in the model and starved the actual town.
He was doctrinaire in print and remarkably practical at home.

document.definition: to record in detail with evidence
sentences: She documented every conversation, which is why she still has a career.
The species was documented once, in 1904, by someone who lost the specimen.

documentary.definition: based on documents or factual record
sentences: The claim has no documentary support beyond a photograph of a photograph.
Documentary evidence beats confident memory in every courtroom on earth.

doff.definition: to take off, especially a hat
sentences: He doffed his cap to the funeral procession and put it back on, carefully.
Doff is "do off" and don is "do on" — English at its laziest and most efficient.
The rumor dogged him through three jobs and two countries.
Injuries dogged the season from the second week onward.
Dogged reporting over four years brought down a minister and a filing system.
Dogged persistence is talent's most reliable substitute.
The card contained six lines of doggerel and one genuinely moving postscript.
Doggerel survives longer than good poetry because it is easier to remember.

dogma.definition: a principle laid down as unquestionably true
sentences: What began as a working hypothesis had hardened into dogma by the third edition.
Dogma is a belief that has stopped taking questions.
He was dogmatic about grammar and cheerfully vague about everything expensive.
The most dogmatic voice in the room is rarely the best informed.
The dog's doleful expression secured a second dinner within minutes.
A doleful trumpet at a wedding suggested the band had opinions.
The dolorous bells rang for an hour, which was three minutes of dignity and fifty-seven of noise.
Her dolorous letters improved dramatically after she got a dog.
The volcano is dormant, a word geologists use to mean "not today."
The dispute lay dormant for eight years and resumed at exactly the same sentence.

dormer.definition: a window projecting from a sloping roof
sentences: Two dormers turned an attic into a bedroom and doubled the house's price.
Dormer comes from sleeping: the window belongs to a bedroom by definition.
In his dotage he confused decades but recited the entire Aeneid.
The family called it dotage; the doctors used a longer word and a worse prognosis.
She doted on the youngest and was fair to the rest, which nobody believed.
They doted on the cat with a devotion the cat received as its due.
Her findings dovetailed with his so precisely that reviewers suspected collaboration.
The joint is named for a bird's tail, and it holds without a single nail.
She dressed dowdy on purpose, having learned what being noticed cost her.
The dowdy little building housed the most expensive art in the county.
The draconian penalties for late returns emptied the library rather than filled it.
Draco's Athenian code punished stealing a cabbage with death, and lent his name to every harsh law since.
By midnight only the dregs of the conference remained, arguing about fonts.
He drank the dregs and pretended, loudly, to enjoy them.

droll.definition: amusing in an odd, dry way
sentences: His droll account of the disaster made everyone laugh and nobody feel better.
A droll remark delivered without a smile is the most efficient joke available.
He earned the dubious honor of being cited most often as a warning.
The dubious expression on her face preceded the objection by a full minute.
The dulcet tones of the announcer failed to make the delay any shorter.
Dulcet shares a root with "dolce": it is sugar for the ear.
Two museums were duped by the same forger using the same catalogue trick.
He was duped by a website whose only flaw was a missing letter in the address.
The duplicitous memo praised the team it was quietly recommending be dissolved.
Duplicitous behavior needs a good memory, which is why most of it fails.
The duplicity was not in what he said but in what he let everyone assume.
Duplicity means twofold: one face for you and one for the room next door.
A confession signed under duress is worth precisely nothing in court.
He claimed duress; the emails suggested enthusiasm.
A dutiful phone call every Sunday for thirty years, never once a minute late.
Dutiful applause is distinguishable from real applause by its punctuality.

dwell.definition: to linger on a subject; to reside
sentences: Do not dwell on the error, said the man who had dwelt on it for nine years.
They dwelt in one room and told the story as if it had been an adventure.
A dwindling audience is quieter than an angry one and much worse.
Dwindling reserves forced a decision three governments had deferred.
The office dynamo organized two conferences and one wedding in a single quarter.
The word borrowed from generators, which is fair: both convert motion into output.
His dyspeptic reviews were feared, quoted, and secretly enjoyed by their victims.
Dyspeptic literally means bad digestion, which explains a great deal of criticism.
His earnest defense of the project was more persuasive than any of its data.
Earnest students ask questions; brilliant ones ask the same question twice.
Support ebbed quietly over two years and vanished in a single vote.
The tide ebbs whether or not the argument on the beach has finished.
Ebullient after the result, he offered to buy dinner for forty people.
The word means boiling over, which is exactly what such moods do to a room.
An eccentric millionaire left his fortune to a cat and his letters to a university.
Eccentric means off-center; the rich get called eccentric and the poor get called something else.

echelon.definition: a level or rank within an organization
sentences: Decisions made in the upper echelons arrived downstairs as weather.
She reached the highest echelon and found the view mostly of meetings.

eclectic.definition: drawing from a wide variety of sources
sentences: His eclectic library held medieval theology beside a manual for outboard motors.
An eclectic playlist is either sophisticated or unfinished, depending on the guests.
Her second novel eclipsed the first so thoroughly that reprints changed the cover.
The scandal eclipsed a genuinely important reform announced the same morning.
His prose is economical: no sentence carries a passenger.
He was economical with the truth, which is the polite phrase for lying.

economy.definition: efficient use of resources; a financial system
sentences: The film's economy is astonishing: ninety minutes, four sets, one idea.
False economy is saving eleven pounds now and spending nine hundred in March.

edict.definition: an official order issued by authority
sentences: The edict banned the practice on Monday and was quietly unenforced by Thursday.
One edict from the head office ended twenty years of local custom.

edifice.definition: a large imposing building or system
sentences: The whole legal edifice rests on a statute nobody has read since 1961.
The edifice took forty years to build and eleven seconds to fall.
The lecture was designed to edify and succeeded mainly in emptying the room.
Edify shares a root with edifice: it is building, but for the mind.
The scandal was not edifying, though everyone found it educational.
An edifying book and an enjoyable one occasionally arrive in the same volume.
Her self-effacing introduction understated a career of considerable brilliance.
Time is effacing the inscription faster than the conservators can read it.
Her effervescence survived a nine-hour flight and two cancelled connections.
The wine lost its effervescence, and the party its point, at roughly the same hour.
The effervescent host kept a difficult table talking for four hours.
Effervescent charm is exhausting to sustain and instantly missed when it stops.
He dismissed the whole department as effete, having failed twice to join it.
An effete aristocracy is the standard villain of every revolution's pamphlets.
The treatment proved efficacious in trials and unaffordable in practice.
A short, efficacious rule beats a long, admirable one.

efficacy.definition: the power to produce a desired result
sentences: Efficacy is what a drug does in the trial; effectiveness is what it does in the world.
The policy's efficacy was assumed rather than measured for eleven years.

effigy.definition: a crude likeness used for mockery
sentences: He was burned in effigy in three towns and re-elected in all of them.
The effigy on the tomb shows him younger, thinner, and considerably kinder.
An effluvium from the drains ended the garden party twenty minutes early.
Victorians blamed disease on effluvium and were wrong about the mechanism, right about the drains.
He had the effrontery to ask for a reference from the man he had sued.
Effrontery is nerve with the shame removed.
The effulgence of the stained glass at four o'clock is the reason people still visit.
Her reputation's effulgence dimmed the moment the archives opened.
The effusive praise in the introduction made the review that followed even crueler.
Effusive thanks for a small favor usually signals a larger one coming.
The egalitarian seating plan lasted until the seniority question arose over dessert.
Egalitarian in principle and hierarchical in practice describes most institutions.
The egotist listened just long enough to find a way back to himself.
An egoist believes in self-interest; an egotist merely talks about himself.
An egregious error on page one survived four rounds of proofreading.
The word once meant outstandingly good, which shows how quickly praise can sour.

egress.definition: a way out; the act of leaving
sentences: Barnum labeled a door "This Way to the Egress," and crowds paid to leave.
The building has one egress for four hundred people, which the inspector underlined.
The elaborate seating plan took a week and was abandoned on the night.
An elaborate excuse is less believable than a short one, and takes longer.
Elated by the acceptance, she reread the email eleven times looking for a catch.
The team was elated for four days and back in training on the fifth.

elegiac.definition: mournful; expressing sorrow for something lost
sentences: The film's elegiac tone mourns a town that is still, technically, inhabited.
His elegiac final chapter reads like a goodbye to a discipline, not a subject.

elegy.definition: a mournful poem, especially for the dead
sentences: Gray's Elegy took seven years to write and about seven minutes to read.
The article was less a report than an elegy for a shuttered factory.
An elementary mistake in the second line invalidated forty pages of algebra.
Holmes never actually said "elementary, my dear Watson," which is elementary trivia.

elevate.definition: to raise in rank, quality, or position
sentences: A single essay elevated her from contributor to the person everyone quoted.
Good lighting elevates a mediocre room the way an accent elevates a mediocre argument.

elicit.definition: to draw out a response or information
sentences: The question elicited a longer silence than any answer would have filled.
Elicit draws out; illicit is illegal. One letter separates the interview from the crime.
The complaint that the museum was elitist was made in a members-only lounge.
Elitist standards and open doors are not actually incompatible, whatever both sides claim.

ellipsis.definition: the omission of words; the three-dot mark
sentences: The quotation used an ellipsis to remove the word "not," which changed everything.
Ellipsis in speech is why "coming?" is a complete sentence.
His eloquence won the debate and cost him the friendship it was aimed at.
There is an eloquence in a well-timed silence that no speech matches.
Her eloquent two minutes changed a vote that four reports had not moved.
The empty chair at the table was eloquent enough without anybody explaining it.
One diagram elucidated what three pages of prose had thoroughly hidden.
He was asked to elucidate and produced a second, longer mystery.

elude.definition: to escape or evade, physically or mentally
sentences: The name eluded her for two days and arrived, unbidden, in the shower.
He eluded capture for nine years by being extremely boring.

elusive.definition: hard to find, catch, or define
sentences: The elusive particle was predicted in 1964 and photographed, so to speak, in 2012.
Happiness is elusive mostly because people keep checking whether they have it.
Two weeks of elysian weather ended the moment the tourists arrived.
The Elysian Fields were the Greek afterlife for heroes, which sets a high bar for a holiday.

emaciate.definition: to make abnormally thin and weak
sentences: Drought emaciated the herds within a single season.
Endless cuts emaciated a service that had been envied across Europe.

embellish.definition: to decorate or add invented details
sentences: He embellished the story with a bear that had not, on the day, existed.
The manuscript is embellished with gold leaf and one very rude marginal drawing.
The slogan was emblazoned on the bus and quietly removed after the audit.
Her name is emblazoned above a door she was never allowed to enter.

emboss.definition: to decorate with a raised design
sentences: The invitation was embossed, which added forty pounds and no information.
Braille is embossed writing, which makes it the most useful decoration ever invented.
A single email embroiled him in a dispute between two departments he had never visited.
Do not embroil yourself in an argument whose stakes you cannot name.
Embroiled in litigation for six years, the company forgot what it originally made.
He was embroiled in the scandal by proximity rather than participation.
The plan was embryonic: two names, one date, and a great deal of confidence.
In its embryonic form the internet connected four computers and nobody's grandmother.
The editor emended a line that had been printed wrong since 1623.
Emend fixes a text; amend fixes a law or a habit.
Ipecac was the household emetic until doctors decided it did more harm than good.
He described the advertisement as an emetic, which the agency framed.
Four eminent scholars signed the letter and none of them had read the book.
Eminent means standing out; imminent means about to arrive. Both can be alarming.

emissary.definition: someone sent on a mission as a representative
sentences: An emissary arrived with a proposal and a strict instruction not to negotiate.
The emissary was chosen for patience, which the assignment consumed entirely.
An emollient statement from the chair calmed a meeting that had begun shouting.
The cream is emollient; the apology was not.
The emoluments clause exists so that officials are paid by their country and nobody else.
His emoluments were modest; his expenses were architecture.
An empathetic doctor explains the same diagnosis in a way the patient can carry home.
Empathetic listening takes longer and saves the entire conversation.

empirical.definition: based on observation rather than theory
sentences: The empirical evidence contradicted a model that was too elegant to abandon.
Empirical means somebody actually went and looked.

empiricism.definition: the view that knowledge comes from experience
sentences: British empiricism insisted the mind begins as a blank sheet, which is charming and probably wrong.
Empiricism made the thermometer more important than the philosopher.

emulate.definition: to imitate in order to match or surpass
sentences: Younger writers emulated his sentences and inherited none of his patience.
The software emulates a machine that stopped being manufactured in 1987.

enamor.definition: to fill with love or fascination
sentences: He was enamored of the idea and considerably less fond of the work it required.
Nobody is enamored with a spreadsheet, though several people have claimed to be.
The exhibition enchanted children and quietly devastated the adults who remembered.
Enchant contains "chant": the magic was originally sung.

enclave.definition: a distinct area enclosed within a larger one
sentences: The village remained a linguistic enclave for four centuries and two border changes.
Every campus has an enclave where the coffee is good and the conversation is unbearable.
The encomium ran twenty minutes and mentioned the honoree's work twice.
An encomium at a retirement is a eulogy the subject gets to hear.

encroach.definition: to intrude gradually on another's territory
sentences: The hedge encroached six inches a year and started a lawsuit in the eleventh.
Work encroached on the weekend so gradually that nobody could name the day it won.

encroachment.definition: gradual intrusion on rights or territory
sentences: Each encroachment was small, and after ten years the beach was private.
Liberties are rarely seized; they are lost to encroachment.
The estate was encumbered by debts older than the current owner.
Encumbered with four bags and a map, he missed the train twice.
His encyclopedic memory for statistics made him unbeatable and unbearable at quizzes.
An encyclopedic footnote in a slim book is a small act of aggression.

endemic.definition: regularly found in a place or group
sentences: The bird is endemic to one valley and has no idea how precarious that is.
Corruption was endemic, which meant nobody could remember it being otherwise.

endow.definition: to provide with a quality or a fund
sentences: The chair was endowed by an alumnus who had failed the subject twice.
She was endowed with perfect pitch and no patience for people who lacked it.
Office endued him with a gravity his friends found frankly hilarious.
Endue is endow's older, more ceremonial cousin.
The enduring appeal of the design is that nothing about it was fashionable.
Their enduring friendship survived four countries and one disastrous business.
The heat enervated the entire crew by noon.
Enervate sounds like energize and means the exact opposite, which has ruined many essays.
Enervated by three days of meetings, the team produced its best work on the fourth.
An enervated economy does not collapse; it just stops answering.

engage.definition: to occupy, involve, or enter into conflict with
sentences: He refused to engage with the criticism and answered a friendlier question instead.
The fleet engaged at dawn and disengaged, badly damaged, by noon.

engender.definition: to give rise to; to cause
sentences: Secrecy engenders exactly the suspicion it was meant to avoid.
Small courtesies engender loyalty that salaries cannot buy.

enhance.definition: to improve or increase the quality of
sentences: Nothing enhanced the room like removing three quarters of what was in it.
The photograph was enhanced until it stopped being evidence.
He remained an enigma to colleagues who had shared an office with him for years.
Churchill called Russia a riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma, and left it there.
Her enigmatic reply could be read as approval or a threat, which was the point.
The enigmatic smile has sold more postcards than any other expression in art.

enjoin.definition: to order someone to do or stop something
sentences: The court enjoined the company from selling the product pending review.
Enjoin is one of those words that can command an act or forbid it entirely.
The enmity between the two villages was founded on a bridge and maintained by habit.
Enmity requires memory, which is why forgetting is sometimes strategic.
A summer of ennui produced three abandoned novels and one very good garden.
Ennui is boredom with a French passport and better clothes.

enormity.definition: extreme wickedness or a monstrous act
sentences: The enormity of the crime was matched by the banality of its planning.
Purists insist enormity means wickedness, not size, and lose that battle daily.
The final movement enraptured an audience that had spent the first half coughing.
He was enraptured by the machine and indifferent to what it produced.
Ensconced in the corner armchair with a blanket, he refused all further requests.
She was ensconced in the department for thirty years and outlasted six restructurings.
Chaos ensued, as it generally does when four people share one microphone.
A silence ensued that was longer than the question deserved.

entertain.definition: to consider an idea; to amuse
sentences: He would not entertain the possibility that the fault lay in his own code.
Aristotle praised the mind that can entertain a thought without accepting it.

enthrall.definition: to capture the complete attention of
sentences: The storyteller enthralled two hundred children for fifty minutes without a single prop.
Enthrall once meant to enslave, which is a dark origin for a compliment.

entice.definition: to tempt by offering something appealing
sentences: Free coffee enticed forty people to a seminar that eleven found useful.
The trap was baited with something enticing and, unusually, nutritious.
The entitled complaint about a delayed flight lasted longer than the delay.
Legally entitled and behaving entitled are very different things.

entitlement.definition: a right to something; a sense of deserving it
sentences: The entitlement is written in the contract; the attitude was acquired elsewhere.
Reforming entitlements is popular in the abstract and lethal in a specific district.
Entomology studies insects; etymology studies words. Confusing them creates memorable errors.
A lifetime in entomology left him with sixty thousand specimens and no dinner invitations.
She entreated the committee for one more week and was granted three days.
He entreated, argued, and finally simply waited, which worked.

entrenched.definition: firmly established and hard to change
sentences: Entrenched habits survive every reorganization, which is why reorganizations keep happening.
The advantage is entrenched: the leader writes the rules of the next round.

enumerate.definition: to list items one by one
sentences: He enumerated his objections in nine parts, and the room aged visibly.
To enumerate the problems took an hour; to solve one took a week.
Mayflies are ephemeral by name and by fact: one day, no mouth, no time to eat.
Internet fame is ephemeral, which is the only mercy in the whole arrangement.

epicure.definition: a person with refined taste in food and drink
sentences: The epicure sent back the wine, the fish, and eventually himself.
Epicurus actually recommended bread, cheese, and friends, which the epicures forgot.
Wilde's epigrams have outlasted the plays that carried them.
An epigram is a whole argument compressed until it sparkles.
Her epiphany arrived on a bus, as most epiphanies do, uninvited.
Joyce borrowed the religious word for the moment an ordinary thing turns luminous.

episodic.definition: occurring irregularly; made of loose episodes
sentences: The novel is episodic: nine excellent chapters and no discernible spine.
His interest was episodic, arriving each spring and departing each autumn.

epistolary.definition: written in the form of letters
sentences: Dracula is an epistolary novel, assembled from letters, diaries, and one ship's log.
Their epistolary friendship survived forty years and one disastrous meeting.
The building is the epitome of a style everyone claims to dislike.
He is the epitome of the competent bore, and the department could not run without him.

eponym.definition: a person after whom something is named
sentences: Sandwich, boycott, and diesel are all people who became things.
The disease's eponym described it in 1817 and never treated a single case successfully.
His equable temper survived four hours of hostile questioning and one broken microphone.
The island's equable climate ruins its inhabitants for anywhere else.
She received the diagnosis with an equanimity that frightened her family.
Equanimity in a crisis is mostly deciding in advance what you will not do.
An equitable split is not always an equal one, which is where the arguing starts.
The settlement was equitable, which meant everyone left mildly dissatisfied.
The test results were equivocal, so they ran it again with the same outcome.
His equivocal endorsement helped neither candidate and offended both.

equivocate.definition: to speak ambiguously to avoid commitment
sentences: Asked a yes-or-no question, he equivocated for six paragraphs.
Politicians equivocate; witnesses who equivocate are usually asked to sit back down.
Smallpox is the one human disease we have actually eradicated, and it took two centuries.
The Latin root is pulling up by the roots, which is the standard for the word.
Each small dishonesty eroded a reputation that had taken decades to build.
The cliff erodes a meter a year, and the houses on it are still for sale.
Err on the side of caution, said the sign, unhelpfully, at the top of the cliff.
To err is human; to blame the intern is management.
An errant comma changed the meaning of a contract by four million pounds.
The errant knight wandered in search of trouble, which is the job description.
His erratic attendance made him impossible to schedule and impossible to replace.
The engine ran erratically for a week and then, considerately, failed at the depot.
The erroneous figure was repeated in nine articles before anyone checked the source.
An erroneous assumption at the start makes every later calculation beautifully wrong.
Wartime ersatz coffee was made from acorns and grim determination.
The apology was ersatz: the shape of the thing without the substance.
His erstwhile allies testified first and at length.
The erstwhile factory is now nine apartments and a coffee shop.
His erudite footnotes were longer, and better, than the chapters above them.
Erudite conversation is delightful for exactly as long as you can keep up.
Her erudition was worn lightly, which made it twice as impressive.
Erudition without judgment produces very well-informed nonsense.
A dispute about parking escalated into a case that reached the high court.
Costs escalated quietly until the total appeared on one very memorable slide.
She eschewed publicity so thoroughly that two obituaries used the wrong photograph.
He eschews adjectives, which makes his praise worth something.

esoteric.definition: understood by only a small group
sentences: The dispute was esoteric enough that only nine people on earth could take a side.
Esoteric knowledge becomes valuable the moment somebody needs it urgently.

espouse.definition: to adopt or support a cause
sentences: He espoused free trade in public and lobbied for tariffs in private.
The word once meant to marry, which explains its air of commitment.

establish.definition: to set up firmly; to prove
sentences: The study established a link that four earlier studies had merely suggested.
The firm was established in 1892 and has moved premises eleven times since.
He was held in high esteem by colleagues and in open suspicion by auditors.
Esteem earned slowly can be spent alarmingly fast.
An estimable career ended in a dispute over a parking space.
The estimable qualities of the plan did not include being affordable.

estrange.definition: to cause to become hostile or distant
sentences: An argument about a will estranged the brothers for twenty-two years.
Success estranged him from everyone who had known him before it.

estranged.definition: no longer close or on good terms
sentences: His estranged sister arrived at the funeral and sat, deliberately, at the back.
Estranged colleagues can still produce excellent work, silently, in shifts.

ethereal.definition: delicate and light, seemingly not of this world
sentences: Her ethereal soprano carried over an orchestra that should have drowned it.
The ethereal light in those paintings comes from a pigment that cost more than gold.

ethos.definition: the characteristic spirit of a group
sentences: The company's ethos was printed on the wall and contradicted in the parking lot.
A newsroom's ethos is set by whoever is willing to stay latest.
Eugenic policies were mainstream science in 1920 and a global disgrace by 1950.
The eugenic argument confused what is heritable with what is desirable.

eulogy.definition: a speech of high praise, especially for the dead
sentences: The eulogy was funny for four minutes and unbearable for the fifth.
A eulogy is the one speech nobody rehearses enough and everyone remembers.

euphemism.definition: a mild word substituted for a harsh one
sentences: "Restructuring" is the euphemism; the letters go out on Friday.
Every profession invents euphemisms for the part of the job it dislikes explaining.
"Cellar door" is often cited as the euphony champion of English.
The poem sacrifices sense for euphony and gets away with it entirely.
The euphoria lasted three days and the paperwork lasted three months.
Post-victory euphoria is famously bad for making decisions.
Euphoric at the finish line, she promised never to do it again and entered twice more.
The market was euphoric for a quarter and educational for a year.

evade.definition: to avoid or escape by cleverness
sentences: He evaded the question by answering the one before it, at length.
Avoiding tax is legal; evading it is a different chapter of the same book.
The scent of rain on hot stone is evanescent and impossible to bottle honestly.
His fame was evanescent: two seasons, one catchphrase, then nothing.
The evasive answers were more damaging than any admission would have been.
Evasive action saved the ship and cost eleven hours.
An evenhanded account satisfied neither camp, which is the usual sign of one.
She was evenhanded with praise and blame, and both landed harder for it.
It was evident from the second paragraph that the author had not visited the country.
The strain was evident to everyone except the person under it.

evoke.definition: to bring a feeling or memory to mind
sentences: Three notes on a piano evoked an entire summer he had not thought about in years.
The painting evokes a place that never existed, convincingly.
The statement exacerbated a crisis it was written to calm.
Sleeping badly exacerbates everything, including the reason you slept badly.
An exacting editor is the cheapest improvement any writer can buy.
The exacting standards were met once, in 1974, and are still displayed.

exalt.definition: to praise highly or raise in rank
sentences: The obituary exalted a man his employees had described in very different terms.
To exalt one colleague publicly is to demote everyone else quietly.
The automated menu exasperated callers into hanging up, which reduced complaints beautifully.
Nothing exasperates a specialist like confident amateur advice.
Exasperated after the fourth transfer, she wrote a letter instead and got results.
His exasperated sigh was audible in the next room and quoted for years.
The editor excised the entire third act and the play improved immeasurably.
Two paragraphs were excised for legal reasons and everyone noticed the gap.
The report excoriated the board in language usually reserved for war crimes.
To excoriate is literally to strip the skin, which reviewers occasionally forget.
The pain was excruciating; the wait for a diagnosis was worse.
An excruciating silence followed the joke about the host's cooking.
The timestamp exculpated him in a single line after two years of suspicion.
Exculpatory evidence must be disclosed, which is the whole point of the rule.
The execrable coffee was the only thing everyone in the building agreed on.
His execrable handwriting cost a patient the correct dose.
The policy was execrated by everyone and repealed by nobody.
He was execrated in his lifetime and has a statue now, which is the usual sequence.

exegesis.definition: a detailed critical interpretation of a text
sentences: A twelve-page exegesis of a four-line poem is either devotion or a career.
Exegesis draws meaning out; eisegesis pushes your meaning in.
The chapel is the exemplar every architecture student is made to draw.
She became an exemplar of the method mainly by surviving its early failures.

exemplify.definition: to be a typical example of
sentences: The episode exemplifies everything wrong and everything right with the process.
He exemplified the profession's virtues and, on Thursdays, its vices.

exert.definition: to apply effort, force, or influence
sentences: The committee exerted pressure so gently that nobody could later identify it.
He exerted himself once, spectacularly, and rested on it for a decade.
After that exertion the team slept through a fire alarm.
The exertion of pretending to listen is underestimated by everyone who talks.
An exhaustive search of the attic produced one glove and a great deal of dust.
The list is exhaustive, exhausting, and, in three places, wrong.
The first ten minutes were exhilarating and the next four hours were paperwork.
There is something exhilarating about a plan that has no chance of working.

exhort.definition: to strongly urge someone to act
sentences: The coach exhorted them for ten minutes and then let the silence do the work.
Editorials exhort; budgets decide.
The exigencies of the moment excused a decision that looked terrible in the report.
Every constitution has a clause for exigencies, and every exigency finds it.
Exigent circumstances allowed entry without a warrant, and the court later disagreed.
The exigent problem crowded out the important one, as it always does.
The exiguity of the evidence did not slow the confident conclusion.
Given the exiguity of the budget, the result was frankly miraculous.

exonerate.definition: to clear of blame or accusation
sentences: He was exonerated after eleven years, and the apology took another three.
The inquiry exonerated everyone senior and blamed a process nobody had designed.
The exorbitant rent explained why the shop sold nothing but very small jewelry.
Exorbitant means out of orbit: the price has left the ordinary path.

exorcise.definition: to drive out an evil spirit or bad memory
sentences: He wrote the book to exorcise a decade he could not otherwise put down.
The new management exorcised the old logo and kept every old problem.

exotic.definition: strikingly unusual, from a distant place
sentences: The exotic fruit at the market was an ordinary vegetable two thousand miles away.
Exotic is a description of the describer's location, not the thing described.
He grew expansive after the second course and revealed the merger by dessert.
The expansive view from the office made the small decisions feel worse.

expatiate.definition: to speak or write at length
sentences: He expatiated on the history of the roof until the tour lost half its members.
Given an opening she would expatiate, brilliantly, for as long as anyone stayed.

expatriate.definition: a person living outside their native country
sentences: The expatriate community met weekly to complain about a country none intended to leave.
Expatriate or immigrant often depends on which passport and which salary.

expedient.definition: convenient and practical, though possibly improper
sentences: It was expedient to blame the software, which could not resign or testify.
The expedient solution buys a year and charges interest afterward.
A single phone call expedited a permit that had waited eight months.
Expedited shipping costs triple and arrives, reliably, on the same Thursday.

expel.definition: to force out or drive away
sentences: He was expelled for an essay that the school now includes in its prospectus.
The engine expels heat, noise, and, occasionally, its own components.
He spent thirty years trying to expiate one afternoon.
Fines expiate nothing; they merely price the offense.
The anomaly was explicable, though the explanation was duller than the mystery.
Everything is explicable afterward, which is the trouble with history.

explicate.definition: to analyze and explain in detail
sentences: She explicated the poem line by line and left it more alive than she found it.
To explicate a joke is to conduct an autopsy on it.
The instructions were explicit and were ignored explicitly.
Make the assumption explicit and half the disagreement disappears.

exploit.definition: to use unfairly for one's own advantage
sentences: The scheme exploited a loophole that had been left open deliberately.
As a noun it means a heroic deed; as a verb, something rather less admirable.

exploitation.definition: unfair use of someone or something for gain
sentences: The report documented exploitation that four inspections had somehow missed.
Exploitation of the resource funded a museum about the people it displaced.
The contract was exploitative in six clauses and illegal in one.
Exploitative pricing during a flood is remembered longer than any flood.
She was the leading exponent of a technique she had once dismissed in print.
An exponent of plain speech should probably avoid the word exponent.

exposition.definition: a clear explanation; a large public display
sentences: The exposition of the theory takes forty pages and rewards every one of them.
Clumsy exposition is why characters explain to each other what both already know.
His expostulations were noted in the minutes and ignored in the decision.
After much expostulation, the fee was reduced by eleven pounds.
He expounded his theory to anyone who paused near the coffee machine.
Asked a simple question, she expounded for forty minutes and answered it beautifully.
The conviction was expunged, though the internet declined to cooperate.
Two names were expunged from the register, which drew more attention than leaving them.

expurgate.definition: to remove objectionable material from a text
sentences: The expurgated edition removed eleven pages and every reason to read it.
Expurgated letters make dull history and comfortable descendants.
Only three copies are extant, and two of them are in private hands.
Extant means still here; extinct means the opposite and sounds worryingly similar.
His extemporaneous remarks were better than the speech he had spent a week writing.
Extemporaneous brilliance usually turns out to have been rehearsed in the car.
When the slides failed she extemporized for thirty minutes and got a standing ovation.
Jazz is extemporizing with rules everyone has agreed not to mention.

extend.definition: to make longer or wider; to offer
sentences: The deadline was extended twice and met, as always, at the last hour.
He extended a hand and an apology, in that order.

extenuate.definition: to make an offense seem less serious
sentences: Nothing extenuated the delay except that the alternative would have been worse.
The lawyer sought to extenuate rather than deny, which the jury noticed.
Extenuating circumstances reduced the sentence and none of the damage.
Everyone believes their own circumstances are extenuating, which is what makes judges necessary.
He extolled the virtues of a system he had never personally had to use.
The brochure extols the view and omits the motorway.

extort.definition: to obtain by force or threats
sentences: They extorted payments for four years by threatening to reveal nothing in particular.
The fee felt extorted rather than charged.
Strip the extraneous detail and the argument fits on a postcard.
Extraneous noise in the recording turned out to be the most important evidence.

extrapolate.definition: to extend a conclusion to unknown cases
sentences: He extrapolated from three months of data and predicted a decade, confidently and wrongly.
Extrapolating a straight line far enough always predicts something absurd.

extrapolation.definition: an estimate extended beyond known data
sentences: The forecast was an extrapolation dressed as a measurement.
Every extrapolation carries an unwritten clause: if nothing changes.
The extravagant claims in the advertisement drew regulators before customers.
One extravagant gesture is remembered; consistent generosity is not.

exuberant.definition: full of lively energy and enthusiasm
sentences: Exuberant applause greeted a speech nobody could later summarize.
"Irrational exuberance" described a market that then rose for four more years.
He fabricated the data and the apology, and only one of them was detected quickly.
The part was fabricated overnight from a photograph and a guess.
His facetious remark at the memorial cost him three friendships.
The word holds all five vowels in order, which is more than its jokes usually manage.
The facile explanation fit on a slide and left every hard question untouched.
Facile can mean effortless, but on the GRE it almost always means too easy to be true.
A single shared calendar facilitated what four meetings had failed to arrange.
To facilitate a meeting is to keep three people from talking at once.

faction.definition: a small dissenting group within a larger one
sentences: Two factions formed over a font choice and did not speak for a year.
A faction becomes a party the moment it wins something.

factious.definition: given to internal conflict and division
sentences: The factious committee split over a font and never reassembled.
A factious party loses to a dull united one every single time.
The outrage was factitious, organized by three accounts and a scheduling tool.
Factitious is manufactured; fictitious is invented. Both are lies with different jobs.
The diet was a fad in 1994, a joke in 1999, and a cookbook again in 2019.
Every fad is a tradition that failed its second year.
The argument was fallacious in a way that took three pages to explain and one line to feel.
A fallacious premise produces a confident, useless conclusion.

fallacy.definition: a mistaken belief or flawed argument
sentences: The sunk-cost fallacy has kept more bad projects alive than any budget.
Naming a fallacy in Latin does not win the argument, though people try.
Memory is fallible in ways that are systematic, which is worse than being random.
A fallible expert who says so is worth two confident ones.
He lay fallow for two years and came back with the best work of his life.
Fields left fallow recover nitrogen; people left fallow recover everything else.
Her voice faltered once, on a name, and then held for the rest of the eulogy.
The campaign faltered in October and collapsed in November.
Fanatical attention to detail built the bridge and ruined four marriages.
A fanatical follower is a liability disguised as an asset.
The fanciful proposal involved a monorail and no visible funding.
Her fanciful drawings of machines predate three of the actual inventions.

fancy.definition: to imagine or take a liking to
sentences: He fancied himself a natural leader, which nobody else fancied at all.
Fancy is a shortened "fantasy," which explains why it means both imagining and liking.

fanfare.definition: a showy public display or flourish
sentences: The product launched with enormous fanfare and was discontinued without a word.
A trumpet fanfare announces the arrival of someone who could have simply knocked.

fare.definition: to get along or turn out in a specified way
sentences: The smaller firms fared better in the crisis because they had less to lose.
How did you fare? is the polite version of what went wrong.

fastidious.definition: very attentive to detail; hard to please
sentences: A fastidious proofreader is worth more to a book than a second author.
He was fastidious about his shoes and cheerfully vague about his taxes.
Nobody could fathom why the timetable had been designed that way.
A fathom measures the depth of water; the verb measures the depth of a mystery.
His fatuous grin survived a question that should have removed it.
A fatuous remark is stupid and pleased with itself, which is the worst combination.
Three deputies fawned over the visitor and one asked a real question.
Dogs fawn honestly; people fawn with an agenda.

fawning.definition: flattering in an excessive, servile way
sentences: The fawning introduction lasted so long the speaker looked embarrassed.
Fawning praise from a subordinate tells you nothing except who is afraid.
The plan was feasible on paper and impossible in February.
Feasible does not mean wise; it only means the physics allows it.
The feckless heir spent four years and the entire estate proving the will right.
Feck is an old word for effect: feckless means, precisely, without effect.
A fecund decade produced nine novels, four of them good.
The delta's fecund soil supported a city for three thousand years.
A feeble excuse delivered confidently often outperforms a good one mumbled.
The signal was too feeble to carry past the second floor.
He feigned surprise so badly that even the cat looked skeptical.
She feigned illness on the day of the exam and caught a real one that evening.

feint.definition: a deceptive move to distract an opponent
sentences: The feint drew defenders left, and the pass went right.
Feint is a fake move; faint is falling over. Boxers do both.
A felicitous phrase in the opening carried the whole essay.
Their meeting was felicitous: two problems that turned out to be each other's solution.
She described the disaster with a felicity that made everyone laugh guiltily.
Domestic felicity is rarely written about because it makes such dull reading.
The phrase "in one fell swoop" preserves an adjective that means murderous.
A fell wind stripped the orchard in a single night.
She ferreted out the discrepancy from a filing cabinet nobody had opened since 1998.
Ferrets were used to flush rabbits from burrows, which is exactly what the verb does.
His fervent defense of the library persuaded a council that had already decided.
Fervent comes from boiling, which is where most convictions live.
The fervid tone of the letter suggested a grievance older than the subject.
Fervid is fervent with the thermostat broken.
Revolutionary fervor lasted eleven months and one very cold winter.
He argued about punctuation with the fervor others reserve for religion.

fester.definition: to worsen through neglect; to become infected
sentences: The grievance festered for six years because nobody wanted an awkward conversation.
A wound festers quietly and then, all at once, urgently.
He was feted in three cities and audited in a fourth.
They feted the retiring caretaker more warmly than any director before him.
The fetid canal was cleaned in 1908 and named after the man who paid for it.
A fetid atmosphere in an office is rarely about the air.
The opening night was a fiasco: two power cuts and a missing lead actor.
Italian for "bottle," and nobody has satisfactorily explained how it came to mean this.
Fickle audiences abandoned the show between two seasons and returned for the reunion.
Fortune is famously fickle, which is the only fair thing about it.
The translation's fidelity to the original made it almost unreadable in English.
High fidelity meant, originally, that the recording resembled the concert.
He meant it figuratively, which the lawyers found insufficiently reassuring.
A figurative bloodbath sells newspapers; a literal one closes them.

filch.definition: to steal something of small value
sentences: Somebody filched the good stapler and the department never recovered.
He filched a peach and paid for it in guilt for thirty years.

filibuster.definition: prolonged speech used to block a vote
sentences: The filibuster ran twenty-four hours and included a recipe for oyster stew.
A filibuster is a speech whose only purpose is its own length.
He finagled an upgrade by knowing the right name and using it sadly.
She finagled the schedule so that every difficult meeting fell on a Friday.

financial.definition: relating to money and its management
sentences: The financial case was flawless and the human case was never made.
Financial literacy is taught nowhere and required everywhere.

finesse.definition: delicate skill in handling a situation
sentences: She handled the resignation with a finesse that left everyone feeling consulted.
The repair needed finesse; it got a hammer.
The finicky printer refused any paper it had not personally approved.
He was finicky about coffee and indifferent to whether the roof leaked.

firebrand.definition: someone who stirs up trouble or passion
sentences: The firebrand of 1968 became the cautious committee chair of 1991.
Every movement needs one firebrand and about forty people who do the paperwork.
A fissure in the party widened into two parties within a year.
Steam escaped from a fissure the survey had marked as sealed.
Fitful sleep before a flight is worse than none at all.
Progress was fitful: three good months, six silent ones, then a breakthrough.
Attention flagged in the third hour and nobody pretended otherwise.
The same word means to mark something for attention, which is confusing at the end of a long meeting.
A flagrant breach of the rules went unpunished, which taught everyone the actual rule.
Flagrant comes from burning: the offense is on fire in plain view.

flail.definition: to wave about wildly; to struggle ineffectively
sentences: The department flailed for a quarter before anyone admitted the strategy had failed.
He flailed at the wasp and hit the lamp.
She had a flair for defusing meetings that had already caught fire.
Flair is talent that wants to be seen.
His flamboyant style hid an accountant's caution about everything that mattered.
Flamboyant means flaming, which is a fair description of the jacket.

flay.definition: to criticize savagely; to strip skin from
sentences: The review flayed the novel and doubled its sales.
To flay in print is legal; to flay in fact has been illegal for some time.
The fledgling company had four employees and one very optimistic sign.
A fledgling is a bird just able to fly, which is exactly the level of confidence involved.
Tourists were fleeced at the border by a man with an official-looking clipboard.
Fleecing a customer once earns more than serving them badly forever, which is why regulation exists.
A fleeting expression crossed his face and was gone before anyone could name it.
Fleeting fame is at least honest about its schedule.
A flip answer to a grieving relative ended his career in customer service.
He gave a flip reply and spent the afternoon apologizing for it.
The flippant tone of the statement made a small problem into a resignation.
Flippant is funny at the wrong moment, which is the only difference between wit and disaster.
His florid prose took four sentences to open a door.
The florid ceiling has more cherubs than the chapel has seats.
A flotilla of fishing boats rescued more people than the navy did that week.
By dawn a flotilla of kayaks blocked the harbor entrance entirely.

flotsam.definition: floating wreckage; worthless odds and ends
sentences: The beach filled with flotsam, and one intact piano.
Flotsam floats off a wreck; jetsam was thrown overboard on purpose.
He floundered through the first ten minutes and then found his footing entirely.
The project floundered for two years and was declared a pilot.
The garden flourished under total neglect, which was humbling.
He flourished the letter above his head as though it were a verdict.
They flouted the ban so publicly that enforcing it became unavoidable.
Flout is to defy; flaunt is to show off. Flouting the difference is common.
Attendance fluctuated with the weather and nothing else anyone could identify.
Prices fluctuate; the explanations offered for it fluctuate faster.
The discovery was a fluke, which the grant application described as a strategy.
Winning twice is skill; winning once is a fluke with a trophy.
The new ticket machine flummoxed commuters and delighted the taxi drivers outside.
One simple question flummoxed a panel of four experts.
Flummoxed by the form, he left it blank and was approved anyway.
The audience looked flummoxed, which the artist took as a compliment.
Flush with grant money, the lab bought a machine it used twice.
The company was flush in spring and borrowing by autumn.
Flustered by the applause, she forgot the name of her own book.
He never looked flustered, which colleagues found either admirable or inhuman.
The department is in flux, which is the official word for nobody knows who reports to whom.
Everything is in flux, said Heraclitus, and has been reliably quoted ever since.
His foibles were catalogued affectionately in a speech he pretended not to enjoy.
Marriage is largely the negotiation of foibles.
The plot was foiled by a locked door nobody had planned for.
As a noun, a foil is the contrast that makes someone else look brighter.

foist.definition: to impose something unwanted on someone
sentences: The extra duties were foisted on the newest hire, as tradition demanded.
He foisted a forgery on two dealers and a museum before anyone checked the frame.
The pamphlet fomented a strike its author had intended merely to describe.
To foment is to apply heat, which is exactly what agitators do to a grievance.
The charge was fomentation of unrest, based on a speech and a rumor.
Fomentation of dissent is only a crime when the dissent succeeds too slowly.
The foolhardy crossing cost two boats and taught the village a permanent lesson.
Courage weighs the risk; foolhardiness has not looked.
His foppish cuffs concealed a man who could rebuild an engine by hand.
The foppish villain in a costume drama is always the second-best character.

forage.definition: to search widely for food or supplies
sentences: They foraged in the fridge and produced dinner from three unlikely ingredients.
Foraging armies feed themselves and empty the countryside behind them.
He forbore to mention the earlier failure, which everyone noticed him not mentioning.
Forbear with an E is patience; forebear with two is your ancestor.
Her forbearance during the interview was mistaken for agreement.
The bank showed forbearance for one quarter and then showed the door.

ford.definition: to cross a river at a shallow point
sentences: They forded the river at dawn and lost only one bag to the current.
Oxford and Frankfurt are both named for places somebody once forded.
Her forebears arrived with one trunk and left an entire street.
We inherit our forebears' habits more reliably than their money.

foreboding.definition: a feeling that something bad will happen
sentences: A sense of foreboding hung over the meeting before a word was spoken.
Foreboding is anxiety that turns out, sometimes, to have been information.
The failure was foreseeable, and two memos had in fact foreseen it.
For the foreseeable future means until somebody changes their mind.

foreshadow.definition: to hint at something that will happen
sentences: The broken clock in chapter one foreshadows everything, as broken clocks do.
Small delays foreshadowed a collapse nobody wanted to name.
A frank memo forestalled a rumor that would have taken months to correct.
To forestall is to get to the market before the seller, which is where the word began.

forfeit.definition: to lose or give up as a penalty
sentences: He forfeited the deposit rather than spend another night in the flat.
The team forfeited the match and won the argument.
A forlorn umbrella stood in the corner for eight months awaiting its owner.
A forlorn hope was originally the first troops into a breach, which explains the tone.
A formal complaint changes everything; an informal grumble changes nothing.
The formal apology was drafted by lawyers and read exactly like it.

formidable.definition: inspiring fear or respect through power
sentences: A formidable opponent in debate, she prepared for arguments nobody had thought to make.
The formidable wall kept out invaders for four centuries and one afternoon.
He forsook a comfortable career for a boat that leaked from the first day.
Wedding vows use forsake because abandon sounds too much like what actually happens.

forswear.definition: to renounce or give up solemnly
sentences: She forswore social media in January and returned, quietly, in March.
He forswore alcohol, sugar, and opinions, and kept two of the three.
Diplomacy was never his forte, which the ambassadorship exposed within a week.
Punctuality is not her forte and never has been, cheerfully.

forthcoming.definition: willing to share information; about to happen
sentences: The witness was less forthcoming after the second cup of coffee, not more.
The forthcoming report has been forthcoming for two years.
His forthright assessment of the budget cost him a friend and saved a department.
Forthright answers make short meetings, which is why they are so rare.

fortify.definition: to strengthen against attack or weakness
sentences: They fortified the argument with data and forgot to make it interesting.
Flour is fortified with iron, which is a quiet public-health triumph.
It took fortitude to sit through the review and thank the reviewers afterward.
Fortitude is courage stretched over months rather than minutes.
The meeting was fortuitous: two strangers, one delayed train, one company.
Strictly it means by chance, though it has quietly acquired the good luck.
Small grants fostered work that no committee would ever have approved directly.
The policy fostered exactly the behavior it was written to prevent.
The merger foundered on a disagreement about which logo survived.
The ship foundered within sight of a harbor it could not enter.
A fracas over seating delayed the ceremony and enlivened the photographs.
The fracas lasted ninety seconds and the inquiry lasted nine months.
A fractious coalition governed for eleven months and agreed on nothing but lunch.
Fractious toddlers and fractious committees respond to identical management.
Human frailty, not conspiracy, explains most institutional failure.
The frailty was physical; the stubbornness was entirely intact.

fraud.definition: deliberate deception for gain; an impostor
sentences: The fraud ran for nine years and required only one unopened envelope to unravel.
He was exposed as a fraud by a student who checked a footnote.
The negotiation was fraught with the history nobody wanted to mention.
A fraught silence at dinner is more informative than any argument.
She entered the fray late and ended it in two sentences.
As a verb it means to unravel, which is what tempers do in a fray.
The frenetic final week produced a report nobody could read.
Frenetic activity is often what an organization does instead of deciding.

fresco.definition: a painting made on wet plaster
sentences: A fresco must be finished before the plaster dries, which is why they are so confident.
The fresco survived because someone whitewashed it in 1660 and forgot.
He fretted about a deadline that had, unknown to him, already been moved.
Fretting is planning with all the useful parts removed.

frieze.definition: a decorative horizontal band on a wall
sentences: The frieze shows a procession that took eleven months to carve and nine minutes to walk past.
Half the frieze is in Athens and half in London, which remains a conversation.

fringe.definition: the outer edge; a marginal group
sentences: The idea lived on the fringe for a decade and is now on the syllabus.
Fringe benefits were originally the small extras at the edge of a wage.
The court dismissed the claim as frivolous and charged the filer for the pleasure.
A frivolous purchase on a bad day is cheaper than most therapies.

frontier.definition: the limit of settled or known territory
sentences: The frontier of the field is wherever the funding was last renewed.
Frontier towns had three saloons and no school, which tells you the priorities.

fructify.definition: to bear fruit or become productive
sentences: The partnership took four years to fructify and then produced everything at once.
Investment fructifies slowly, which is why patience outperforms cleverness.
Frugal by habit rather than necessity, she saved a fortune and mentioned it to nobody.
The frugal meal turned out to be the best one of the trip.
His frugality was legendary and, in the end, entirely pointless.
Frugality practiced only in public is called austerity.
A fruitful hour on the phone replaced a month of email.
The collaboration was fruitful for both and pleasant for neither.
Bad weather frustrated an attempt that had been three years in planning.
Nothing frustrates a plan like another plan filed on the same day.

fulcrum.definition: the pivot point on which something turns
sentences: The single clause was the fulcrum of the entire negotiation.
Give me a lever and a fulcrum, said Archimedes, and I will move the earth.
He fulminated against the reform for a decade and voted for its successor.
Fulminate is to explode: the word means literally to strike with lightning.
A functionary with a stamp can delay you longer than a minister can help you.
The decision was blamed on a functionary who had followed the rules exactly.
Oil is fungible; a good colleague is not, whatever the org chart implies.
Money is fungible, which is why earmarked funding rarely stays earmarked.
The archive furnished the one document the defense had insisted did not exist.
He furnished the flat with three chairs and a piano.
A furtive glance at the door told everyone what the answer would be.
Furtive shares a root with "thief," which is exactly the manner it describes.
Arguing with the parking algorithm was futile and, briefly, satisfying.
The gesture was futile and made anyway, which is often the point of gestures.

gadfly.definition: a persistent critic who provokes others
sentences: Socrates called himself the gadfly of Athens, and Athens executed the insect.
Every board needs one gadfly and cannot survive two.
The gaffe was minor, the apology was worse, and the clip was permanent.
A political gaffe is when someone accidentally says what they think.
Nobody could gainsay the figures, so they questioned the person who found them.
There is no gainsaying her record, however irritating her manner.

gale.definition: a very strong wind; an outburst
sentences: A gale took the roof, the fence, and the argument about who owned the fence.
The joke produced gales of laughter and one very offended trustee.
He had the gall to ask for a refund on a meal he had finished.
Gall was one of the medieval humors, which is why bitterness and nerve share a word.
The photograph galvanized a public that had ignored four years of reports.
Galvani made a dead frog's leg twitch, and the word has been jolting people ever since.

gambit.definition: a calculated opening move involving risk
sentences: Resigning was a gambit; being accepted was the part he had not planned.
In chess a gambit sacrifices a pawn for position, which is also true of most careers.
Lambs gambol for about three weeks and then discover standing still.
The dog gamboled across the lawn and into the pond it had not seen.

garble.definition: to distort a message so it is unclear
sentences: The transmission was garbled and the order was carried out anyway.
One garbled sentence in the summary reversed the finding entirely.
The garish carpet was chosen deliberately so nobody would linger in the corridor.
Garish under fluorescent light and rather lovely by candle, as it turned out.
The film garnered awards abroad and empty cinemas at home.
She garnered support one conversation at a time and won the vote unanimously.
The garrulous barber added twenty minutes and no information to every haircut.
Garrulous witnesses are a lawyer's nightmare and a journalist's dream.
Asking the fee at the funeral was gauche even by his standards.
Gauche is French for left, which is unfair to half the population.

gaunt.definition: thin and haggard from illness or hardship
sentences: He came back gaunt, cheerful, and unwilling to discuss any of it.
The gaunt outline of the mill against the sky is on every local postcard.
Drivers slowed to gawk, which caused a second accident behind the first.
It is possible to gawk politely, though nobody has managed it yet.
The gawky teenager grew into someone the camera followed around a room.
A gawky first draft can still contain the whole book.

generate.definition: to produce or bring into existence
sentences: The policy generated more paperwork than electricity.
One good question generates ten more, which is how research eats decades.

genesis.definition: the origin or beginning of something
sentences: The genesis of the project was an argument in a corridor about a chart.
Everyone claims to have been present at the genesis of anything successful.
His genial manner disguised the fact that he never conceded anything.
A genial host makes even a bad dinner memorable for the right reasons.
Genteel poverty means good furniture and no heating.
The genteel refusal took four sentences to say no.
The hotel's faded gentility was its entire selling point.
Gentility survives longest in the details nobody can afford to replace.

gentry.definition: people of high social class below nobility
sentences: The local gentry opposed the railway until they saw the compensation.
Country gentry produced most of the naturalists and nearly all of the diaries.

germane.definition: relevant to the matter at hand
sentences: The anecdote was entertaining and not remotely germane.
Germane and german both mean closely related; only one now applies to arguments.

gerrymander.definition: to redraw boundaries for political advantage
sentences: The district was gerrymandered into a shape that resembled a salamander, hence the name.
Gerrymandering lets representatives choose their voters instead of the reverse.
The idea gestated for six years in a notebook nobody else could read.
Let it gestate, said the editor, meaning put it in a drawer until January.

gestation.definition: a period of development before emergence
sentences: The law had a gestation of eleven years and a life of eighteen months.
After a long gestation, the design arrived fully formed and immediately obsolete.
The gibe about his accent was repeated so often it became his nickname.
A gibe is a jab; a jibe is a sailing maneuver, though few now distinguish them.

gird.definition: to prepare oneself for something difficult
sentences: The department girded itself for a review that turned out to be a formality.
Gird your loins is ancient advice meaning tuck in your robe before running.
The gist of forty pages was that nobody knew and everybody was busy.
Give me the gist, she said, and received the whole thing anyway.
Progress was glacial, which in this case meant visible only in photographs years apart.
Her glacial silence at dinner was more effective than any argument.
From three interviews she gleaned one fact that changed the whole story.
Gleaning was the right of the poor to gather what the harvest left behind.
The glib answer satisfied the room and none of the people who checked it.
Glib is what fluent sounds like when nothing is behind it.
He glowered at the vending machine as though it had insulted his family.
She glowered through the entire ceremony and applauded, once, at the end.
A glum silence followed the announcement of the new mandatory workshop.
He looked glum for a week and then bought a boat.
A glut of graduates in one field creates a shortage in another five years later.
The glut of tomatoes ended in nine jars of chutney nobody wanted.
He was goaded into a response that cost him considerably more than silence.
A goad was a spiked stick for driving cattle, which is exactly the manner intended.

goosebumps.definition: bumps on the skin from cold or emotion
sentences: The final chord gave four hundred people goosebumps simultaneously.
Goosebumps are a vestige of fur we no longer have, raising hair that no longer helps.
The evidence was gossamer: suggestive, beautiful, and unable to bear any weight.
Gossamer threads across the field are visible only for an hour after dawn.

gouge.definition: to overcharge; to cut out roughly
sentences: Hotels gouged travelers during the storm and were named in the paper for it.
The flood gouged a channel through what had been the main street.

gradation.definition: a gradual step or shading between stages
sentences: Between the two positions lie forty gradations, and every meeting occupies a different one.
The gradation of color from the horizon upward is the whole point of the painting.

graft.definition: corruption for personal gain; a transplant
sentences: Graft in the contracting office cost the city more than the projects were worth.
The skin graft took, and the scandal did not.
Egypt was the granary of Rome, which explains a great deal of Roman politics.
The granary burned in August, which is the worst possible month for a granary to burn.
The grandiloquent toast lasted eleven minutes and mentioned the couple twice.
Grandiloquent prose is a small idea in a very large coat.

grandstand.definition: to behave showily to impress onlookers
sentences: He grandstanded for the cameras and let the committee do the actual work.
Grandstanding at a hearing is free; governing afterward is not.
Granted, the timing was poor — but the decision was still correct.
The council granted permission and withheld the money, which amounted to refusal.

grapple.definition: to struggle with a problem or opponent
sentences: The essay grapples honestly with a question it never manages to answer.
Two committees grappled with the same problem in separate rooms for a year.
It gratified him enormously that the correction ran on the front page.
Instant gratification is expensive precisely because it is instant.
His grating laugh was audible through two doors and one very thick wall.
The grating cheerfulness of the hold music made the wait longer.
The advice was gratis and worth approximately that.
They offered the venue gratis, which turned out to include a bill for cleaning.
Her gratitude took the form of a letter that the recipient framed.
Gratitude expressed late is still better than gratitude felt silently.
The gratuitous insult in the footnote was the only part anyone quoted.
Gratuitous means both free of charge and uncalled for, which says something.
He failed to grasp the gravity of the situation until the lawyers arrived.
The gravity of his expression was undermined slightly by the party hat.
Gregarious to a fault, he knew everyone's name and nobody's phone number.
Gregarious animals form herds; gregarious people form committees.

grievance.definition: a real or imagined cause for complaint
sentences: The grievance was filed in March and resolved, sort of, in November.
An unaddressed grievance compounds faster than any debt.
A grievous error in the dosage was caught by a pharmacist who happened to look twice.
The loss was grievous and the statement about it was four lines long.
They griped about the coffee for years and organized nothing about the pay.
Griping is complaint with no intention of resolution.
The grisly details were omitted from the report and included in the podcast.
Grisly means horrifying; grizzly is a bear. Meeting the second can produce the first.
He groused about the new system and used it more than anyone else.
Soldiers grouse; when they stop, the officers worry.
Plato taught in a grove, which is why academies still pretend to have gardens.
The olive grove had been in the family since a war nobody could name.
He groveled by email, which is the most excruciating available medium.
Groveling rarely restores what honesty would have preserved.
Grudging respect from a rival is worth more than easy praise from a friend.
The grudging apology managed to blame the carpet.
Oliver Twist asked for more gruel, which tells you how bad the alternative was.
The soup was gruel with ambitions.
A single guffaw from the back row rescued a joke that had died on delivery.
His guffaw could be identified from another floor of the building.
He won the contract by guile and lost the renewal by reputation.
Guile is intelligence with the ethics removed.
Her guileless question exposed the whole scheme in one sentence.
Guileless in a negotiation is either a weakness or a very advanced technique.
The scam targeted the gullible and caught, as usual, the merely busy.
Everyone believes they are the one person too sharp to be gullible.
It took gumption to walk into that office without an appointment and a plan.
She had the gumption to ask and got what forty politer people did not.
The meal was a gustatory event and a financial one.
Gustatory memory outlasts almost every other kind, which is why smell ambushes you.
He attacked the buffet with a gusto the hosts had not budgeted for.
She sang badly and with such gusto that nobody minded.
A gusty afternoon ended the picnic and started a tradition of indoor ones.
Gusty conditions delayed the landing by an hour and the apology by three.
The speech was a chain of hackneyed phrases held together by pauses.
A hackney was a horse for hire, worn out by everyone — hence the word.
They haggled for forty minutes over a sum smaller than the coffee they drank afterward.
In some markets refusing to haggle is the rudest thing you can do.
The paper hailed the discovery as a breakthrough and buried the retraction.
He hailed a taxi and, in the same gesture, ended the argument.
The halcyon days of the department lasted from 1994 to a specific Tuesday in 1997.
The halcyon was said to calm the sea while nesting, which is where the word got its peace.

hale.definition: healthy and robust, especially in old age
sentences: Hale at ninety, he still cycled to the shop for a newspaper he did not read.
Hale and hearty is redundant and has survived anyway.
Understatement was the hallmark of her prose and the despair of her publisher.
Hallmarks were literal stamps applied at Goldsmiths' Hall to certify purity.
His halting delivery made the audience listen harder than any polish would have.
The negotiations resumed in a halting way and stopped again by Thursday.
Fog hampered the search for two days and then lifted, unhelpfully, at dusk.
The investigation was hampered by files that had been filed correctly, once, in 1978.

hamstrung.definition: severely restricted in ability to act
sentences: The agency was hamstrung by a budget that arrived nine months late.
To hamstring is to cut the tendon; the metaphor has not softened.
He had a hankering for the town he had spent his youth escaping.
A hankering for salt at midnight has ended many otherwise sound diets.
The filing was haphazard, which meant everything was findable by exactly one person.
A haphazard search found what a systematic one had missed twice.
The hapless intern was blamed for a decision made three levels above him.
Hapless means without hap, an old word for luck.
The harangue lasted forty minutes and converted precisely nobody.
A harangue differs from a speech mainly in the exits people take during it.

harbinger.definition: a sign of something to come
sentences: The first crocus is a harbinger of spring and, usually, of one more frost.
Falling orders were the harbinger; the closure took another eighteen months.

hardy.definition: tough and able to endure difficult conditions
sentences: The hardy little plant survived a winter that killed everything around it.
A hardy few stayed to the end of the meeting and shaped the entire policy.
The harried waiter took four orders, corrected two, and never once stopped smiling.
A harried expression at the airport is the most universal human experience.
The testimony harrowed a courtroom that had heard a great deal already.
A harrow breaks up soil; the verb does something similar to a person.
The harrowing account was read aloud once and never printed.
A harrowing journey makes for a terrible week and an excellent book.
Creditors harried the firm for a year before anyone senior returned a call.
Light cavalry harried the retreat and did more damage than the battle.
Her haughty dismissal of the question was quoted for a decade.
Haughty comes from "high": the nose is doing the talking.
The hauteur of the concierge suggested the hotel was doing you a favor.
Hauteur is arrogance that has been to finishing school.

haven.definition: a place of safety or refuge
sentences: The reading room was a haven from a building otherwise dedicated to noise.
A tax haven offers a different kind of shelter to a different kind of refugee.
They rushed headlong into a merger that took nine years to unwind.
He fell headlong down the stairs and blamed the carpet, correctly.

headstrong.definition: stubbornly determined to have one's way
sentences: The headstrong young captain ignored the chart and discovered a reef.
Headstrong is admirable in a founder and exhausting in a colleague.
The heady early months of the startup ended with the first payroll they nearly missed.
Heady praise from a stranger is more dangerous than criticism from a friend.
Nobody hearkened to the engineer, who had been right in 1998 as well.
The phrase "hearken back" preserves a verb that otherwise died two centuries ago.
He hectored the witness until the judge intervened on the witness's behalf.
Homer's Hector was the hero; the verb, unfairly, remembers only his menace.

hedge.definition: to avoid committing; to limit risk
sentences: He hedged so thoroughly that both sides quoted him as an ally.
The fund hedged its position and lost less than everyone who had been certain.

hedonism.definition: devotion to pleasure as the highest good
sentences: The city's reputation for hedonism outlasted the clubs that earned it.
Philosophical hedonism is more disciplined than the holiday brochure version.
He called himself a hedonist and went to bed at ten every night.
The hedonist's problem is that pleasure requires increasingly expensive maintenance.
Had anyone heeded the second memo, there would have been no third one.
Heed the small warning and you rarely meet the large one.

hegemony.definition: dominance of one group over others
sentences: Naval hegemony bought a century of trade terms nobody else could refuse.
Cultural hegemony works best when it is mistaken for common sense.
Cleaning the archive was a herculean task and, like the labors, mostly unwitnessed.
Hercules had twelve labors; the intern had a filing cabinet.

heretic.definition: one who dissents from accepted belief
sentences: The heretic of one century is the syllabus of the next.
He was treated as a heretic for suggesting the data be published.
The heretical suggestion that meetings could be shorter was never raised again.
Heretical ideas travel fastest where they are most forbidden.

hermetic.definition: airtight; sealed off from outside influence
sentences: The hermetic world of the department admitted no outside evidence for twenty years.
Hermetically sealed jars and hermetically sealed disciplines both eventually spoil.
He built a hermitage at the end of the garden and called it an office.
