The hermitage held one bed, one book, and forty years of silence.
Her heterodox methods produced results the orthodox ones had missed entirely.
Heterodox means other-teaching; orthodox means straight-teaching. Both are claims, not verdicts.
A heterogeneous committee argues more and decides better.
The sample was heterogeneous, which made the average meaningless.

hew.definition: to cut with blows; to adhere to closely
sentences: The steps were hewn from the rock by people whose names went unrecorded.
He hewed to the party line until the party changed it.
In its heyday the mill employed half the town and named the other half's streets.
Every heyday is identified only after it is over.
The hierarchical structure was drawn on one page and ignored on all the others.
Hierarchical organizations are efficient at obeying and terrible at noticing.
The formal hierarchy was on the wall; the real one met for coffee at eleven.
Every flat organization grows a hierarchy within eighteen months.
Bureaucracy hindered the rescue more effectively than the weather did.
Do not hinder someone doing your job for you.

hireling.definition: someone who works purely for pay
sentences: The hirelings did exactly what was contracted and not one minute more.
Calling an employee a hireling says more about the employer.
The histrionic resignation letter was leaked, framed, and quoted for years.
Histrionic grief at a public funeral raises questions no one is allowed to ask.

hoary.definition: old and stale; grey with age
sentences: He opened with a hoary joke that the audience had heard from his predecessor.
Hoary frost and hoary jokes share the same whiteness of age.
Sanctions hobbled the industry without ever quite closing it.
He hobbled to the finish line and refused a wheelchair on principle.
The regulation is a hodgepodge of three eras and four compromises.
Dinner was a hodgepodge of leftovers and, unexpectedly, excellent.
The film pays homage to four directors and steals openly from a fifth.
Homage was once a formal oath of loyalty; now it is a knowing camera angle.
His homespun wisdom charmed voters and alarmed economists.
The homespun aesthetic of the campaign cost four hundred thousand to produce.
The staff meeting ended with a homily about ownership that owned nothing.
A good homily is six minutes long; almost none are.
A homogeneous team agrees quickly and misses the same things together.
Milk is homogenized so the cream stops separating, which is a fair metaphor.
The neighborhood is architecturally homogenous and socially anything but.
Homogenous is technically a biology term that has swallowed homogeneous whole.
Investors were hoodwinked by a prospectus that mentioned the risk in a footnote.
To hoodwink was to blindfold someone before robbing them, which is honest etymology.
A horde of tourists arrived at eleven and the village disappeared until three.
Horde comes from a Mongol word for camp, which the camps earned.
The claim was hotly denied and quietly settled.
Two candidates hotly contested a seat that was abolished the following year.
Reporters hounded the family for a comment that never came.
He was hounded out of the job by a campaign nobody would admit to running.

hubbub.definition: a loud confused noise or commotion
sentences: The hubbub in the corridor made it clear the decision had leaked.
After the hubbub died down, the actual policy remained entirely unchanged.
It was hubris to name the ship unsinkable and hubris to sail it fast through ice.
Greek tragedy runs on hubris the way engines run on fuel.

humble.definition: to lower in pride or status
sentences: The result humbled a team that had spent the week explaining why it would win.
Nothing humbles a writer like reading their own first draft aloud.
The humdrum work of checking references is what keeps the exciting work honest.
He escaped a humdrum job for an exciting one and missed the humdrum one by March.
Correcting him publicly humiliated him and fixed nothing.
The scoreline humiliated a side that had been favorites for a decade.
They pitched the tent on a hummock and stayed dry while the field flooded.
Every hummock in that field marks a building nobody living has seen.
The trolley hurtled down the ramp and into a display of very expensive glass.
The deadline hurtled toward them at the usual, unstoppable rate.
She husbanded her energy through the first four rounds and won the fifth.
The estate husbanded its timber for two centuries and sold it in one.

husbandry.definition: careful management of resources or farming
sentences: Good husbandry kept the farm solvent through two droughts and one bank.
Financial husbandry is the least glamorous and most effective form of strategy.
"I've told you a million times" is hyperbole, and it has been said about that often.
Advertising is hyperbole with a legal department.
The coverage grew hysterical while the actual risk stayed unchanged.
Hysterical comes from the Greek for womb, which is a whole chapter of medical history.
The iconoclast of 1975 was giving keynote addresses by 1995.
Iconoclasts literally smashed images; now they merely smash assumptions on podcasts.
His iconoclastic first book made his name and his second one apologized for it.
Iconoclastic design ages faster than the conventions it mocked.

ideological.definition: based on a system of beliefs
sentences: The objection was ideological, which meant no amount of data would settle it.
Ideological purity and electoral arithmetic rarely share a room.

ideology.definition: a system of beliefs guiding action
sentences: An ideology explains everything, which is precisely the problem with it.
The party had an ideology at founding and a marketing department by year ten.
His one idiosyncrasy was writing every draft in green ink.
Idiosyncrasies are charming in a colleague and unbearable in a housemate.
Her idiosyncratic filing system was unusable by anyone else and flawless for her.
An idiosyncratic style is only called a style once it succeeds.
The idolatrous devotion of his fans made honest criticism impossible.
An idolatrous attitude to founders has killed more companies than competition.
The idolatry of growth crowded out every other measure of success.
Idolatry of the past is called heritage; idolatry of the future is called vision.
The idyllic photograph omits the motorway forty meters to the left.
Two idyllic weeks were followed by a bill nobody had discussed.
An ignoble motive can still produce a useful outcome, which complicates the moral.
It was an ignoble end to a career of genuine service.
The ignominious exit involved a taxi, a cardboard box, and a security escort.
An ignominious defeat is remembered longer than a narrow one.
He suffered the ignominy of being escorted from a building he had designed.
Ignominy fades; the photograph of it does not.
The illiberality of the committee showed in what it refused to discuss.
Illiberality with money is stinginess; with ideas it is worse.
The illicit trade moved through the same ports as the legal one and paid better.
Illicit is forbidden; elicit is drawing out. Confusing them creates strange sentences.
The gains were illusory: the currency had moved and nothing else had.
Illusory progress is more dangerous than none, because it stops the search.
An illustrious career ended over a dispute about a parking permit.
Illustrious predecessors make a difficult inheritance.
He imbibed the assumptions of the field before he could name any of them.
They imbibed rather more than intended and agreed to everything by midnight.
The whole imbroglio began with a misfiled expense claim for eleven pounds.
An imbroglio is a scandal that is too complicated to summarize.
The teacher imbued a whole generation with a suspicion of easy answers.
The room was imbued with the smell of coffee and old paper.
His immaculate record was the reason the accusation caused such disbelief.
The workshop was immaculate, which told you something about how little was built there.
Whether he liked the policy is immaterial; he signed it.
The objection was immaterial and consumed forty minutes anyway.
The collapse was imminent for three years before it finally arrived.
Imminent is about to happen, eminent is distinguished, immanent is dwelling within.

immure.definition: to shut away as if in prison
sentences: He immured himself in the library for a winter and emerged with the manuscript.
The word contains "wall": to immure is to build one around someone.
The laws of physics are immutable; the interpretations are revised annually.
Nothing in the contract was immutable except the fee.
Four hours of sleep impairs judgment as much as a legal limit of alcohol.
The injury impaired his grip and not, notably, his ambition.
The best teachers impart a method rather than a set of facts.
A drop of vanilla imparts more than its size suggests.
An impartial chair is worth two clever ones.
He claimed to be impartial and was seen dining with one side twice.

impasse.definition: a deadlock with no way forward
sentences: The talks reached an impasse over a word that appeared once in an annex.
An impasse is broken by a new fact or a new person, rarely by a new argument.
He remained impassive through the verdict and wept in the corridor.
The impassive face of the negotiator was the most valuable thing in the room.
Her timing was impeccable, arriving exactly as the objection was being formed.
Impeccable literally means incapable of sin, which is a lot to ask of a haircut.
The impecunious student ate the same meal for a year and learned to cook it well.
Impecunious poets are a cliché that the rent has kept remarkably accurate.
Roadworks impeded the ambulance for four crucial minutes.
The Latin root is "in the feet": to impede is to shackle.
The only impediment to the plan was that it required money nobody had.
A speech impediment ended his broadcasting career and started a better one in print.

impel.definition: to drive or urge into action
sentences: Curiosity impelled her to open a file that had been sealed for forty years.
Impel pushes from behind; compel forces from in front.
A sense of impending reorganization hung over the office all autumn.
Nothing focuses a team like an impending audit.

impenetrable.definition: impossible to pass through or understand
sentences: The prose was impenetrable, which some reviewers mistook for depth.
The hedge was impenetrable to everything except the neighbor's cat.
One careless email imperiled a negotiation that had taken two years.
Cutting the inspections imperiled everyone and saved almost nothing.
An imperious wave sent the waiter across the room and the guests into silence.
Imperious manners work exactly as long as the authority behind them lasts.
The clay layer is impermeable, which is why the reservoir holds at all.
He was impermeable to advice from anyone paid less than he was.
The impertinent question was the only one worth answering.
Impertinent originally meant simply irrelevant, and rudeness attached itself later.
The imperturbable clerk processed the complaint, the shouting, and the apology identically.
Imperturbable is not the same as uncaring, though it is often mistaken for it.
He is impervious to criticism, which is a strength for a novelist and a flaw in a manager.
The coating is impervious to salt water and, apparently, to seagulls.
An impetuous resignation over lunch became a two-year legal matter.
Impetuous in youth and cautious in office is the usual sequence.

impetus.definition: a force that drives something forward
sentences: The scandal gave the reform an impetus that ten years of argument had not.
The impetus faded within a year and the committee met on.
He was charged with impiety, which in Athens covered almost any inconvenient question.
There is a mild impiety in laughing at your own field, and it is usually healthy.

impious.definition: showing no respect for the sacred
sentences: The impious joke was cut from the broadcast and circulated widely regardless.
An impious remark in the wrong century could cost a great deal more than a job.
An implacable creditor pursued the estate for nineteen years.
Time is implacable, which is the entire subject of most poetry.
The alibi was implausible and, inconveniently for the prosecution, true.
Real life is full of implausible coincidences that no editor would permit.
The receipts implicated three people who had insisted they never met.
He implicated himself by explaining something nobody had asked about.
The implication of the memo was clear and its wording was carefully not.
Consider the implications before congratulating yourself on the finding.
The implicit assumption was that someone else would do the checking.
She had implicit trust in her editor, which he had earned over twenty years.
The company imploded in six weeks, taking four suppliers with it.
Buildings are imploded on purpose so they fall on their own footprint.
It was impolitic to mention the audit at the retirement dinner.
Impolitic honesty ends more careers than dishonesty does.
The forecast handles the numbers and ignores the imponderables entirely.
Weather, mood, and traffic are the three imponderables of any launch day.
The importunate emails arrived nightly until somebody finally answered.
An importunate request eventually gets what a reasonable one could not.
He importuned the committee weekly until it created a rule about him.
Importuned by both sides, she published the data and satisfied neither.
The imposed deadline was met and the imposed method was quietly abandoned.
Order imposed from outside lasts exactly as long as the imposing.
The imposing entrance hall led to nine very small offices.
He was physically imposing and, in argument, entirely harmless.
Staying an extra hour was framed as a favor and functioned as an imposition.
The imposition of the levy was announced on a Friday afternoon, as always.

imposture.definition: the act of deceiving by pretending to be someone else
sentences: The imposture lasted eleven years and included two published papers.
An imposture is undone by one person who actually knows the field.
He muttered an imprecation at the printer and, briefly, felt better.
The letter ended with an imprecation that the lawyers advised removing.

impregnable.definition: unable to be captured or broken into
sentences: The impregnable fortress fell to a bribe rather than a siege.
His argument seemed impregnable until somebody checked the first citation.

improbable.definition: unlikely to be true or happen
sentences: An improbable sequence of small errors produced a completely predictable disaster.
Improbable things happen constantly, because there are so many of them available.

improvident.definition: failing to plan for the future
sentences: Improvident spending in the good years made the bad ones unsurvivable.
The improvident grasshopper is the villain of a fable written by ants.
When the projector died she improvised with a whiteboard and did better.
Improvising well requires knowing the material better than reading it would.

imprudence.definition: lack of care or good judgment
sentences: The imprudence was not the investment but the failure to read anything about it.
Youthful imprudence is forgiven; the same act at fifty is called character.
It was imprudent to sign before the survey and expensive to discover why.
An imprudent remark in a small town outlives the person who made it.
The impudent reply got him fired and quoted approvingly for a decade.
Impudent children grow into either comedians or defendants.

impugn.definition: to attack as false or questionable
sentences: He impugned her motives rather than address a single one of her figures.
To impugn a witness is a strategy; to refute one is an argument.
They dumped waste with impunity for eleven years and a fine of nine thousand.
Impunity is not the absence of rules but the absence of enforcement.

impute.definition: to attribute a fault or quality to
sentences: Never impute malice where a missed email will do.
The court declined to impute knowledge to a director who had signed the page.
An inadvertent copy-and-paste sent the salary list to the whole company.
Inadvertent harm still requires an apology, however sincere the surprise.
The panel discussion achieved a level of inanity rare even for conferences.
The inanity of the slogan was its greatest commercial strength.
He was inarticulate in meetings and devastating on paper.
Inarticulate rage is the hardest kind to answer or to help.
An inborn resistance to the disease protects about one person in three hundred.
Nothing about the talent was inborn; the willingness to practice may have been.
Her incandescent performance carried a production that was otherwise a shambles.
He was incandescent with rage, which was more informative than his usual calm.
Macbeth imagines the seas turned incarnadine, which is Shakespeare showing off.
The incarnadine sky at sunset made everyone stop and take the same photograph.
The incendiary speech was delivered to two hundred people and read by four million.
An incendiary device burns; an incendiary remark spreads faster.
The dismissal of the complaint incensed a group that had been merely annoyed.
One word in the second paragraph incensed the entire readership.
The incentive scheme rewarded speed and produced, predictably, a great deal of rework.
People respond to incentives, including the ones you did not intend to create.
The incessant drilling next door made working from home a theoretical option.
Incessant complaint achieves less than one well-timed letter.

inchoate.definition: just begun and not fully formed
sentences: The movement was inchoate: real anger, no leadership, and three competing hashtags.
An inchoate idea should not be judged by the standards of a finished one.
The incidental costs exceeded the main budget line by a factor of two.
An incidental detail in the footnote turned out to be the actual story.
Incipient cracks in the coalition were visible to everyone except the coalition.
Incipient panic in a crowd is quieter than you expect.
Her incisive summary reduced a three-hour argument to one printable sentence.
Incisive means cutting: it removes what does not matter.
The match was abandoned due to inclement weather and a flooded car park.
Inclement conditions revealed which of the tents had been tested.
I am inclined to agree, which is as close to a yes as he ever came.
She was inclined to caution and, on this occasion, spectacularly wasn't.
The price is inclusive, which is why the total surprised nobody at checkout.
An inclusive process takes longer and produces decisions that survive.

inconclusive.definition: not leading to a definite result
sentences: The tests were inconclusive, which the headline reported as a discovery.
Two inconclusive studies do not add up to one conclusive one.

incongruity.definition: a lack of harmony or fit
sentences: The incongruity of a chandelier in a garden shed was the whole joke.
Comedy is largely engineered incongruity delivered with a straight face.
His cheerful tie was incongruous at a hearing about mass redundancy.
The incongruous glass extension is either the building's ruin or its rescue.
The change looked inconsequential and altered every downstream calculation.
Meetings expand to fill the time with inconsequential detail.
The inconstancy of the funding made planning beyond a year impossible.
He was accused of inconstancy by people who had changed their minds twice as often.
The video evidence was incontrovertible and the denial continued anyway.
Very little is incontrovertible; a great deal is merely inconvenient to controvert.

incorporate.definition: to include as part of a whole
sentences: The final draft incorporated three objections and ignored the fourth entirely.
The design incorporates the old wall, which was cheaper than removing it.
He is an incorrigible optimist, which has cost him money and saved his health.
The word literally means uncorrectable, which teachers use fondly and courts use plainly.
The incredulous silence lasted long enough for him to repeat the number.
Incredulous is the listener; incredible is the claim.

incubation.definition: a period of development before emergence
sentences: The incubation of the idea took four years and its execution took six weeks.
The incubation period explains why the outbreak was invisible until it was everywhere.
The school inculcated punctuality so thoroughly that alumni arrive early to funerals.
Inculcate comes from stamping with the heel, which is how repetition feels.
The incumbent lost to a challenger who had campaigned for eleven months.
It is incumbent on the author to check what the footnote actually says.
She remained indebted to a teacher who never learned what she had done.
The company was indebted to three banks and loyal to none.
It was thought indecorous to celebrate before the results were confirmed.
The indecorous joke was cut from the speech and told in the bar.
The indefatigable volunteer answered letters for thirty years without pay.
Indefatigable means literally not able to be tired out, which few people qualify for.

indemnify.definition: to compensate for loss or protect from liability
sentences: The contract indemnified the supplier against everything except doing the job badly.
He was indemnified for the loss and never for the inconvenience.
The painting is of indeterminate date, which lowered the price and raised the interest.
Sentenced for an indeterminate period is a phrase that should alarm everybody.

indication.definition: a sign or piece of evidence
sentences: There was no indication of trouble until the third quarter, when there was nothing else.
An early indication is not a conclusion, though headlines disagree.

indict.definition: to formally charge with a crime
sentences: A grand jury would indict a ham sandwich, as the saying goes.
The report does not indict individuals; it indicts a system that produced them.

indictment.definition: a formal charge; a damning criticism
sentences: The waiting list is an indictment of a decade of decisions, not of any one nurse.
The indictment ran ninety pages and rested on a single spreadsheet.
Public indifference killed the proposal more efficiently than opposition would have.
The opposite of love is indifference, which requires no maintenance at all.
The service was indifferent and the food was worse, which the review said politely.
He was indifferent to praise and unusually sensitive to being ignored.
He died in indigence, and three museums now compete for his sketches.
Indigence is poverty severe enough to require someone else's decision.
The indigenous oak supports six hundred species; the imported ornamental supports four.
Indigenous knowledge of the coast predates every map of it.
Free legal representation exists for indigent defendants and is funded like an afterthought.
The indigent scholar dined on invitations for two years.
He was indignant about the accusation and specific about nothing else.
Indignant letters to the editor are the most reliable free content in publishing.
Public indignation lasted four days and changed one line of the policy.
Righteous indignation is the most enjoyable emotion and the least useful.
Indiscriminate cuts removed the waste and the two people who understood the system.
Indiscriminate praise is worth exactly as much as indiscriminate criticism.
The indispensable colleague went on leave and the department discovered it was true.
Graveyards are full of indispensable people, as the French say.
He indited a letter of complaint that took three days and was never sent.
Indite is to write; indict is to charge. They are pronounced identically, which is cruel.
An indolent summer produced nothing but a suntan and one very good idea.
He was indolent about everything except the one hobby he pursued fanatically.
Her indomitable insistence outlasted four ministers and won the inquiry.
Indomitable spirit is what we call stubbornness once it succeeds.
The industrious apprentice outlasted three clever ones.
Industrious is not the same as productive, as many long days demonstrate.

ineffable.definition: too great to be expressed in words
sentences: He described the ineffable for two pages, which rather undercut the claim.
The ineffable quality of the performance was, by definition, missing from every review.
The ineluctable arithmetic of the pension fund defeated every clever proposal.
Ineluctable means you cannot wrestle your way out, which is the literal root.
The inept cover-up drew more attention than the original error would have.
He was inept at small talk and formidable in a crisis.
The inequity was measurable, documented, and defended as tradition.
Inequity is unfairness; iniquity is wickedness. A single letter and a moral world apart.
He argued for the inerrancy of the text and against reading it closely.
Nobody has ever claimed inerrancy for a timetable, which shows some sense.
The committee was inert for two years and then, alarmingly, decisive.
Argon is inert, which is why it is used to protect things from air.
The inexorable rise of the water made the argument about drainage academic.
Inexorable means unmoved by pleading, which describes both glaciers and deadlines.
No system is infallible, and the ones described as such fail most spectacularly.
His infallible method worked twice and was retired quietly after the third attempt.
The infelicitous phrase in the press release cost a week of clarification.
An infelicitous choice of venue put the grief counselors next to the bar.
From the silence she inferred that the decision had already been made.
The speaker implies; the listener infers. Swapping them is the commonest error in English.
Moths infested the archive and ate exactly the box that mattered.
The comment section was infested with accounts created that morning.
Inflammable and flammable mean the same thing, which has caused actual fires.
The inflammable mood in the hall needed only one careless sentence.
The inflammatory headline was corrected on page nineteen a week later.
Inflammatory language in a crowded room is a physical act, not a verbal one.

inform.definition: to give shape to; to tell
sentences: A deep reading of the archives informs every page of the book without being visible.
Nobody informed the night staff, who discovered the closure on the door.
The ingenious solution used two paperclips and one insight nobody else had.
Ingenious is inventive; ingenuous is innocent. The two get swapped constantly.
She was cast as the ingenue at nineteen and refused the part at twenty.
The ingenue role has ruined more careers than it has launched.
Wartime ingenuity built a working radio from a razor blade and a pencil.
Ingenuity is what a small budget produces and a large one buries.
Her ingenuous question about the accounts emptied the room.
An ingenuous manner is the most effective disguise available, which is why it is suspected.

ingrained.definition: deeply fixed and hard to change
sentences: Ingrained habits survived the reorganization, the merger, and the motivational posters.
The stain was ingrained, as was the argument about who caused it.
He called them ingrates for not thanking him for a favor nobody had requested.
Every benefactor eventually suspects the world is full of ingrates.
He ingratiated himself with the board and never once spoke to the staff.
Ingratiating behavior is obvious to everyone except its intended target.

inherent.definition: existing as an essential part of something
sentences: The risk is inherent in the design and cannot be trained away.
Inherent limitations are the ones that survive every version of the plan.
Fear of looking foolish inhibits more questions than ignorance does.
The drug inhibits an enzyme, which sounds modest and changes everything downstream.
Constant interruption is inimical to the kind of thought the job requires.
The climate is inimical to olives and generous to everything else.
His inimitable style was imitated by four hundred writers, none successfully.
The inimitable thing about her lectures was that nobody left.
The iniquitous tax fell hardest on those least able to pay and stayed for forty years.
An iniquitous system rarely needs iniquitous individuals to operate it.
The pamphlet catalogued the iniquities of the mill and was banned within a month.
Iniquity is wickedness; inequity is unfairness. Both were present.
Nobody had an inkling of the resignation until the email arrived at seven.
She had an inkling in March and confirmation in September.
An innate sense of direction is mostly a well-practiced one.
The debate over what is innate has outlasted every generation of evidence.
The innocuous-looking clause let either party walk away without penalty.
An innocuous question at the right moment can end a career.
The fire alarm chose an inopportune moment during the marriage proposal.
An inopportune truth is still a truth, told badly.
An inordinate amount of the meeting concerned the biscuits.
He took inordinate pride in a hedge that took eleven years to grow.

inquest.definition: an official inquiry, especially into a death
sentences: The inquest found systemic failure and named nobody, as inquests do.
After the defeat came the inquest, which lasted longer than the season.
An inquisitive child asks the question the adults have agreed to leave alone.
Inquisitive is a compliment right up until it becomes a complaint.
His inscrutable expression during the negotiation was worth several million.
The rules were inscrutable, which was either incompetence or design.
Insensate rage broke a window and solved nothing.
The machinery grinds on, insensate, whatever the quarterly report says.
He was insensible to the offense he had caused and cheerfully repeated it.
By the third hour the audience was insensible to any further statistics.

insidious.definition: harmful in a gradual, hidden way
sentences: The most insidious errors are the ones that produce plausible results.
Insidious comes from ambush: the harm is waiting rather than charging.

insinuate.definition: to suggest slyly; to work in gradually
sentences: He insinuated that the results were convenient and refused to say so plainly.
She insinuated herself into the committee by volunteering for the worst subcommittee.
The insipid sequel kept the cast and lost whatever had made the first one work.
Insipid means without flavor, which applies to soup and to prose.
She insisted on seeing the raw data and found the error in twenty minutes.
He insisted he was calm, at volume.
The insolence of the reply was noted by everyone and punished by nobody.
Insolence from the powerless is bravery; from the powerful it is something else.
His insolent shrug ended a conversation that had been going quite well.
The insolent letter was framed by its recipient, which was the best possible answer.
The firm was insolvent for eleven months before anyone was legally required to say so.
Insolvent means the arithmetic has stopped working, whatever the confidence says.
He accepted the verdict with an insouciance that infuriated the prosecution.
Insouciance is charming in a friend and terrifying in a pilot.
The lecture inspired four students and irritated the other two hundred.
Inspire means to breathe in, which is a fair description of what a good idea feels like.
In this instance the rule was applied; in the four before it, it was not.
One instance is an anecdote; forty is a pattern.

institute.definition: to establish or set in motion
sentences: They instituted proceedings on a Friday, which delayed everything by a weekend.
The policy instituted in 1974 was reviewed for the first time in 2009.
He was insufferable after the promotion and, oddly, delightful before it.
The insufferable heat emptied the office by two o'clock.
The insular department cited only itself for a decade.
Insular literally means island-like, which is exactly the mental geography.
The insularity of the profession is its greatest defense and its permanent weakness.
Two conferences a year cured a decade of insularity.
The insurgents held the valley for three years and the roads for none of it.
Party insurgents won the primary and inherited a machine built to stop them.
The insurrection lasted nine days and rewrote the constitution for ninety years.
An insurrection that succeeds is renamed a revolution by its own historians.
The instructions became intelligible only after the device was already assembled.
Making a hard idea intelligible is harder than having it.

intemperance.definition: lack of moderation, especially in drinking
sentences: His intemperance cost him a liver, a marriage, and eventually a knighthood.
Intemperance in argument loses more cases than weak evidence does.

intend.definition: to plan or mean to do
sentences: He intended the remark kindly, which the transcript entirely failed to convey.
The road to trouble is paved with things people intended to do on Monday.
Two weeks of intensive study beat six months of the leisurely kind.
Intensive farming produces more per acre and fewer birds per hedgerow.
He was interred in a village churchyard beside a rival he had outlived by a week.
The report was interred in an appendix and never exhumed.

interchangeable.definition: able to be swapped without difference
sentences: The parts are interchangeable, which is why the repair took nine minutes.
The candidates' policies were interchangeable and their accents were not.
The court interdicted the sale pending a full valuation.
Naval patrols interdicted the shipments and quadrupled the price.
An intermediary carried messages between two people in the same building.
Removing the intermediary saves a fee and loses a translator.
The interminable introduction outlasted two audience members and one microphone battery.
Interminable means literally without end, which is how the meeting felt at hour three.
Intermittent faults are the worst kind: they vanish whenever an engineer arrives.
Intermittent rain ruined the match without ever stopping it.

internecine.definition: destructive to both sides within a group
sentences: Internecine feuding cost the party three elections and one entire generation.
Internecine conflict is the only kind where both sides can lose completely.

interplay.definition: the way things affect each other
sentences: The interplay of light and shadow does more work in that film than the dialogue.
Policy is the interplay of intention and whatever the ministry can actually implement.

interpolate.definition: to insert something between existing parts
sentences: A later scribe interpolated three lines that theologians argued over for centuries.
You interpolate between known points and extrapolate beyond them, at your own risk.

interregnum.definition: a gap between two reigns or governments
sentences: During the interregnum, three deputies each behaved as though they had been chosen.
The interregnum lasted eight months and produced the department's best work.
The two families' fortunes were intertwined through four generations and one lawsuit.
Their careers were intertwined so tightly that neither could be described alone.
He intimated that funds might be found, and nothing was ever written down.
The verb intimates; the adjective is close and private. Same spelling, different stress.
The first intimation of trouble was a supplier asking to be paid in advance.
There was no intimation in the letter of what the meeting would actually decide.
The problem was intractable for forty years and then dissolved in one paper.
An intractable colleague is more expensive than an incompetent one.
Both sides were intransigent, which is why the mediator lasted nine days.
Intransigence is principle when you agree with it and obstruction when you do not.
The intrepid reporter filed from a rooftop with a satellite phone and a bad cough.
Intrepid means not trembling, which is a lower bar than it sounds.
Court intrigue consumed more energy than governing ever did.
The department's intrigue was conducted entirely by calendar invitation.
The problem is intrinsic to the design and no amount of training will fix it.
Intrinsic motivation outlasts every bonus scheme ever invented.
A week of introspection produced one useful decision and four abandoned ones.
Introspection is unreliable evidence about a mind and the only evidence available.
The office was inundated with applications and staffed by two people.
The river inundated the water meadows, which is what water meadows are for.
Ten years of night shifts inured him to a schedule nobody else could survive.
You can be inured to bad news and still notice when it changes.
Inured to rejection, she submitted the manuscript for the twenty-third time.
Nurses grow inured to the sights and never to the families.
The invasive species arrived in ballast water and rewrote the whole lake.
Invasive questions at an interview reveal more about the interviewer.
The letter descended into invective by the second paragraph and never recovered.
Invective is the sound of an argument that has run out of arguments.

inveigle.definition: to persuade by flattery or deceit
sentences: He inveigled his way onto the guest list with a name that resembled someone important's.
She inveigled two colleagues into a project neither had time for.
The investiture took forty minutes and the actual handover took a year.
Investiture disputes between kings and popes shaped medieval Europe more than most battles.
An inveterate note-taker, he filled sixty notebooks and read none of them twice.
Inveterate liars are undone by memory, not by conscience.

invidious.definition: likely to cause resentment; unfairly discriminating
sentences: Ranking colleagues publicly puts the manager in an invidious position.
The invidious comparison to her predecessor followed her for a decade.
A cold walk invigorated a discussion that had died indoors.
New funding invigorated a department that had been coasting since 2011.

inviolable.definition: never to be broken or violated
sentences: The inviolable rule about Sunday lunch survived three house moves and one divorce.
Diplomatic immunity treats an embassy as inviolable, which occasionally strains everyone's patience.
The seal remained inviolate for four hundred years and eleven minutes.
His privacy stayed inviolate until the biography arrived.

invocation.definition: an appeal to authority or a higher power
sentences: The invocation of national security ended the questioning immediately.
The ceremony opened with an invocation nobody under forty could follow.

invoke.definition: to call on for support or authority
sentences: He invoked a precedent from 1931 that turned out to have been overturned in 1932.
To invoke tradition is to hope nobody looks up when it started.
The explanation was too involved to fit in the summary, which is usually a warning.
She was involved in four projects and finishing none of them.
He believed his position invulnerable right up until the audit began.
Achilles was invulnerable except at one tendon, which is now a proverb.
The irascible chef ran the best kitchen and the highest staff turnover in the city.
Irascible before coffee and merely difficult after it.
The parking policy drew the ire of everyone who had ever owned a car.
Ire is short, old, and much loved by headline writers for exactly that reason.
It irked him that the correction never received the attention the error had.
Small things irk; large things enrage. The small ones do more cumulative damage.
The irksome requirement to log every hour produced logs nobody ever read.
An irksome colleague is survivable; an irksome commute is not.
The ironclad guarantee had one exception, and it was the one that occurred.
An ironclad alibi is generally the most suspicious kind.

irony.definition: an outcome contrary to what was expected
sentences: The irony of the fire station burning down was noted by absolutely everyone.
Irony survives translation badly, which is why treaties avoid it.
The logic was irrefutable and the premise was invented.
Irrefutable evidence still requires somebody willing to look at it.
An irresolute leader is worse in a crisis than a wrong one.
He stood irresolute in the doorway until the decision made itself.
The irreverent obituary was the only one the family actually liked.
Irreverent humor is the immune system of an institution.
The transfer was irrevocable, as the terms had said in a font nobody read.
Very few decisions are truly irrevocable, and those are worth a second night's sleep.

issue.definition: to send out or publish officially
sentences: The ministry issued a denial that raised more questions than the story had.
Passports are issued in four weeks and, in emergencies, in four hours.

itinerant.definition: traveling from place to place for work
sentences: An itinerant teacher covered six villages and slept in a different one each night.
Itinerant work suits the young and punishes everyone else.

itinerary.definition: a planned route or travel schedule
sentences: The itinerary allowed eleven minutes between two airports in different cities.
A good itinerary is mostly the things you decided to leave out.

itinerate.definition: to travel from place to place
sentences: Preachers itinerated between market towns, drawing crowds and complaints in equal number.
He itinerated for a decade and then bought a shop.
The jargon exists to save time among specialists and to exclude everyone else.
Strip the jargon and the memo said: we don't know yet.

jaundice.definition: bitterness or prejudice; a yellowing condition
sentences: Twenty years in the industry left him with a jaundice toward every press release.
The jaundiced eye sees corruption in every coincidence.
The jejune conclusion undid three chapters of genuinely careful work.
Jejune comes from a Latin word for fasting: the writing is undernourished.
Publishing early would jeopardize the patent, so the paper waited eleven months.
One careless sentence jeopardized four years of quiet negotiation.
Her jet hair in the portrait is the only thing the restorer did not touch.
Jet is a fossilized wood, which is why jet-black is a mineral color.
The plan jettisoned its most interesting feature to satisfy a regulator's footnote.
Ships jettison cargo to stay afloat, which is where the word and the wisdom come from.

jibe.definition: to agree or be consistent with
sentences: His story did not jibe with the timestamps, which ended the interview.
As a noun it is a taunt; as a verb, agreement. English enjoys this sort of thing.
The editorial's jingoism embarrassed the paper within a decade.
Jingoism comes from a music-hall song, which is a fittingly cheap origin.
The jingoist demanded a war he had no intention of attending.
Every jingoist is certain he speaks for a silent, agreeing nation.
His jocular tone at the disciplinary hearing was a serious miscalculation.
A jocular aside can carry a criticism that a direct one could not.
Wordsworth found the daffodils jocund, which is a lot to ask of a flower.
The jocund mood at breakfast did not survive the agenda.
The jovial doorman knew four hundred names and every one of the dogs.
Jovial comes from Jupiter, whose astrological influence was supposed to make you cheerful.
Jubilant supporters filled a square that had been empty an hour earlier.
The jubilant press release was withdrawn when the result was recounted.
A judicious edit removed the one paragraph that would have caused a lawsuit.
Judicious silence has saved more careers than eloquence.
The retail juggernaut opened four hundred stores and closed a thousand smaller ones.
The word comes from a temple cart said to crush those in its path.
At this juncture, the polite phrase for right now, the money ran out.
The company reached a juncture where doing nothing was the most expensive option.

junket.definition: a trip taken at someone else's expense
sentences: The fact-finding junket found four facts and one very good beach.
Journalists on a junket rarely write anything the host will regret.

junta.definition: a military group ruling after seizing power
sentences: The junta promised elections within a year and held them within eleven.
A junta always announces that it acted reluctantly, and always at dawn.

justify.definition: to show to be right or reasonable
sentences: The results justified a method that had looked reckless for two years.
If you have to justify it three times, it may not be justified.

juxtapose.definition: to place side by side for contrast
sentences: The exhibit juxtaposes the sketch and the finished work, to the sketch's advantage.
Juxtaposing the two budgets made the argument without a word of commentary.
A keen observer noticed that the shadows in the photograph fell two ways.
He was keen to start and keener still to be finished.

kindle.definition: to start a fire or arouse feeling
sentences: One good teacher kindled an interest that lasted fifty years.
It takes dry wood to kindle a fire and dry facts to kindle an argument.
The sculpture is kinetic, which means the museum employs someone to oil it.
Her kinetic style of teaching left the front row exhausted.

knack.definition: a natural skill or clever trick
sentences: She had a knack for asking the question that unlocked the whole interview.
There is a knack to the door, which the landlord mentions only after you move in.

knell.definition: a sound signaling the end of something
sentences: The supplier's withdrawal sounded the knell for the whole project.
A knell is a bell rung slowly, which is why the metaphor is so heavy.

knight.definition: to confer an honorary title on
sentences: He was knighted for services to a charity he had joined the previous year.
Being knighted changes the name on the letters and nothing else whatsoever.
They picnicked on a knoll with a view of the road they had escaped.
One grassy knoll has done more for conspiracy theories than any document.
He refused to kowtow to a board that had never read the research.
Kowtowing began as a literal forehead-to-floor bow at the Chinese court.
Kudos went to the department that announced the work, not the one that did it.
Kudos is singular in Greek, which has not stopped anyone.
Once labeled difficult, she found every disagreement read as proof.
Labeling a problem is often mistaken for solving it.

labor.definition: to work hard; to belabor a point
sentences: He labored the analogy until it collapsed under its own weight.
They labored for six months on a report the minister read in the car.
The laborious transcription took a year and revealed one crucial sentence.
His laborious prose is the sound of someone working very hard in the wrong direction.
The review lacerated the book and made its author famous.
Barbed wire lacerated the coat and, eventually, the argument for shortcuts.
The lachrymose finale had the audience reaching for handkerchiefs and the critics for adjectives.
Lachrymose comes from the Latin for tear, which the word does look like.
A lackluster first half was followed by a second half that was worse.
Lackluster literally means without shine, which is a kinder way to say boring.
Asked to describe the disaster, the laconic engineer said only: "It fell."
Sparta was so laconic that a threat of invasion drew a one-word reply: "If."
The laggards in the adoption curve turned out to have been right to wait.
One laggard on a group hike sets the pace for everyone.
He lambasted the plan in public and adopted it in November.
Lambast and lambaste are the same word arguing about a silent E.
The auditors lambasted a process that three previous audits had merely noted.
Being lambasted in the trade press did the company less harm than the silence before it.
Editors have lamented the decline of attention since roughly the invention of print.
He lamented the loss of the old building while approving its replacement.
The cartoon lampooned all four candidates and offended only the one it flattered.
Being lampooned is the surest evidence of having arrived.
The lancet gave the medical journal its name and its founder's reputation for sharpness.
A lancet window is tall, narrow, and pointed like the blade.

landmark.definition: a decisive event or notable feature
sentences: The ruling was a landmark and, for eleven years, entirely unenforced.
The pub is a landmark for everyone except the map, which omits it.
A languid afternoon in August produced nothing except the idea for the whole book.
Her languid delivery made every sentence sound like a favor.

languish.definition: to grow weak or be neglected
sentences: The proposal languished in a drawer for four years and passed in a week.
He languished on the waiting list while healthier people were seen faster.

lapidary.definition: elegantly concise, as if carved in stone
sentences: Her lapidary style fits an argument into a sentence you cannot forget.
Lapidary prose is written for stone, which is why it survives paper.
Petty larceny in the stockroom cost less than the surveillance system installed to stop it.
Grand larceny is petty larceny with a higher price tag on the item.
The larder held four jars of chutney and no explanation for any of them.
A well-stocked larder is the difference between a storm and an inconvenience.
The department survived on the largess of one alumnus and the fear of losing it.
Political largess before an election is called investment and after it, a deficit.
His largesse funded the wing, the chair, and the plaque listing his largesse.
Largesse from the powerful always arrives with an unspoken invoice.
The lascivious remark was reported, denied, and confirmed by the recording.
Lascivious material in the eighteenth century would now barely qualify as flirtation.
A general lassitude settled over the office in the third week of August.
Lassitude after a crisis is the body sending an invoice.
The latent demand appeared the moment the price dropped four percent.
Latent talent stays latent without somebody willing to notice it.

latitude.definition: freedom to act as one chooses
sentences: Junior staff were given latitude on method and none at all on deadline.
The contract allowed latitude that the client had not intended to grant.
The obituaries lauded a career whose difficult middle decade went unmentioned.
He was lauded abroad and audited at home, in the same month.
The aim was laudable and the execution was a catastrophe.
"Laudable effort" in a review means the result was not.
The lavish launch party cost more than the product's first year of revenue.
He was lavish with praise and extremely careful with credit.
Lax security meant the door had been propped open since March.
Lax standards do not fail immediately, which is exactly the problem.
Explaining it to a layperson forced him to discover he did not understand it either.
The jury is twelve laypersons deciding what four experts could not agree on.
The two firms were in league long before the merger was announced.
A league was also three miles, which is why old maps are so confusing.
Investors were leery of a forecast that assumed nothing would ever go wrong.
He was leery of anyone who agreed with him immediately.
Accounting legerdemain moved the loss into a subsidiary nobody consolidated.
Legerdemain is French for "light of hand," which is a generous name for cheating.
The lethargic response to the first warning made the second one inevitable.
A heavy lunch makes a lethargic afternoon, which every scheduler ignores.

levee.definition: an embankment holding back a river
sentences: The levee held for two days and failed at the one point nobody had inspected.
Building the levee higher moved the flooding downstream to a poorer parish.

level.definition: to direct an accusation; to make flat
sentences: Serious charges were leveled at a department that had already been abolished.
The storm leveled the fence and left the greenhouse untouched.
A moment of levity at the funeral was exactly what the family needed.
Levity in a crisis is either leadership or negligence, depending on the timing.

levy.definition: to impose a tax or fine
sentences: The council levied a charge on empty properties and halved the number of them.
Taxes are levied; the resentment is voluntary.
Johnson called lexicography harmless drudgery, which was false modesty and mostly accurate.
Modern lexicography records how words are used, not how they ought to be.

liability.definition: a legal obligation or a disadvantage
sentences: His candor was an asset in research and a liability in negotiation.
The liability was capped at the contract value, which the lawyers noticed and the client did not.
He was liberal with other people's time and careful with his own.
A liberal interpretation of the rules kept everyone employed and nobody safe.
Automating the report liberated four hours a week that immediately filled with meetings.
The town was liberated twice in one month by opposing armies.
The libertine of the memoirs turns out, in the letters, to have been rather lonely.
A libertine in one decade is merely fashionable in the next.
The libretto is silly and the music has carried it for two centuries.
Librettists get one line in the program and none of the applause.
The licentious court was described in detail by chroniclers who clearly enjoyed the research.
Licentious originally meant simply unlicensed, which is a mild beginning for the word.
The first draft was cut by half; the second was likewise treated.
"Likewise" is the standard reply of someone who did not catch what you said.
Her limpid prose explains quantum mechanics without a single equation.
The limpid pool was four feet deeper than it looked, as limpid pools are.

lineament.definition: a distinctive feature, especially of a face
sentences: The lineaments of the old policy are visible in every line of the new one.
The portrait captures his lineaments and none of his manner.
London lionized him for one season and forgot him during the next.
To be lionized is to be admired by people who have not read the work.
The lissome dancer made the difficult sequence look like a decision rather than a feat.
Lissome is lithesome with the middle worn away.
A listless second half emptied the stands before the final whistle.
He was listless for a month and then, without explanation, entirely himself.
The complaint was a litany of small grievances stretching back eleven years.
A litany in church is a prayer; in an argument it is exhausting.

litigation.definition: the process of taking legal action
sentences: Six years of litigation cost more than the disputed contract was ever worth.
The threat of litigation settles more disputes than litigation does.

livelihood.definition: the means of earning a living
sentences: The closure removed the livelihood of half a village in a single announcement.
He turned a hobby into a livelihood and lost the hobby in the process.
She was livid about the leak and icily polite for the entire meeting.
Livid also means bluish-grey, which is the color of a bruise and, apparently, of rage.
He was loath to admit the earlier estimate had been invented.
Loath is reluctant; loathe is to hate. The E does all the work.
She loathed the phrase "circle back" and used it four times that afternoon.
He loathed the work and did it beautifully for thirty years.

lode.definition: a rich source or vein of ore
sentences: The archive proved a lode of material nobody had thought to mine.
The lode ran out in 1904 and the town emptied within a decade.

lofty.definition: elevated in position or ideals; haughty
sentences: The lofty aims of the charter were reduced to a car parking policy by June.
His lofty tone at the meeting cost him the vote he was certain of.
She logged every call, which is why the inquiry took four days instead of four months.
Ships log their speed with an actual log on a rope, which is where the word comes from.
The loquacious taxi driver delivered a complete history of the city in nine minutes.
Loquacious witnesses give away what careful ones protect.
A pair of louts ruined an evening that four hundred other people had enjoyed.
The lout at the back of the bus is a permanent feature of urban life.
His lucid explanation of the tax change was the only useful thing on the news.
She had lucid intervals in which she named every visitor correctly.
The lucrative side business quietly became the main one.
Lucrative work and interesting work occasionally overlap, usually by accident.
His lugubrious delivery made the good news sound like a diagnosis.
The lugubrious hound in the painting is doing most of the emotional work.
In the lull between the two waves, everyone assumed it was over.
The lull in the storm is when experienced sailors do the most work.
The old bus lumbered up the hill at a speed that permitted conversation.
The process lumbers along and arrives, eventually, at the same place.
Four luminaries were invited and one turned up, brilliantly.
Every field has luminaries who publish and workhorses who make the results replicate.
The luminous dial had been painted with radium, which killed the women who painted it.
Her luminous performance made a thin script feel like literature.
The lurid details filled four pages and the correction filled one paragraph.
Lurid was originally a sickly yellow, which the tabloids have improved upon.
The luxuriant garden was the result of total neglect and excellent drainage.
Luxuriant is abundant growth; luxurious is expensive comfort.
The museum's macabre collection is its most visited and least photographed room.
Macabre humor is how emergency workers survive their own week.
They machinated for a year to remove a director who resigned voluntarily anyway.
To machinate is to run a machine of plots, which is exactly how it feels.
The machination required six people to keep one secret, which is five too many.
Every reorganization is explained as strategy and remembered as machination.
The machinations behind the appointment took four months and one leaked email to unravel.
History remembers the machinations and forgets who did the actual work.
The madrigal group met on Tuesdays and disagreed about tempo for thirty years.
Madrigals are polyphonic, which means everyone is singing something slightly different on purpose.

maelstrom.definition: a violent whirlpool or turbulent situation
sentences: He walked into a maelstrom of accusations that had been building for months.
The original Maelstrom is a real current off Norway that terrified real sailors.
The magisterial three-volume history has not been superseded in fifty years.
His magisterial tone worked in the lecture hall and failed completely at home.
Magnanimity in victory costs nothing and buys the next decade.
His magnanimity extended to everyone except the one critic who had been right.

magnanimous.definition: generous and forgiving, especially to rivals
sentences: The magnanimous concession speech was the best thing he ever wrote.
Being magnanimous when you have lost is much harder and much rarer.
The shipping magnate endowed a library and named it after his mother.
Every magnate's biography contains one chapter that the lawyers shortened.

maintain.definition: to assert firmly; to keep in condition
sentences: He maintained his innocence for eleven years and was proved right in the twelfth.
Maintaining the building cost more than building it had.
A majority of one is still a majority, and it governed for four years.
The silent majority is silent partly because nobody has asked it anything.
The makeshift repair lasted nineteen years, which embarrassed the engineers who costed the real one.
A makeshift solution becomes permanent the moment it works twice.
The maladroit apology managed to insult two more people.
Maladroit is French for badly-right-handed, which is unkind on several fronts.
Short-termism is the malady of every organization judged quarterly.
The malady was diagnosed correctly in 1931 and treated correctly in 1954.

malaise.definition: a general feeling of unease or discontent
sentences: A malaise settled over the industry that no single figure explained.
Malaise is what a doctor writes when the patient is unwell and the tests are not.

malapropism.definition: a comic misuse of a similar-sounding word
sentences: "Dance a flamingo" is a malapropism that has entered the family permanently.
Mrs. Malaprop in the play gave her name to a lifetime of accidental comedy.
Management dismissed them as malcontents, and the malcontents turned out to be right.
Every organization labels its early warning system a group of malcontents.
He left the meeting with a malediction that the minutes recorded as "comments."
Malediction is bad-speaking; benediction is good-speaking. Both were once thought to work.
The malevolent rumor was traced to one anonymous account and four willing repeaters.
Most harm is careless rather than malevolent, which is somehow less comforting.
The inquiry found malfeasance at three levels and prosecuted at none.
Malfeasance is doing the wrong thing; nonfeasance is doing nothing at all.
The verdict required proof of malice, which the emails supplied abundantly.
Never attribute to malice what incompetence explains, but do not rule it out either.

malign.definition: to speak evil of; to slander
sentences: He was maligned for a decade and rehabilitated in an appendix.
The much-maligned regulation turned out to have prevented two disasters.

malinger.definition: to fake illness to avoid work
sentences: He was accused of malingering and diagnosed, three weeks later, with something serious.
Malingering is a real problem and a much-abused accusation.

malingerer.definition: one who fakes illness to avoid duty
sentences: The sergeant treated everyone as a malingerer until the third case of pneumonia.
One malingerer costs a team less than a manager who suspects everyone.
Gold is malleable enough to be beaten into a sheet you can see through.
A malleable committee is convenient for exactly as long as you are the one shaping it.
The malodorous fridge united a hostile office in a single afternoon.
Malodorous is what a report says when "stinks" is unavailable.
The debt manacled the company to a supplier it could not afford to leave.
The prisoner was manacled for a hearing about a parking offense.
The unfairness was manifest to everyone except the committee that designed it.
The disagreement became manifest only when the budget arrived.
The strike was a manifestation of a grievance nobody had bothered to record.
Rust is the manifestation; the water got in years ago.
His mannered delivery divided audiences into devotees and deserters.
The mannered prose of the period reads now like everyone was performing.
He manumitted eleven people in his will and none during his life.
The word means "to send from the hand," which is precisely the gesture of release.
A single typo on the cover marred an otherwise flawless edition.
The evening was marred by a speech that had been warned against twice.
Gulls marauded the picnic with a coordination that suggested planning.
Marauding bands took the harvest and left the seed corn, which was strategic.
The improvement was marginal and the press release was not.
Marginal seats decide elections, which is why they get all the new roads.

marginalize.definition: to push to the edges of importance
sentences: The reorganization marginalized a team that had produced most of the revenue.
You can marginalize a person without ever saying a word to them.

martial.definition: relating to war or the military
sentences: Martial law was declared at midnight and lifted, quietly, four years later.
His martial bearing came from twelve years in a band, not an army.
The martinet in charge of scheduling ran the only department that never missed a deadline.
Martinet was a French drillmaster whose name became a complaint.
Gladstone reportedly masticated every mouthful thirty-two times, which cannot have improved conversation.
The machine masticates the waste into a pulp nobody wants to look at.

matriarch.definition: a woman who heads a family or group
sentences: The matriarch settled disputes at Sunday lunch and nowhere else.
Elephant herds are led by a matriarch whose memory of water holes keeps everyone alive.
Two glasses in, he became maudlin about a school he had disliked intensely.
The maudlin final scene undoes an hour of restraint.
The reviewers mauled the first act and praised the second.
The bear did not maul the tent; it removed it entirely.
He maundered through twenty minutes of anecdote before reaching the agenda.
Maundering in a memoir is charming; in a meeting it is theft.
The maverick of the department was right twice and unemployable by the third time.
Samuel Maverick refused to brand his cattle, which is how unbranded people got his name.
The mawkish tribute video made even the honoree wince.
Mawkish once meant nauseating, which explains what too much sentiment does.
"Measure twice, cut once" is a maxim that has saved more wood than skill has.
Every maxim has a contradicting maxim, which is why judgment still exists.
The conversation meandered for an hour and arrived somewhere neither had expected.
Rivers meander because water is lazy in a very precise way.

mediate.definition: to intervene to settle a dispute
sentences: She mediated between two departments that had communicated only by memo for a year.
To mediate you must be trusted by people who trust nobody.
A pleasant melancholy settles over the coast in late September.
Melancholy was once a medical diagnosis involving black bile and no evidence.
The exhibition is a melange of three collections and no discernible argument.
Dinner was a melange of what four households had left in their fridges.
The melee at the gate lasted four minutes and dominated the coverage for a week.
In the melee somebody's shoe was lost and never claimed.
His mellifluous voice made even the safety announcements sound like poetry.
Mellifluous literally means flowing with honey, which is a fair description of a good broadcaster.
The cell membrane decides what enters, which makes it the busiest doorman in biology.
A thin membrane of politeness separated the two factions at dinner.
The mendacious prospectus described a factory that had never been built.
A mendacious witness is easier to handle than a sincerely mistaken one.
The mendacity was not in the numbers but in the sentence introducing them.
Mendacity ages badly, because records outlive memories.

mendicant.definition: a beggar, especially a religious one
sentences: Mendicant orders owned nothing and organized everything.
The mendicant at the cathedral door had been there longer than the current bishop.
His motives were mercenary and his results were excellent, which complicated the moral.
A mercenary interest in the outcome is not the same as a corrupt one, quite.
The mercurial director was adored on set and unemployable between films.
Mercury the god was quick and Mercury the metal will not stay still either.
The meretricious charm of the prospectus survived exactly one site visit.
Meretricious comes from a word for a prostitute, which is harsh on the profession and the prose.
The proposal has merit and no chance, which is a common combination.
Promotion on merit requires somebody willing to define merit before the vacancy.

meritocracy.definition: rule by those judged most able
sentences: The word meritocracy was coined as satire and adopted as a compliment.
Every meritocracy eventually has to explain why the same families keep qualifying.
The medal is for meritorious service, which usually means twenty unglamorous years.
A meritorious argument still loses to a well-connected one.
The plot mesmerized viewers who could not have summarized a minute of it.
Franz Mesmer hypnotized Vienna and left his name behind when the theory collapsed.
The pilot project metamorphosed into a department of ninety within four years.
A caterpillar metamorphoses by dissolving almost entirely, which is a lot to ask of anyone.
The building's metamorphosis from mill to museum took nine years and three architects.
Kafka's Metamorphosis begins with the transformation and spends the rest on the family.
He said the department was on fire in the metaphorical sense, twice, before anyone checked.
Most everyday language is metaphorical and has forgotten that it is.

metaphysical.definition: concerning abstract reality beyond the physical
sentences: The dispute turned metaphysical, which meant no experiment could settle it.
The metaphysical poets compared love to compasses and got away with it.
Her meteoric rise took eleven years, which nobody mentions in the profile.
Meteoric ought to imply falling and burning up, which the metaphor cheerfully ignores.
Meticulous record-keeping saved the department when the inquiry finally arrived.
He was meticulous about the footnotes and vague about the argument.
The third day tested everyone's mettle and revealed two natural leaders.
Mettle and metal were once the same word, which the metaphor still remembers.
The mettlesome young lawyer took the case nobody senior would touch.
A mettlesome horse is admired by everyone except the person riding it.

microcosm.definition: a small world representing a larger one
sentences: The village was a microcosm of the country's argument about itself.
A departmental meeting is a microcosm of every political system ever devised.
His grave mien at the door told them the news before he spoke.
She kept a cheerful mien through a week that deserved none.
Transplanted from his milieu, the charm stopped working entirely.
The novel captures a literary milieu that lasted about four years.

militate.definition: to work against or in favor of something
sentences: Everything about the timetable militated against actually finishing the work.
Militate against is to argue against; mitigate is to soften. They are not the same verb.

milk.definition: to exploit for all it is worth
sentences: He milked the anecdote for three minutes past its natural life.
The franchise was milked until audiences finally stopped turning up.
The harmless snake mimics a venomous one and is left alone by everything.
He mimicked the accent so well that nobody noticed until he laughed.
His mincing delivery made a plain instruction sound like an insult.
She used no mincing words and none were needed.
The minute differences between the samples turned out to be the whole finding.
He gave a minute account of a journey that had taken twelve minutes.
The project was mired in approvals for so long that the technology changed.
Mired in detail, the committee lost sight of what it had been asked.
The typo caused general mirth and one very quiet resignation.
There was no mirth in the room, only the sound of people waiting.
The misanthrope volunteered at the animal shelter and got on famously.
A misanthrope in a small village is a tourist attraction.
His misanthropic column ran for twenty years and was widely loved.
Misanthropic on Monday and cheerful by Thursday is just a normal week.

misappropriate.definition: to take dishonestly for one's own use
sentences: Funds were misappropriated over eleven years in amounts too small to flag.
He misappropriated the phrase and the credit in a single paragraph.
A single sentence was misconstrued and cost two weeks of clarification.
Do not misconstrue silence as agreement; it is usually exhaustion.
The miscreants were identified from a photograph and a very distinctive coat.
Miscreant once meant unbeliever, and drifted into general wrongdoing.

miser.definition: one who hoards money and hates spending
sentences: The miser left three million pounds and a house with no working heating.
Miser shares a root with miserable, which is an ancient piece of moralizing.
The miserly budget for the project produced miserly results, to universal surprise.
He was miserly with praise and lavish with corrections.
"Rush hour" is a misnomer for something that lasts three hours and involves no rushing.
Calling it a working group was a misnomer on both counts.

misogynist.definition: one who hates or despises women
sentences: The misogynist's memoir accidentally documented his own career decline.
Misogynist is from Greek roots meaning hatred of women, and the word carries no ambiguity.

missive.definition: a letter, especially a formal one
sentences: A four-page missive from head office announced a policy in one sentence.
The missive arrived by courier, which told everyone how serious it was.

mite.definition: a very small amount or creature
sentences: He was a mite optimistic about the timeline, by roughly a year.
The widow's mite was tiny and, the parable insists, the largest gift given.
Planting the embankment mitigated the flooding without preventing it.
Mitigate softens a bad thing; militate argues against one.

mode.definition: a way or manner of doing something
sentences: The department switched into crisis mode, which mainly meant longer meetings.
Mode of transport, mode of address, mode in statistics — one word, three careers.
A modest proposal, in Swift's hands, was neither.
The modest raise was accompanied by an immodest description of it.
A modicum of preparation would have prevented the entire disaster.
He asked for a modicum of respect and received the minimum viable amount.
The modish jargon of the report dates it precisely to 2014.
Modish theories arrive with conferences and leave without obituaries.
Nothing mollified the residents except an actual apology, which took two years.
He tried to mollify her with flowers and made an excellent situation worse.

molt.definition: to shed feathers, skin, or shell
sentences: The crab molts its shell and hides for a week while the new one hardens.
The company molted three names in five years and kept the same problems.
A decision of great moment was taken by four people on a Friday afternoon.
The moment passed and nobody moved to reclaim it.
A momentary lapse in attention put the wrong figure into the final table.
The relief was momentary and the paperwork was not.
He kept a monastic routine: one desk, one meal, no telephone.
The monastic silence of the reading room ended when the café opened downstairs.
Monetary policy moved slowly and the prices did not.
The monetary cost was manageable; the reputational one was not.
The monotonous drone of the presentation put three people visibly to sleep.
Monotonous work is bearable with company and unbearable alone.
The monotony of the coastline was broken once, by a lighthouse and a sheep.
Monotony is what makes a five-hour flight longer than a five-hour hike.
The question became moot when the building was sold in March.
Whether it was moot or crucial depended entirely on which side you were on.
The contract dragged them into a morass of subclauses and cross-references.
A morass is a swamp, and the metaphor keeps every bit of the mud.
A moratorium on new hires lasted eleven months and cost two departments their best candidates.
The moratorium on drilling expired quietly on a bank holiday.

morbid.definition: unhealthily preoccupied with death or gloom
sentences: He took a morbid interest in the accident statistics of his own commute.
Morbid curiosity is why the crash makes the front page and the recovery does not.
Her mordant wit made the obituary the most-read piece of the year.
Mordant comes from biting, which is exactly how the humor lands.
The plan was late; moreover, it was based on figures from a previous decade.
"Moreover" in a letter usually signals the paragraph that actually matters.

mores.definition: the accepted customs of a community
sentences: The mores of the office were never written down and were enforced ruthlessly.
Changing laws is easier than changing mores, which is why one lags the other.
The moribund industry was revived by a technology it had spent a decade dismissing.
A moribund committee still meets; that is how you tell it is moribund and not dead.
He grew morose after the verdict and cheerful the day the appeal was filed.
The morose waiter delivered excellent food with visible regret.

morph.definition: to change gradually into something else
sentences: The support group morphed into a lobbying organization over four years.
The complaint morphed, with each retelling, into a much better story.
It mortified him to be corrected by someone he had taught.
Mortify literally means to make dead, which is roughly how embarrassment feels.
Motes of dust hung in the projector beam like a small weather system.
The parable warns about the mote in your brother's eye and the beam in your own.

mountebank.definition: a charlatan who sells false remedies
sentences: The mountebank sold a tonic containing sugar, alcohol, and confident phrasing.
Mountebanks mounted a bench to draw a crowd, which is where the word comes from.

mulct.definition: to fine or swindle out of money
sentences: Investors were mulcted of their savings by a fund with excellent stationery.
The court mulcted him a sum that was, for him, a rounding error.
The problem is multifaceted, which is the polite way to say nobody knows where to start.
A multifaceted career sounds better in a eulogy than it feels at the time.
His multifarious interests filled a house and emptied a bank account.
The multifarious duties of the role were listed on four pages and performed by one person.
A multitude of small errors produced one large and entirely predictable failure.
Charity, says the proverb, covers a multitude of sins.
The mundane detail of the timetable turned out to be the key to the whole case.
Mundane means "of the world," which is either an insult or a description.
A munificent bequest funded the wing and a decade of arguments about its name.
Munificent giving in public is sometimes matched by private meanness.
He mused aloud about resigning and was taken seriously by the wrong person.
She mused for a week and acted in a morning.
She mustered enough support to force a vote and lost it by two.
He could not muster the enthusiasm to finish a sentence about it.

muted.definition: subdued in sound, color, or reaction
sentences: The muted response to the announcement was itself the story.
A muted palette makes a small room feel considerably larger.
The mutiny began over food and ended with a change of management.
Most mutinies are about conditions; the flags come later.
The myopic focus on this quarter cost the company the next decade.
Myopic is literally nearsighted, which is exactly the metaphor intended.
The myriad small kindnesses of that week are what she actually remembers.
Myriad was originally exactly ten thousand, which is disappointingly specific.
The nadir came in March, when even the optimists stopped forecasting.
Nadir is the point directly beneath you; zenith is directly above.
It was naive to assume the deadline meant the same thing to both parties.
Naive questions from a newcomer are the most valuable thing in any meeting.
The narcissist described the disaster mostly in terms of how it had affected him.
Narcissus fell in love with a reflection and gave psychology a permanent word.
The nascent industry had four companies and one very optimistic trade association.
A nascent friendship survives disagreement better than an established one sometimes does.
A natty bow tie made him identifiable in every photograph for forty years.
He arrived natty and left, after the storm, considerably less so.
The strategy was nebulous enough that every department read it as approval.
A nebulous complaint is impossible to answer and impossible to dismiss.
The nefarious scheme required nine accomplices and collapsed under its own logistics.
Nefarious purposes are usually simpler and duller than the word suggests.
One line in the appendix negated the entire conclusion.
The gains were negated by an exchange rate nobody had modeled.
The garden flourished under benign neglect and died under enthusiastic attention.
Neglect ruins buildings more thoroughly and more cheaply than vandalism.
